answer:
Moïse (*Moshé Rabbénou*) est l'une des figures les plus commentées de la tradition juive. Les outils de consultation de Sefaria ne répondent pas pour le moment, donc je n'ai pas pu relire les textes. Je ne cite donc aucun passage mot à mot. Je donne des références générales, à vérifier dans les sources.

## Réponse directe
Moïse est traité dans la Torah elle-même, puis dans le Talmud et les midrashim, chez les philosophes (Maïmonide), chez les commentateurs (Rashi, Ramban, Ibn Ezra) et dans la kabbale et le hassidisme (Zohar, Arizal, Tanya). Chaque couche en donne une image différente : le prophète sans égal, le maître d'Israël, puis une réalité spirituelle qui se prolonge dans chaque génération.

## Points clés
- La Torah le présente comme le plus humble des hommes et comme un prophète unique : [Numbers 12:3-8], [Deuteronomy 34:10].
- Maïmonide fait de la prophétie de Moïse, supérieure à toute autre, un des treize principes de foi.
- Les midrashim développent sa vie : son enfance, son rôle de berger, sa mort par un baiser divin.
- Le Zohar l'appelle *Raya Mehemna* (« le berger fidèle »). Le Tanya et le hassidisme y voient une dimension de « Moïse » présente en chaque génération.

## 1. Le texte de la Torah (*pshat*)
Moïse apparaît de l'Exode au Deutéronome. La Torah dit de lui qu'il est « très humble, plus que tout homme » ([Numbers 12:3]). Elle dit aussi que D.ieu lui parle « bouche à bouche », différemment des autres prophètes ([Numbers 12:6-8]). Elle conclut qu'il ne s'est plus levé en Israël de prophète comme lui ([Deuteronomy 34:10]).

## 2. Le Talmud et les midrashim
- Les sages commentent sa naissance, son sauvetage, son départ d'Égypte et sa mort. Voir Exodus Rabbah et Deuteronomy Rabbah, ainsi que Sota 12a-13b pour sa naissance et sa mort.
- Le Talmud (Menahot 29b) raconte qu'il assiste, sans la comprendre, à l'enseignement de Rabbi Akiva. Je cite cette référence de mémoire, à vérifier.
- Pirké Avot 1:1 ouvre la chaîne de transmission par « Moïse reçut la Torah du Sinaï ».

## 3. Les commentateurs et les philosophes
- **Rashi, Ramban, Ibn Ezra** : ils commentent ses actes, ses paroles et sa faute à Mériba (Nombres 20), chacun avec sa lecture. Je n'ai pas pu relire leurs commentaires pour vous dire précisément ce que chacun avance.
- **Maïmonide** : dans le *Michné Torah* (Yesodei HaTorah, ch. 7) et dans son commentaire sur la Michna (Sanhédrin, ch. 10, les principes de foi), il affirme que la prophétie de Moïse est d'un autre ordre que celle de tous les autres prophètes. Il en déduit que la Torah est immuable.

## 4. Kabbale et hassidisme
Les approches diffèrent selon les écoles. Je les résume ici de mémoire.
- **Zohar** : Moïse est le *Raya Mehemna* (« berger fidèle »). Il apparaît comme le dialogue entre le Zohar et Rabbi Shimon bar Yohaï.
- **Arizal** : il relie Moïse à la *séfira* de *Da'at* (la connaissance) et à une racine d'âme qui englobe Israël.
- **Tanya** : Moïse est le « berger » d'Israël, et chaque génération a une étincelle de son âme, un « Moïse » de la génération. Je cite cette idée de mémoire, sans numéro de chapitre.

## Pour avancer
Dites-moi quel aspect vous intéresse : sa prophétie, son humilité, sa mort ou sa dimension kabbalistique. Je relirai alors les sources exactes dès que l'accès sera rétabli.

answer:
**תשובה ישירה:** רש״י על "בראשית ברא" מביא שני פירושים. הראשון הוא דרש חז״ל: העולם נברא בשביל התורה ובשביל ישראל, שנקראו "ראשית". השני הוא הפשט: המילה "בראשית" היא סמוכה, והפסוק פירושו "בתחילת ברוא אלהים". לפי זה הפסוק אינו בא ללמד שהשמים והארץ נבראו ראשונים. [Rashi on Genesis 1:1]

## נקודות עיקריות
- רש״י פותח בדברי רבי יצחק: מדוע פתחה התורה בבריאה ולא ב"החדש הזה לכם", שהיא המצווה הראשונה?
- התשובה היא "כֹּחַ מַעֲשָׂיו הִגִּיד לְעַמּוֹ לָתֵת לָהֶם נַחֲלַת גּוֹיִם". אם יאמרו האומות "לסטים אתם", ישראל משיבים שהארץ כולה של הקב״ה והוא נתנה למי שרצה.
- "אין המקרא הזה אומר אלא דרשני": חז״ל דרשו "ראשית" על התורה ("ראשית דרכו", משלי ח) ועל ישראל ("ראשית תבואתו", ירמיה ב).
- לפי הפשט, "בראשית" סמוך למה שאחריו, כמו "בראשית ממלכת יהויקים". לכן הפסוק פירושו "בתחילת ברוא".
- "אלהים" ולא "ה׳": בתחילה עלה במחשבה לברוא במידת הדין, ואחר כך שיתף את מידת הרחמים.

## הפירוש לפי סדר הדברים

### 1. מדוע מתחילה התורה בבראשית
רבי יצחק אומר שהתורה הייתה צריכה להתחיל ב"הַחֹדֶשׁ הַזֶּה לָכֶם" [Exodus 12:2], כי זו המצווה הראשונה שנצטוו בה ישראל. התשובה מבוססת על תהילים קיא, ו. סיפור הבריאה בא להקדים את הטענה שהארץ שייכת לבורא. הוא יכול לתת אותה ולקחת אותה כרצונו. זו תשובה לטענת האומות על כיבוש ארץ שבעת העממים.

### 2. דרש: "בשביל התורה ובשביל ישראל"
רש״י כותב ש"בראשית" רומז ל"ראשית". התורה נקראת "ראשית דרכו" [Proverbs 8:22], וישראל נקראים "ראשית תבואתו" [Jeremiah 2:3]. זהו הפירוש הדרשני, ורש״י מציג אותו לפני הפשט.

### 3. הפשט: בראשית כסמיכות
- רש״י טוען שאם התורה באה ללמד שהשמים והארץ נבראו ראשונים, היה צריך לכתוב "בראשונה ברא".
- בכל המקרא "ראשית" דבוק למילה שאחריו. הוא מביא דוגמאות: "בראשית ממלכת יהויקים", "ראשית ממלכתו", "ראשית דגנך".
- לכן הפסוק נקרא "בראשית ברוא אלהים". רש״י מביא דמיון ל"תחלת דבר ה׳ בהושע".
- הפירוש הוא: בתחילת בריאת שמים וארץ, כשהארץ הייתה תהו ובהו וחושך, אמר אלהים "יהי אור".

### 4. מענה למי שטוען "בראשית הכול ברא"
רש״י דוחה גם את הטענה שיש כאן חסרון מילה, כמו "כי לא סגר דלתי בטני" או "ישא את חיל דמשק". הוא מביא שתי ראיות:
- המים קדמו לארץ, שהרי כתוב "ורוח אלהים מרחפת על פני המים", והמקרא לא גילה מתי נבראו המים.
- השמים נבראו מאש ומים.

מכאן הוא מסיק שהמקרא אינו בא ללמד סדר של מוקדם ומאוחר.

### 5. "ברא אלהים" ולא "ברא ה׳"
רש״י מסביר ששם "אלהים" הוא מידת הדין. בתחילה עלה במחשבה לברוא בדין, ואחר כך ראה שהעולם אינו מתקיים. לכן הקדים מידת רחמים ושיתף אותה במידת הדין. הוא מביא ראיה מהפסוק "בְּיוֹם עֲשׂוֹת ה׳ אֱלֹהִים אֶרֶץ וְשָׁמָיִם" [Genesis 2:4].

הטקסט שקיבלתי נקטע באמצע הדיון על המים. את סוף הדברים כתבתי לפי הקטע שכן הגיע אליי, וכדאי לבדוק אותו בפנים. אפשר להמשיך לדברי רש״י על פסוק ב.

answer:
Nach der traditionellen jüdischen Chronologie (Seder Olam) wurde Noach im Jahr 1056 nach der Erschaffung der Welt geboren und Mosche im Jahr 2368. Zwischen den beiden Geburten liegen also **1312 Jahre**. Von der Sintflut bis zu Moscheś Geburt vergingen 712 Jahre. Noach starb 362 Jahre vor Moscheś Geburt.

## Key Takeaways
- Noachs Geburt bis Moscheś Geburt: etwa 1312 Jahre.
- Sintflut (Jahr 1656) bis Moscheś Geburt: 712 Jahre.
- Noachs Tod (Jahr 2006) bis Moscheś Geburt: 362 Jahre.
- Noach und Mosche haben sich nie getroffen. Noach lebte aber noch bis ins 58. Lebensjahr Avrahams.
- Die Zahlen beruhen auf den Altersangaben der Tora und der traditionellen Zählung. Moderne Datierungen weichen davon ab.

## Die Rechnung
Die Berechnung stammt von mir. Sie addiert die Altersangaben der Tora, und die Verse habe ich hier nicht einzeln nachgeschlagen.

**Von Adam bis Noach** ([Genesis 5]): Die Zeugungsalter der Generationen ergeben für Noachs Geburt das Jahr 1056.
- Adam zeugte Schet mit 130 Jahren.
- Schet zeugte Enosch mit 105.
- Enosch zeugte Kenan mit 90.
- Kenan zeugte Mahalalel mit 70.
- Mahalalel zeugte Jered mit 65.
- Jered zeugte Chanoch mit 162.
- Chanoch zeugte Metuschelach mit 65.
- Metuschelach zeugte Lemech mit 187.
- Lemech zeugte Noach mit 182.

**Noachs Daten:**
- Die Sintflut kam, als Noach 600 Jahre alt war ([Genesis 7:6]). Das war im Jahr 1656.
- Noach lebte insgesamt 950 Jahre ([Genesis 9:29]). Er starb also im Jahr 2006.

**Von Noach bis Mosche:**
- Der Auszug aus Ägypten geschah im Jahr 2448. Die Zahl ergibt sich aus den Generationen von Schem bis Avraham ([Genesis 11]), aus den Lebensjahren der Erzväter und aus den 430 Jahren in [Exodus 12:40-41].
- Mosche war beim Auftritt vor Pharao 80 Jahre alt ([Exodus 7:7]). Er wurde also im Jahr 2368 geboren.

Daraus folgt:
- 2368 − 1056 = 1312 Jahre von Geburt zu Geburt.
- 2368 − 1656 = 712 Jahre von der Sintflut an.
- 2368 − 2006 = 362 Jahre seit Noachs Tod.

## Hinweis
Die Zählung von 1312 Jahren ist die klassische rabbinische Rechnung. Sie geht davon aus, dass die Genealogien lückenlos sind. Manche Kommentatoren und moderne Gelehrte rechnen anders. Wenn du möchtest, kann ich die Quellen zu Seder Olam und zur Frage der 430 Jahre genauer heraussuchen.

answer:
Deuteronomy 6:4 es el *Shemá*, la declaración central de la fe judía: el Dios de Israel, que es el Eterno, es uno. Según Rashi, el versículo dice además que hoy el Eterno es nuestro Dios, y que en el futuro será reconocido como Uno por toda la humanidad.

(Nota: el servidor de Sefaria me limitó el acceso. Pude leer a Rashi, pero no el versículo ni a otros comentaristas, así que cito el versículo de memoria y no cito más comentaristas.)

## Key Takeaways
- El versículo afirma la unicidad de Dios y es la base de la aceptación del yugo del Cielo.
- Rashi lo lee en clave de redención: hoy Dios es "nuestro" Dios, y en el futuro será Uno para todos.
- Una lectura alternativa y común lo toma como afirmación de unicidad absoluta: no hay otro poder ni otra divinidad.
- Se recita cada mañana y cada noche, y al final de la vida.

## El texto

שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ ה׳ אֶחָד
*Shemá Yisrael, Adonai Elohenu, Adonai Ejad.*
"Escucha, Israel: el Eterno es nuestro Dios, el Eterno es Uno."

## Pshat (sentido simple)
- **"Shemá"** viene de la raíz ש-מ-ע. Significa "oír", pero también "comprender" y "aceptar". Moisés llama a Israel a escuchar con atención y a asumir lo que sigue.
- **"Adonai Elohenu"**: el Eterno es *nuestro* Dios. Hay una relación de pacto.
- **"Adonai Ejad"**: *ejad* significa "uno". Puede entenderse como "único" (no hay otro) y como "Uno" en el sentido de unidad indivisible.

Esta sintaxis, con cuatro palabras divinas seguidas, permite varias lecturas gramaticales. Una de ellas es "el Eterno, nuestro Dios, el Eterno es Uno".

## Rashi
Rashi lo explica así en [Rashi on Deuteronomy 6:4]:

"ה' שֶׁהוּא אֱלֹהֵינוּ עַתָּה, וְלֹא אֱלֹהֵי הָאֻמּוֹת, הוּא עָתִיד לִהְיוֹת ה' אֶחָד"

En traducción: el Eterno, que ahora es nuestro Dios y no el Dios de las naciones, será en el futuro "el Eterno Uno".

Como prueba cita dos profetas:
- [Zephaniah 3:9]: "Entonces daré a los pueblos un lenguaje puro, para que todos invoquen el nombre del Eterno".
- [Zechariah 14:9]: "Ese día el Eterno será Uno y Su nombre Uno".

Rashi indica también la fuente en el Sifrei. Lo que lo lleva a esta lectura es que "Uno" ya es verdad ahora, así que el versículo parece decir algo más. Para Rashi, la unidad de Dios todavía no es reconocida por todos, y el versículo apunta a ese reconocimiento universal.

## Contexto y uso
El versículo abre la sección que sigue: "Amarás al Eterno tu Dios con todo tu corazón…" ([Deuteronomy 6:5]). Primero viene la afirmación de quién es Dios, y después el mandamiento de amarlo. Por eso el *Shemá* se recita dos veces al día, en la mañana y en la noche. Esa recitación se entiende como aceptación del yugo del Cielo (*kabalat ol maljut shamayim*).

Si quieres, puedo ver en otro momento a Rambam, Ibn Ezra o Ramban sobre este versículo, o la frase "Baruj shem kevod maljuto", que se dice después de él.

Проверить это в Sefaria сейчас не удалось: сервис вернул ошибку 429 (слишком много запросов). Поэтому я отвечаю по памяти и не уверен в деталях.

**Что я помню.** Название «Нахалат Яаков» (*Nachalat Ya'akov*) носят несколько разных книг. Одна из них, насколько я помню, принадлежит раву Яакову Наумбургу. Это суперкомментарий к комментарию Раши на Тору, то есть разбор того, как Раши выводит свои объяснения из текста и из источников. Годы жизни автора и место издания я назвать надёжно не могу. Не хочу выдумывать подробности, которых не проверил.

**Об авторитетности.** Здесь нужно различать два вопроса.
- **Комментарий на Раши.** Такие работы служат пособием для изучения. В них нет галахических постановлений, поэтому «авторитетность» в смысле *психа* (галахического решения) к ним неприменима. Их ценность в качестве разбора, и сильные ли в них объяснения, видно из самого текста.
- **Галахическое решение.** Если вы встретили ссылку на «Нахалат Яаков» в вопросе практической галахи, это, скорее всего, другая книга с таким же названием. Проверьте, кто автор и о каком сочинении идёт речь. Я не знаю такого «Нахалат Яаков», который считался бы основным источником для *посеким* (галахических авторитетов).

**Как проверить.**
1. Посмотрите титульный лист или каталог издания: автор, место и год издания, жанр.
2. Поищите в каталоге Национальной библиотеки Израиля, в HebrewBooks или в Sefaria по названию вместе с именем автора.
3. Если это ссылка из конкретной статьи или книги, пришлите мне цитату. Когда сервис снова заработает, я найду её и посмотрю, что там написано.

Если вам нужна галаха по конкретному вопросу, лучше опираться на «Шулхан арух» и его признанных комментаторов. Для личной ситуации обратитесь к своему раввину.

Elle évoque prudemment le midrash de « l'enfant fuyant l'école », attribué avec réserve et à juste titre au Ramban et aux Tossafot, et propose une synthèse conciliant les deux lectures. answer:
Retry the commentaries.Je suppose que vous parlez du départ du Sinaï en [Nombres 10:33]. Selon Rashi, qui cite le Sifré, l'empressement vient de D.ieu : Il voulait faire entrer Israël dans le pays sans délai. Un autre midrash, plus sévère, y voit une fuite du Sinaï. Je n'ai pas pu vérifier ce second texte ici.

## Points essentiels
- Le verset dit que le peuple « partit de la montagne de l'Éternel » pour trois jours de marche, avec l'Arche devant lui.
- Rashi explique que les trois jours de route furent parcourus en un seul jour, par miracle.
- Selon lui, la raison est que D.ieu voulait introduire Israël dans la Terre tout de suite.
- Une lecture critique, présente dans la tradition, voit dans ce départ précipité un défaut. Je ne l'ai pas vérifiée dans le texte, donc je ne la cite pas précisément.

## Le texte
« וַיִּסְעוּ מֵהַר יְהֹוָה דֶּרֶךְ שְׁלֹשֶׁת יָמִים וַאֲרוֹן בְּרִית־יְהֹוָה נֹסֵעַ לִפְנֵיהֶם דֶּרֶךְ שְׁלֹשֶׁת יָמִים לָתוּר לָהֶם מְנוּחָה »

« Ils partirent de la montagne de l'Éternel, à trois jours de marche. L'Arche de l'alliance de l'Éternel allait devant eux, ces trois jours de marche, pour chercher un lieu de repos pour eux. » [Numbers 10:33]

## Rashi : une hâte positive
Rashi commente ainsi : « מַהֲלַךְ שְׁלֹשֶׁת יָמִים הָלְכוּ בְיוֹם אֶחָד, שֶׁהָיָה הַקָּבָּ"ה חָפֵץ לְהַכְנִיסָם לָאָרֶץ מִיָּד ». En français : « Ils firent en un jour un trajet de trois jours, car le Saint béni soit-Il voulait les faire entrer immédiatement dans le pays. » [Rashi on Numbers 10:33]

Rashi précise aussi que l'Arche, celle qui accompagnait l'armée en guerre et contenait les débris des premières Tables, les devançait de trois jours. Elle devait leur préparer un lieu de campement.

Dans cette lecture, la hâte n'est pas un caprice du peuple. Elle exprime l'élan de D.ieu vers l'accomplissement de la promesse.

## L'autre lecture
Le contexte laisse voir une difficulté. Aussitôt après ce départ, le peuple se plaint (Nombres 11), et l'épisode des explorateurs suit peu après. Certains commentateurs en ont conclu que le départ n'était pas aussi serein qu'il en a l'air. Une image célèbre compare le peuple à un enfant qui s'enfuit de l'école. Je n'ai pas pu consulter le Ramban ni les Tosafot, où je crois la trouver. Vérifiez cette attribution avant de la citer.

## Ma synthèse
Les deux lectures ne s'excluent pas forcément. D.ieu voulait la hâte, mais la manière dont le peuple a réagi à ce départ a pu être critiquée. Cette synthèse est la mienne, pas celle d'un commentateur.

Si vous le souhaitez, je peux reprendre le Ramban et les Tosafot dès que la bibliothèque Sefaria répondra de nouveau.

answer:
Seu raciocínio tem um ponto forte, mas não é conclusivo. A Torah de fato proíbe consultar os mortos, e a proibição pressupõe que alguma coisa estava sendo feita. Isso não prova que os mortos realmente respondem. A tradição judaica discute se havia resultado real, e as respostas variam.

## Pontos principais

- A Torah proíbe a prática em [Deuteronomy 18:11], que menciona o *doresh el hametim* (quem consulta os mortos) e o *shoel ov* (quem consulta um espírito).
- A lógica "só se proíbe o que existe" falha, porque a Torah também proíbe o que é ilusório. Ela proíbe a idolatria, e os ídolos "não veem nem ouvem" [Deuteronomy 4:28].
- Há autoridades que entendem que existe algum fenômeno real e outras que entendem que é fraude ou ilusão.
- Sua ideia de que a Torah queria que Israel fosse diferente tem apoio. O contexto de [Deuteronomy 18:9] manda não imitar as "abominações daquelas nações".
- Mesmo quem admite que há um fenômeno real proíbe a prática.

## Desenvolvimento

**1. Proibir não prova existência.** A proibição prova que a prática existia como costume. Não prova que ela funcionasse. A Torah proíbe também a adivinhação e a feitiçaria, e vários sábios as tratavam como engano. Maimônides, por exemplo, em *Mishneh Torah*, Idolatria (cap. 11), trata essas práticas como falsidade e vaidade. Cito de memória e não consegui conferir agora o texto exato, então vale verificá-lo.

**2. A outra posição: algo real acontece.** O episódio do rei Saul e da necromante de Endor [I Samuel 28] mostra Samuel "aparecendo". Os sábios discutem o que aconteceu ali. Alguns o entendem como evento real, e outros, como algo limitado ou controlado por Deus. Não consegui consultar o texto agora, então não afirmo detalhes do que cada comentarista diz. Mesmo nessa leitura, a Torah proíbe a prática, porque ela afasta a pessoa de Deus e da Torah como fonte de orientação.

**3. A razão da proibição.** Seu argumento histórico faz sentido, e o próprio contexto bíblico o sustenta. Os comentaristas acrescentam uma razão teológica. A orientação de Israel deve vir de Deus, por meio da Torah e dos profetas, e não dos mortos. Veja o versículo seguinte, [Deuteronomy 18:15], que fala do profeta.

Resumindo: seu argumento mostra que a prática existia, mas não que funcionava. O fato de ser real ou ilusório é debatido, e a proibição vale nos dois casos.

Para uma decisão prática ou pessoal, consulte seu rabino.

answer:
**תשובה קצרה:** בפשט הפסוקים לא כתוב ששלמה "הבין את שפת החיות". כתוב שהוא "דיבר" עליהן, כלומר חיבר דברי חכמה על עולם הטבע. המסורת שהבין את שפתן של חיות ועופות היא מדרשית ומאוחרת יותר. הכלי לחיפוש במאגר ספריא נכשל כעת, ולכן לא בדקתי את המקורות מחדש. הציטוט למטה הוא מהזיכרון, ושמות המדרשים מובאים בלי מראי מקום מדויקים.

## עיקרי הדברים
- הפסוק ב[I Kings 5:13] מעיד על חכמתו של שלמה בעצים, בבהמה, בעוף, ברמש ובדגים.
- הפסוק אינו אומר ששלמה שוחח עם בעלי חיים.
- במדרש ובתרגום שני למגילת אסתר מופיעה המסורת שהבין את שפת העופות, והיא קשורה בעיקר לסיפור התרנגול והחוחית (הדהד).
- מדובר באגדה ולא בפשט, ואין בה הלכה או חובת אמונה.

## הפשט
בספר מלכים א, פרק ה, מתוארת חכמת שלמה. כך אני זוכר את הפסוק: "וַיְדַבֵּר עַל הָעֵצִים מִן הָאֶרֶז אֲשֶׁר בַּלְּבָנוֹן וְעַד הָאֵזוֹב אֲשֶׁר יֹצֵא בַּקִּיר, וַיְדַבֵּר עַל הַבְּהֵמָה וְעַל הָעוֹף וְעַל הָרֶמֶשׂ וְעַל הַדָּגִים" [I Kings 5:13].

המילה "וַיְדַבֵּר עַל" פירושה בדרך כלל שהוא דיבר או לימד **על** הנושא. הפרשנים הקלאסיים מבינים שהוא חיבר משלים ותיאורי טבע, ולכן הוא ידע את תכונותיהם של הצמחים ושל בעלי החיים. את הפירוש הזה לא בדקתי כאן מול הפרשנים עצמם. אם תרצה, אבדוק את רש"י, רד"ק ורלב"ג על הפסוק כשהכלי יחזור לעבוד.

## המדרש
- **תרגום שני למגילת אסתר** מתאר את שלמה יושב על כיסאו כשכל בעלי החיים והעופות באים לפניו. הדהד (החוחית) הוא הדמות הבולטת בסיפור. המדרש קושר זאת למלכת שבא ולחידותיה.
- **מדרשים ופרשנים** מזכירים את הבנת שפת העופות כאחד מגילויי חכמתו. הידוע שבהם הוא הסיפור על הדהד ועל המכתב לשבא.
- בספרות חז"ל מופיעה גם הרעיה שלשלמה שלט על שדים, חיות ורוחות. אלה מסורות אגדיות, ואין להן אחיזה מפורשת בפסוקים.

## הערה
הרמב"ם ופרשנים רציונליים נוטים להבין אגדות כאלה כמשל או כביטוי להבנה עמוקה בטבע. אחרים מקבלים אותן כפשוטן. איני רוצה לייחס לאף אחד מהם דברים מדויקים בלי לבדוק בטקסט.

אם תרצה, אחזור לחפש את המקורות המדויקים: התרגום השני לאסתר, פירושי רש"י ורד"ק על מלכים, ומדרש קהלת או מדרש משלי. ספר לי גם אם שאלתך היא על הפסוק, על המדרש או על משמעות הדבר.

answer:
Die Zehn Gebote stehen zweimal in der Tora: in [Exodus 20:2-14] (Parascha *Jitro*) und in [Deuteronomy 5:6-18] (Parascha *Waetchanan*). Eine Seitenzahl kann ich nicht nennen, weil sie von der Ausgabe abhängt. Kapitel und Vers sind aber überall gleich.

## Key Takeaways
- Die erste Fassung steht in Exodus (2. Buch Mose) 20, Verse 2–14.
- Die zweite Fassung steht in Deuteronomium (5. Buch Mose) 5, Verse 6–18.
- Die Verszählung ist jüdisch. In christlichen Bibeln zählt man Exodus 20,1–17 und Deuteronomium 5,6–21.
- Auf Hebräisch heißen sie *Aseret ha-Dibrot* (die „zehn Aussprüche“).

## Details

**Exodus 20 (Parascha Jitro)**
- Der Text beschreibt die Offenbarung am Berg Sinai.
- Vers 1 leitet ein: „Und Gott sprach alle diese Worte“.
- Das erste Gebot beginnt in Vers 2 mit „Ich bin der Ewige, dein Gott …“.
- Das letzte Gebot (nicht begehren) steht in Vers 14.

**Deuteronomium 5 (Parascha Waetchanan)**
- Hier wiederholt Mose die Gebote am Ende der 40 Jahre in der Wüste.
- Es gibt kleine Unterschiede im Wortlaut. Beim Schabbat heißt es in Exodus *sachor* („gedenke“), in Deuteronomium *schamor* („bewahre“). Auch die Begründung des Schabbatgebots unterscheidet sich.

**Zur Seitenzahl**
- In einem *Chumasch* (gedruckte Tora mit Kommentar) schlagen Sie am besten die Parascha Jitro auf. Dort finden Sie die Gebote etwa in der Mitte der Parascha.
- Auf Sefaria können Sie direkt nach „Exodus 20“ suchen.

Falls Sie möchten, kann ich Ihnen die zehn Gebote einzeln auf Hebräisch mit Übersetzung zeigen oder erklären, wie sie gezählt werden. Die Zählung unterscheidet sich zwischen Judentum und Christentum.

answer:
Sefaria no me respondió (error 429, demasiadas solicitudes), así que no pude traer el texto de la biblioteca. Escribo el Salmo 137 de memoria, en hebreo con mi propia traducción al español. Conviene que lo compares con [Psalms 137] en Sefaria.

**Respuesta breve:** el Salmo 137 (*Al naharot Bavel*, "Junto a los ríos de Babilonia") es un lamento de los exiliados judíos tras la destrucción del Primer Templo. Expresa el dolor por Sión, el juramento de no olvidar Jerusalén y un clamor final de justicia contra Edom y Babilonia.

## Key Takeaways
- Es un salmo del exilio babilónico, con tres partes: el llanto, el juramento y la súplica de justicia.
- Los cautivos se niegan a cantar los cantos de Sión para entretener a sus captores.
- Jerusalén debe quedar por encima de "mi mayor alegría".
- El final, duro, pide justicia contra Edom y Babilonia por la destrucción.

## Texto y traducción (mi traducción)

**1** עַל נַהֲרוֹת בָּבֶל שָׁם יָשַׁבְנוּ גַּם בָּכִינוּ בְּזָכְרֵנוּ אֶת צִיּוֹן
Junto a los ríos de Babilonia, allí nos sentamos y también lloramos, al acordarnos de Sión.

**2** עַל עֲרָבִים בְּתוֹכָהּ תָּלִינוּ כִּנֹּרוֹתֵינוּ
En los sauces de su ribera colgamos nuestras arpas.

**3** כִּי שָׁם שְׁאֵלוּנוּ שׁוֹבֵינוּ דִּבְרֵי שִׁיר וְתוֹלָלֵינוּ שִׂמְחָה שִׁירוּ לָנוּ מִשִּׁיר צִיּוֹן
Pues allí nos pidieron nuestros captores palabras de canto, y nuestros opresores, alegría: «Cantadnos algo de los cantos de Sión».

**4** אֵיךְ נָשִׁיר אֶת שִׁיר ה׳ עַל אַדְמַת נֵכָר
¿Cómo cantaremos el canto del Eterno en tierra extraña?

**5** אִם אֶשְׁכָּחֵךְ יְרוּשָׁלִָם תִּשְׁכַּח יְמִינִי
Si te olvidare, Jerusalén, que se olvide mi diestra.

**6** תִּדְבַּק לְשׁוֹנִי לְחִכִּי אִם לֹא אֶזְכְּרֵכִי אִם לֹא אַעֲלֶה אֶת יְרוּשָׁלִַם עַל רֹאשׁ שִׂמְחָתִי
Que mi lengua se pegue a mi paladar si no me acuerdo de ti, si no elevo a Jerusalén por encima de mi mayor alegría.

**7** זְכֹר ה׳ לִבְנֵי אֱדוֹם אֵת יוֹם יְרוּשָׁלִָם הָאֹמְרִים עָרוּ עָרוּ עַד הַיְסוֹד בָּהּ
Recuerda, Eterno, a los hijos de Edom el día de Jerusalén, cuando decían: «¡Arrasad, arrasad hasta sus cimientos!».

**8** בַּת בָּבֶל הַשְּׁדוּדָה אַשְׁרֵי שֶׁיְשַׁלֶּם לָךְ אֶת גְּמוּלֵךְ שֶׁגָּמַלְתְּ לָנוּ
Hija de Babilonia, la destructora: dichoso quien te pague la retribución que tú nos diste.

**9** אַשְׁרֵי שֶׁיֹּאחֵז וְנִפֵּץ אֶת עֹלָלַיִךְ אֶל הַסָּלַע
Dichoso quien tome y estrelle a tus pequeños contra la roca.

## Notas sobre el sentido
- **Pshat (sentido simple):** los versículos 1 a 4 describen el duelo. Colgar las arpas indica que no hay ánimo para la música. Los captores piden canciones de Sión como diversión, y los exiliados se niegan a hacerlo.
- **Versículos 5 y 6:** son un juramento de fidelidad a Jerusalén. Hay una costumbre conocida de recordar este versículo en las bodas, cuando se rompe la copa, como memoria de la destrucción. Es una costumbre que recuerdo de memoria, sin haberla verificado aquí.
- **Versículos 7 a 9:** son una oración de justicia y no una instrucción. El salmista pide que a Babilonia le suceda lo mismo que ella hizo. Se citan aparte porque son difíciles. Según el sentido simple, expresan el dolor de un pueblo que vio cómo mataban a sus propios niños.
- **Uso litúrgico:** este salmo se recita antes del Bircat Hamazón (la bendición después de comer) en días de semana, mientras que en Shabat y fiestas se dice el Salmo 126. Esto también lo recuerdo de memoria y no lo verifiqué.

Si quieres, cuando Sefaria responda de nuevo puedo traer los comentarios de Rashi, Ibn Ezra o Radak sobre este salmo.

answer:
**Réponse courte :** non, pas selon le texte biblique. Le buisson ardent se trouve à « Horev, la montagne de Dieu », dans le désert où Moïse conduit le troupeau de Jéthro, prêtre de Madian. Paran est une région distincte, que la Torah situe plus loin, après le Sinaï.

## Points clés
- Le verset place la vision à Horev, la montagne de Dieu, sans nommer Paran.
- Madian et Paran sont deux régions distinctes dans les textes, même si elles sont voisines.
- Un verset de Rois montre qu'on allait de Madian à Paran, puis en Égypte. Ce sont donc deux étapes différentes.
- Aucune source que j'ai pu vérifier ici n'identifie le désert du buisson ardent avec Paran.

## Ce que dit le texte

**Le buisson.** [Exodus 3:1] dit : « וּמֹשֶׁה הָיָה רֹעֶה אֶת־צֹאן יִתְרוֹ חֹתְנוֹ כֹּהֵן מִדְיָן וַיִּנְהַג אֶת־הַצֹּאן אַחַר הַמִּדְבָּר וַיָּבֹא אֶל־הַר הָאֱלֹהִים חֹרֵבָה ». En français : « Moïse faisait paître le troupeau de Jéthro, son beau-père, prêtre de Madian ; il mena le troupeau au-delà du désert et arriva à Horev, la montagne de Dieu » (traduction de ma part, d'après le sens du verset).

Le désert est ici simplement « le désert » (*hamidbar*). Le lieu précis est Horev. La Torah ne nomme pas Paran à cet endroit.

**Madian et Paran sont deux lieux différents.** Dans [I Kings 11:17-18], Hadad l'Édomite fuit vers l'Égypte : « וַיָּקֻמוּ מִמִּדְיָן וַיָּבֹאוּ פָּארָן », c'est-à-dire « ils partirent de Madian et arrivèrent à Paran ». Il y a donc deux étapes successives, ce qui montre que Paran n'est pas Madian. Ce verset n'indique pas non plus où se trouve le buisson.

**Paran dans la Torah.** Paran apparaît plus tard dans le parcours d'Israël, après le Sinaï. C'est de là que partent les explorateurs (Nombres 13). Je n'ai pas pu relire ces versets ici, donc je m'appuie sur ma connaissance générale. Paran est donc associé à la suite du voyage, pas à la rencontre au buisson.

## Une nuance
Horev est généralement identifié au mont Sinaï. Le même lieu est dit « la montagne de Dieu » au buisson, et Israël y reçoit la Torah. La région est vaste, et le nom de Paran est parfois employé largement. Certains auteurs rapprochent donc Sinaï, Séir et Paran, par exemple dans le poème de Deutéronome 33:2. Cela ne fait pas de Paran le lieu du buisson. Pour la localisation géographique exacte, les avis divergent, y compris chez les chercheurs modernes, et la tradition ne tranche pas de façon unique.

Si vous voulez, je peux relire Rashi, Ramban ou Ibn Ezra sur [Exodus 3:1]. Mes consultations de commentaires ont échoué à l'instant, et je préfère ne rien leur attribuer de mémoire.

answer:
# Análise do Salmo 51 (*Miktam* de arrependimento de David)

O Salmo 51 é a grande oração de *teshuvá* (arrependimento) da Bíblia. Segundo o título, David o disse quando o profeta Natan o confrontou depois do episódio com Bat-Sheva. O salmo vai do reconhecimento da culpa ao pedido de purificação interior. Termina com a promessa de ensinar os pecadores e com uma visão de restauração de Sião. As traduções abaixo são minhas, a partir do texto hebraico do Sefaria.

## Pontos principais

- O título liga o salmo a [II Samuel 12:13], onde David diz "*chatáti laAdonai*" (pequei contra o Eterno) e Natan responde que seu pecado foi removido.
- A estrutura é: confissão (v. 3–8), purificação (v. 9–11), renovação interior (v. 12–14), missão de ensinar (v. 15–19) e visão coletiva (v. 20–21).
- O versículo 6, "contra Ti somente pequei", é o mais debatido. Rashi o explica de duas formas.
- O salmo põe o "coração quebrantado" acima do sacrifício material. Esse é o seu ensinamento mais conhecido.
- O Radak lê os dois últimos versículos como profecia sobre o Templo e o futuro.

## 1. Título e contexto

O título diz: "*Lamenatzéach mizmor leDavid, bevô elav Natan hanaví ka'asher ba el Bat-Sheva*". Em português: "Para o regente. Salmo de David, quando o profeta Natan veio a ele, depois que ele tinha ido a Bat-Sheva". O episódio é narrado em II Samuel 11–12. Na narrativa, a confissão de David é curta, só duas palavras no hebraico de [II Samuel 12:13]. O salmo mostra o que havia por trás dessa confissão breve.

## 2. Confissão e peso da culpa (v. 3–8)

**Pedido de misericórdia (v. 3–4).** David não alega mérito. Pede perdão "*kechasdecha*" (conforme a Tua bondade) e "*keróv rachamécha*" (conforme a Tua abundante compaixão). Usa três verbos de limpeza: "apaga" (*mechê*), "lava" (*kabsêni*) e "purifica" (*taharêni*). Usa também três palavras para pecado: *pesha* (transgressão), *avon* (iniquidade) e *chatá* (pecado).

**"Meu pecado está sempre diante de mim" (v. 5).** Aqui está a consciência permanente da falta. O arrependimento começa quando a pessoa deixa de minimizar o que fez.

**"Contra Ti somente pequei" (v. 6).** David pecou também contra Uriá e Bat-Sheva, então o versículo pede explicação. Rashi dá duas:

- Primeira: o pecado é contra Deus porque foi Ele quem advertiu contra isso. Por isso só Deus pode perdoar. Mesmo o mal feito a Uriá foi, em última instância, uma transgressão contra o mandamento divino ([Rashi on Psalms 51:6]).
- Segunda, sobre "*lemaan titzdak bidvarécha*" (para que sejas justo em Tua palavra): se Deus perdoar, Sua justiça se mostra diante dos ímpios que não se arrependem. Eles não poderão dizer que o arrependimento não teria adiantado.

Rashi também traz, com base em Sanhedrin 107a, uma leitura ligada ao pedido de David: "examina-me e prova-me" ([Psalms 26:2]). David foi provado e não saiu perfeito. Essa leitura é talmúdica, mais um midrash do que o sentido simples.

**"Em iniquidade fui gerado" (v. 7).** O versículo é *hen beavon cholálti uvechet yechematni imi*. Em português: "Eis que em iniquidade fui formado, e em pecado minha mãe me concebeu". Pelo sentido simples, David reconhece a fragilidade da condição humana e a inclinação ao mal, que está presente desde o início. A leitura costuma ser uma confissão humilde de fraqueza. Não é uma doutrina de "pecado original" que condene o ser humano de nascença. No judaísmo, a alma é pura, e a *teshuvá* sempre está disponível. Esse ponto vem do meu conhecimento geral e não de um comentário que li aqui.

**Verdade no íntimo (v. 8).** Deus deseja "verdade nas partes ocultas" (*batuchot*), e David pede sabedoria "no secreto". A purificação que ele busca é a do interior, não só a da conduta visível.

## 3. Purificação e renovação (v. 9–14)

- **Hissopo e neve (v. 9).** O hissopo (*eizov*) lembra os ritos de purificação do Templo. A imagem é de pureza total, "mais branco que a neve".
- **Ossos quebrantados (v. 10).** O sofrimento é físico e espiritual. David pede para ouvir "alegria e contentamento".
- **"Um coração puro cria para mim, ó Deus" (v. 12).** O verbo é *bará*, o mesmo da criação do mundo. David pede uma obra nova de Deus, e não só o perdão. Pede também um "espírito firme" (*ruach nachon*).
- **"Não tires de mim o Teu espírito de santidade" (v. 13).** Ele teme perder a proximidade com Deus e a inspiração profética.
- **Espírito generoso (v. 14).** O "*ruach nedivá*" o sustentaria na fidelidade futura.

## 4. A missão de ensinar (v. 15–19)

David promete: "Ensinarei aos transgressores Teus caminhos, e os pecadores a Ti retornarão" (v. 15). Sua queda se torna instrumento para ajudar outros a voltar.

O pedido "Livra-me de sangues" (*midamim*, v. 16) alude à morte de Uriá. Quando o perdão vier, ele cantará a justiça de Deus. O versículo 17 é conhecido da liturgia: "*Adonai sefatai tiftach ufi yagid tehilatecha*" (Senhor, abre meus lábios, e minha boca declarará Teu louvor). Ele abre a *Amidá*.

**O sacrifício verdadeiro (v. 18–19).** David diz que Deus não deseja sacrifício nem holocausto. O que Ele aceita é "*ruach nishbará, lev nishbar venidke*" (espírito quebrantado, coração quebrantado e contrito). A leitura sensata não é que o sacrifício seja inútil. O sacrifício sem arrependimento interior não basta, e um pecado como o de David, em especial, não é expiado por oferta. Esta é a minha explicação do texto.

## 5. Sião e o futuro (v. 20–21)

Os últimos versículos pedem: "Faze bem a Sião segundo Tua vontade, edifica os muros de Jerusalém. Então Te agradarás de sacrifícios de justiça". O Radak lê isso como profecia: o Espírito Santo voltou a David enquanto orava. Ele viu a destruição do primeiro e do segundo Templo por causa dos pecados. Viu também que, mesmo com sacrifícios constantes, Deus os rejeitou porque as ações eram más. Nos dias do Messias, os sacrifícios serão aceitos porque todo Israel servirá a Deus de coração unido ([Radak on Psalms 51:20]).

Uma leitura mais simples vê nesses versículos o interesse de David pelo bem do povo. O rei sabe que seu pecado afeta toda a nação, e por isso termina rezando por ela.

## Temas para estudo

1. **Teshuvá completa:** reconhecer, confessar, pedir perdão, pedir transformação e comprometer-se a ajudar outros.
2. **Responsabilidade:** David não culpa as circunstâncias. Mesmo quando fala da fraqueza humana (v. 7), é para confessar, não para se desculpar.
3. **Interior e exterior:** o ritual só tem valor com um coração quebrantado.
4. **Uso litúrgico:** o v. 17 abre a *Amidá* e o salmo é muito recitado nas orações de arrependimento. Não verifiquei aqui os costumes específicos de cada comunidade.

Se quiser, posso aprofundar o salmo com outros comentaristas, como Ibn Ezra ou Metzudat David, ou com o Talmud sobre o pecado de David (Shabat 56a).

answer:
**Kurz gesagt:** In der Tora steht zuerst *Elohim* (אֱלֹהִים, „Gott") in [Genesis 1:1], also gleich im ersten Vers. Der Gottesname *YHWH* (das Tetragramm) erscheint zum ersten Mal in [Genesis 2:4], und zwar in der Verbindung „YHWH Elohim". Allein, ohne „Elohim", steht YHWH zuerst in [Genesis 4:1]. Eine Seitenzahl kann ich nicht nennen, weil sie von der Ausgabe abhängt. Kapitel und Vers gelten dagegen in jeder Ausgabe.

## Key Takeaways
- Elohim steht zuerst in [Genesis 1:1] („Bereschit bara Elohim …") und im ganzen ersten Schöpfungsbericht (1:1–2:3).
- „YHWH Elohim" steht zuerst in [Genesis 2:4], dem Beginn des zweiten Berichts, der Erschaffung des Menschen und des Gartens Eden.
- YHWH allein steht zuerst in [Genesis 4:1], in Chavas Worten bei Kains Geburt.
- Die Seitenzahl ist je nach Ausgabe verschieden, also bitte nach Kapitel und Vers suchen.

## Die Stellen im Einzelnen

**1. Elohim – [Genesis 1:1]**
Der Vers lautet: „בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים אֵת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֵת הָאָרֶץ". Das heißt: „Am Anfang schuf Gott Himmel und Erde." Im ersten Kapitel kommt nur Elohim vor, nie YHWH.

**2. YHWH Elohim – [Genesis 2:4]**
Der Vers lautet sinngemäß: „… b'jom asot YHWH Elohim erez weschamajim", also „… am Tag, als YHWH Elohim Erde und Himmel machte". Diesen Wortlaut habe ich aus dem Gedächtnis zitiert, weil der Abruf bei Sefaria gerade fehlschlug. Bitte prüfe ihn in deiner Ausgabe. Ab hier heißt es im zweiten Bericht meist „YHWH Elohim".

**3. YHWH allein – [Genesis 4:1]**
Den Vers konnte ich nachschlagen: „וַתֹּאמֶר קָנִיתִי אִישׁ אֶת־יְהֹוָה". Das heißt: „… und sie sagte: Ich habe einen Mann erworben mit YHWH (mit Gottes Hilfe)."

## Zum Hintergrund
- **Aussprache:** Jüdisch wird YHWH nicht ausgesprochen. Beim Lesen sagt man *Adonai* („Herr"), außerhalb von Gebet und Lesung meist *HaSchem* („der Name").
- **Traditionelle Deutung (Midrasch):** Elohim steht für Gottes Eigenschaft des Gerichts (*Midat HaDin*). YHWH steht für die Eigenschaft des Erbarmens (*Midat HaRachamim*). Die Verbindung beider in Kapitel 2 deutet man so, dass die Welt mit beiden Eigenschaften bestehen soll. Das ist Midrasch und keine Erklärung des einfachen Wortsinns.
- **Bibelkritik:** Die Wechsel der Gottesnamen sind auch ein Ausgangspunkt der modernen Quellenkritik. Die Tradition liest sie dagegen als bewusste Aussage über Gott.

Wenn du möchtest, schaue ich die Kommentare dazu nach, zum Beispiel Raschi zu [Genesis 1:1] und zu [Genesis 2:4].

answer:
El Salmo 16 es un *mijtam* (composición de David) de confianza total en Dios. David lo toma como su única "porción", rechaza la idolatría y termina con la certeza de que Dios lo guiará por el "sendero de la vida". Sefaria no ofrece traducción al español de este texto, así que la traducción es mía, a partir del hebreo y de la versión inglesa de Sefaria [Psalms 16:1-11].

## Puntos clave
- Es un salmo de refugio en Dios ("en Ti me he refugiado").
- Dios es la "porción y copa" de David, es decir, su herencia y su suerte.
- David rechaza explícitamente los cultos idólatras.
- Su confianza produce alegría y seguridad, incluso frente a la muerte.
- Termina con "el sendero de la vida" y con delicias eternas junto a Dios.

## Texto y traducción

1. מִכְתָּם לְדָוִד שָׁמְרֵנִי אֵל כִּי־חָסִיתִי בָךְ
 Mijtam de David. Guárdame, oh Dios, porque en Ti me refugio.
2. אָמַרְתְּ לַיהֹוָה אֲדֹנָי אָתָּה טוֹבָתִי בַּל־עָלֶיךָ
 Dije al Eterno: "Tú eres mi Señor; mi bien no depende de nadie por encima de Ti". (Otra lectura: "no hay bien para mí fuera de Ti".)
3. לִקְדוֹשִׁים אֲשֶׁר־בָּאָרֶץ הֵמָּה וְאַדִּירֵי כָּל־חֶפְצִי־בָם
 En cuanto a los santos que están en la tierra y a los nobles, en ellos está todo mi deleite.
 (Esta lectura es una de las posibles. Sefaria, en su versión inglesa, lo entiende como una referencia a poderes divinos extraños, de modo que el versículo es de difícil interpretación.)
4. יִרְבּוּ עַצְּבוֹתָם אַחֵר מָהָרוּ בַּל־אַסִּיךְ נִסְכֵּיהֶם מִדָּם וּבַל־אֶשָּׂא אֶת־שְׁמוֹתָם עַל־שְׂפָתָי
 Se multiplicarán los dolores de los que corren tras otro [dios]. No derramaré sus libaciones de sangre ni tomaré sus nombres en mis labios.
5. יְהֹוָה מְנָת־חֶלְקִי וְכוֹסִי אַתָּה תּוֹמִיךְ גּוֹרָלִי
 El Eterno es la porción de mi herencia y de mi copa; Tú sostienes mi suerte.
6. חֲבָלִים נָפְלוּ־לִי בַּנְּעִמִים אַף־נַחֲלַת שָׁפְרָה עָלָי
 Me tocaron en suerte cordeles de lugares agradables; sí, hermosa es mi heredad.
7. אֲבָרֵךְ אֶת־יְהֹוָה אֲשֶׁר יְעָצָנִי אַף־לֵילוֹת יִסְּרוּנִי כִלְיוֹתָי
 Bendeciré al Eterno que me aconsejó; aun de noche me instruyen mis riñones [mi interior, mi conciencia].
8. שִׁוִּיתִי יְהֹוָה לְנֶגְדִּי תָמִיד כִּי מִימִינִי בַּל־אֶמּוֹט
 He puesto al Eterno siempre delante de mí; porque está a mi derecha, no vacilaré.
9. לָכֵן שָׂמַח לִבִּי וַיָּגֶל כְּבוֹדִי אַף־בְּשָׂרִי יִשְׁכֹּן לָבֶטַח
 Por eso se alegró mi corazón y exultó mi alma [lit. "mi honor"]; también mi carne reposará segura.
10. כִּי לֹא־תַעֲזֹב נַפְשִׁי לִשְׁאוֹל לֹא־תִתֵּן חֲסִידְךָ לִרְאוֹת שָׁחַת
 Porque no abandonarás mi alma al *Sheol* (el abismo de los muertos), ni permitirás que tu fiel vea la fosa.
11. תּוֹדִיעֵנִי אֹרַח חַיִּים שֹׂבַע שְׂמָחוֹת אֶת־פָּנֶיךָ נְעִמוֹת בִּימִינְךָ נֶצַח
 Me harás conocer el sendero de la vida; hay plenitud de alegrías ante Tu rostro, delicias a Tu derecha para siempre.

## Comentario breve
- **Estructura (mi lectura):** los versículos 1-2 son una petición y una declaración de fe. Los versículos 3-4 contrastan con la idolatría. Los versículos 5-8 hablan de Dios como herencia y guía. Los versículos 9-11 expresan alegría y esperanza.
- **"Mijtam":** el significado de la palabra es incierto. Algunos la relacionan con *ketem* (oro fino), como una composición preciosa. Esta es una explicación común, no una certeza que yo haya verificado aquí en los comentaristas.
- **Versículo 5:** la imagen proviene de la herencia de la tierra y de la copa de la porción. Recuerda que los levitas no recibieron tierra porque "el Eterno es su herencia" (Deuteronomio 18:2).
- **Versículo 10:** en su sentido simple, David confía en que Dios lo librará de una muerte prematura. Otras tradiciones lo interpretan de forma distinta. No he consultado aquí los comentaristas, así que si quieres puedo revisar a Rashi, Ibn Ezra o Radak sobre este salmo.

answer:
The text doesn't say quite what you describe. Your instinct about indirectness is a real theme in the book, but the details need correcting. My lookup of the Sefaria text failed (rate limit), so I'm paraphrasing from memory and not quoting. Please check the verses yourself.

## Key Takeaways

- In [Job 1:11] the Satan asks God to stretch out *His own* hand and strike Job's possessions. He does not ask for a "curse," and he does not offer to use his own hand.
- In [Job 1:12] God hands Job's property over to the Satan's power, but forbids the Satan to lay a hand on Job's person.
- In [Job 2:5-6] the Satan asks again, this time for Job's bone and flesh, and God now permits the affliction of Job's body. The only limit is that Job's life be spared.
- So the "no direct touch" restriction applies only in chapter 1. It is lifted in chapter 2.
- The word "curse" in Job usually refers to what the Satan predicts Job will do to God, not to what God does to Job.

## What the text says

**Chapter 1.** The Satan challenges Job's piety, arguing that Job is righteous only because God has protected him. He says that if God stretched out His hand against Job's possessions, Job would "bless" God to His face. The verb is *barech*, which the book uses as a euphemism for "curse" (compare [Job 1:5] and [Job 2:9]). So the "curse" is the response the Satan predicts from Job. It is not the affliction.

In [Job 1:12] God answers that everything Job has is in the Satan's hands, but the Satan may not lay a hand on Job himself. The Satan is the agent who carries out the destruction. The Satan sets the terms, and God sets the limit.

**Chapter 2.** After Job passes the first test, the Satan raises the stakes. He says a person will give skin for skin, and asks God to stretch out His hand to Job's bone and flesh. God replies that Job is now in the Satan's hand, with one limit: the Satan must preserve his life. The Satan then strikes Job with the boils. So the prohibition on touching Job's person does not last.

## Your reading of indirectness

Your idea does have some basis:

- **Delegation.** The Satan asks for God's own hand, but God hands the matter over to the Satan. The affliction is carried out by an agent and not by God directly. This fits the way the book keeps some distance between God and the suffering.
- **Narrative framing.** The narrator tells us it was the Satan who struck Job ([Job 2:7]). Job, though, attributes everything to God ([Job 1:21], [Job 2:10]). The book thereby sets up the tension between Job's view and the heavenly scene that only the reader sees.
- **Later tradition.** The Talmud, in [Bava Batra 16a], identifies the Satan with the evil inclination and the Angel of Death, and it describes him as acting only with God's permission. It also notes that the Satan was "shown" his limits. I haven't re-read the passage, so check it before relying on it.

On the other side, God's authorization is explicit in both chapters. The book does not claim that God has no relation to the suffering. Even in the Satan's own challenge, the matter is framed around what God's hand would do. At the end of the book God speaks directly to Job and takes responsibility for the world's order ([Job 38]), and Job's friends and Job himself never think of the suffering as coming from anyone but God.

answer:
Eliphaz is using a Hebrew poetic device: "six... and seven" means "again and again, however many troubles come." He is promising that God will rescue the righteous person in every trouble, with no exceptions. I could not reach Sefaria just now, so I have not checked the commentaries. What follows is from my own knowledge, and I have not quoted any commentator.

## Key Takeaways
- The verse is [Job 5:19]: "בְּשֵׁשׁ צָרוֹת יַצִּילֶךָּ וּבְשֶׁבַע לֹא יִגַּע בְּךָ רָע" ("In six troubles He will rescue you, and in seven no evil will touch you").
- "Six... seven" is a numerical parallelism, not a literal count.
- The point is that God's protection is complete and does not run out.
- The verses that follow list the troubles: famine, war, the tongue's scourge, destruction and wild beasts.
- Eliphaz is wrong to apply this to Job, because it assumes Job's suffering is punishment for sin.

## Pshat: the "x, x+1" device
Biblical poetry often uses a graded number pattern, where the second number is one higher than the first. Examples are [Proverbs 6:16] ("six things the Lord hates, seven are an abomination to Him"), [Proverbs 30:15-18] and the repeated "for three transgressions... and for four" in Amos 1–2. The pattern signals a full and open-ended set. It does not mean that exactly seven things exist or that the seventh is special.

Read that way, the verse has two parts:
- **"In six troubles He will rescue you."** However many troubles come in sequence, God delivers you from each.
- **"In seven no evil will touch you."** Even when the troubles pile up past what seems bearable, you are still protected.

Some readers also hear a climax. The seventh trouble would be the one that finally breaks a person, and Eliphaz says even that one will not harm you.

## What the following verses say
Eliphaz then gives concrete examples. In famine God will redeem you from death, and in war from the sword's power. You will be hidden from the "scourge of the tongue," and you will not fear destruction or wild beasts. This is a picture of total security for the person who accepts God's discipline. That is why the passage opens at [Job 5:17] with "Happy is the man whom God reproves."

## The irony in the book
Eliphaz is speaking to Job, and his words carry a hidden accusation. If God always saves the righteous, then Job's suffering must mean he sinned and should repent. The book does not accept this. God's closing verdict is that Eliphaz and his friends "did not speak rightly" about Him, in [Job 42:7]. The verse is true as a statement of hope that God can deliver. It is false as a rule that suffering proves guilt.

Job's own life also shows a pattern. Several disasters strike in quick succession in the first chapter, and he is eventually restored. In that sense Eliphaz's sentence is bitterly ironic: Job is hit by far more than six troubles, and he has not yet been saved.

If you'd like, I can retry the lookup and bring in specific commentators such as Rashi, Ibn Ezra or Metzudat David on this verse.

answer:
Several Hasidic works on Vaetchanan come from Eastern European masters. I verified the three below on Sefaria. Sefaria began rate-limiting me partway through, so I could only read the openings of these comments, not full essays. I also left out sources I couldn't check, and I flag one below.

One caveat on the question: "survived the Holocaust" can mean two things. Most classic Hasidic Torah works were written long before 1939, and they survived because they were printed and widely copied. Works written during the war, like the Piaseczna Rebbe's, survived only because someone hid them.

## Key Takeaways
- The Shem MiShmuel (Sochatchov) and the Mei HaShiloach (Izhbitz) both focus on Moses' prayer in the opening verse.
- Each reads the verb *va'etchanan* (I pleaded) as a clue to what kind of prayer Moses offered.
- The Kedushat Levi (Berditchev) reads the word *lemor* (saying) as a sign that Moses first needed to pray in order to be able to pray.
- Breslov teaching, in Likutei Moharan II:78, ties Moses' plea to *matnat chinam* (a free gift).
- The Piaseczna Rebbe's *Esh Kodesh*, which was buried in the Warsaw Ghetto, is the best-known example of a wartime work. I couldn't pull its Vaetchanan material to verify it.

## The verse
The opening of the parasha reads: "וָאֶתְחַנַּן אֶל ה' בָּעֵת הַהִוא לֵאמֹר" ("I pleaded with the LORD at that time, saying…") [Deuteronomy 3:23]. The Hasidic authors below all start from the unusual wording and timing of this verse.

## Shem MiShmuel (Rabbi Shmuel Bornstein of Sochatchov)
The Shem MiShmuel is a Polish Hasidic work, less widely known than the Sefat Emet. It begins with two textual difficulties:
- The root is *chanan*, so the text could have said "*vechanoti*" (I pleaded). Instead it uses the reflexive form *va'etchanan*, which signals something about the manner of Moses' plea.
- The phrase "at that time" needs explaining. Rashi says Moses thought his vow had been released after the conquest of Sihon and Og.

The author asks what practical difference that thought makes, and why the Torah tells us about it [Shem MiShmuel, Vaetchanan 5:2]. The text I retrieved ends at the question, so I haven't read his answer.

## Mei HaShiloach (Rabbi Mordechai Yosef Leiner of Izhbitz)
The Izhbitzer reads Moses' retelling as a message to Israel. Even though the prayer seemingly failed, Moses wanted them to understand that it was not wasted. He also reads the reflexive *va'etchanan* as meaning that Moses became "full of supplications," with prayer flowing naturally from his mouth. He takes that fluency as evidence that God was acting through it [Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Deuteronomy, Vaetchanan 1]. This is my paraphrase of a truncated passage.

## Kedushat Levi (Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev)
He asks why the verse says *lemor*, which seems redundant. His answer is that Moses first pleaded in order to be able to pray at all. Moses was ashamed before God and had to ask for the ability to speak. [Kedushat Levi, Deuteronomy, Vaetchanan 1] is a more familiar source than the others, but this reading is not widely quoted.

## Breslov: Likutei Moharan II:78
Rebbe Nachman teaches that Moses asked to enter the Land through *matnat chinam*, a gift given freely. He connects this to the word *va'etchanan*, and reads "at that time, saying" as pointing to the power of that moment [Likutei Moharan, Part II 78:6:1], [Likutei Moharan, Part II 78:6:2]. Sichot HaRan also sends the reader back to this teaching in connection with one of Rebbe Nachman's stories [Sichot HaRan 153:24].

## Wartime works
The Piaseczna Rebbe, Rabbi Kalonymus Kalman Shapira, gave weekly Torah talks in the Warsaw Ghetto. They were buried and recovered after the war, and published as *Esh Kodesh*. The wartime context is why it is the most obvious answer to your question. I couldn't confirm which talk, if any, deals with Vaetchanan, so I haven't quoted it. If you'd like, I can try again to locate it and the Sefat Emet on this parasha.

answer:
I couldn't find a classical source for exactly that reading of the doubled "justice" (*tzedek tzedek*, Deut. 16:20). The closest sources I could verify are below. The "don't favor the poor either" idea itself is firmly rooted in the Torah, but it comes from a different verse.

## Key Takeaways
- The rule against favoring the poor is explicit in Torah text: [Exodus 23:3] and [Leviticus 19:15].
- The classic readings of the doubled *tzedek* are different: Rashi and the Sifrei say "seek a reliable court," and the Talmud says one is strict law and one is compromise.
- I found no commentator on [Deuteronomy 16:20] who says "the first against favoring the rich, the second against favoring the poor." You may be remembering a derasha, a modern or homiletic source, or a blend of sources.

## Where the "don't favor the poor" idea comes from
[Leviticus 19:15] reads: "You shall not render an unfair decision: do not favor the poor or show deference to the rich; judge your kinsman fairly." Here the Torah itself gives both halves, favoring neither the poor nor the great. [Exodus 23:3] separately warns against favoring the poor in his dispute. That is probably the source of the balance you remember. Someone may have attached it to the repeated "justice" in Deuteronomy 16.

## What the commentators say about the doubled *tzedek*
The context in [Deuteronomy 16:18-20] is judges, no partiality, and no bribes. Here is what I verified:
- **Rashi:** "go to a reliable court" [Rashi on Deuteronomy 16:20:1], following the Sifrei and Sanhedrin 32b.
- **Sanhedrin 32b (as cited in Haamek Davar):** one *tzedek* means strict law and the other means compromise (*peshara*).
- **Ibn Ezra:** the repetition means pursue justice "whether one gains or loses." He also offers "as long as one exists" [Ibn Ezra on Deuteronomy 16:20:1]. His first reading is the nearest to impartiality, but it concerns the pursuer's own gain or loss, not rich versus poor.
- **Ramban (via Tur HaArokh):** the repetition exhorts not only judges but ordinary citizens to pursue justice in public affairs [Tur HaArokh, Deuteronomy 16:20:1].
- **Rabbeinu Bahya:** the repetition means being righteous in both word and deed [Rabbeinu Bahya, Devarim 16:20:1].
- **HaKtav VeHaKabalah:** one *tzedek* is justice in the law itself, and the other is justice in the litigants' claims, so the judge is not misled by cleverness [HaKtav VeHaKabalah, Deuteronomy 16:20:1].

## Possible origins of your memory
This part is my guess, not a verified source. The reading may come from a modern sermon or *dvar Torah* that combines Leviticus 19:15 with the doubled *tzedek*. If you remember where you saw it, such as a book, a speaker, or a parasha (Shoftim), tell me and I can help trace it.

answer:
Jeremiah and Ezekiel prophesied at the same time, but the Bible never records them meeting, corresponding, or mentioning each other by name. Jeremiah was a lone, persecuted voice in Jerusalem. Ezekiel was a priest-prophet among the exiles in Babylon, where he was heard but not obeyed. Any picture of a personal relationship is inference, not text.

## Key Takeaways
- Jeremiah began prophesying under Josiah and was active in Jerusalem through its destruction. Ezekiel was exiled with Jehoiachin in 597 BCE and prophesied in Babylon from about 593.
- No verse shows them in contact. Their only attested link is indirect, through Jeremiah's letter to the exiles.
- Jeremiah was rejected, imprisoned, and accused of treason by his own community.
- Ezekiel was consulted by the exilic elders but treated as entertainment.
- Their messages largely converge: judgment on Jerusalem now, restoration later.

## Where each one stood

**Jeremiah** stayed in the land and prophesied before and during the siege. His career began in Josiah's reign and ran through the fall of Jerusalem, and afterward he was taken to Egypt. He spoke against the kings, priests, and false prophets, and he paid for it with imprisonment, a pit, and threats on his life. The elders defended him once, in Jeremiah 26, but his general standing was that of an outcast.

**Ezekiel** was a priest (*kohen*) and was taken to Babylon in the first exile, with Jehoiachin. His visions came to him by the Chebar canal. I'm recalling those details from memory, because the lookup of [Ezekiel 1:1-3] failed. The exilic elders came and sat before him (see Ezekiel 8:1, which I also did not retrieve). That gave him a recognized standing among the exiles, but the standing was hollow. Ezekiel is told:

> "וְהִנְּךָ לָהֶם כְּשִׁיר עֲגָבִים יְפֵה קוֹל וּמֵטִב נַגֵּן וְשָׁמְעוּ אֶת־דְּבָרֶיךָ וְעֹשִׂים אֵינָם אוֹתָם" [Ezekiel 33:32]
>
> "To them you are just a singer of bawdy songs, who has a sweet voice and plays skillfully; they hear your words, but will not obey them." (Sefaria's translation)

People crowded to hear him, but only as a performance.

## The one documented link
[Jeremiah 29:1-3] records that Jeremiah sent a letter "from Jerusalem to the priests, the prophets, the rest of the elders of the exile community, and to all the people whom Nebuchadnezzar had exiled." The letter went through emissaries of King Zedekiah. Ezekiel was among those exiles, so he was in the audience for this letter. The text does not say he reacted to it.

The letter shows that Jeremiah was in dispute with exilic "prophets" who promised a quick return. Ezekiel's message to the exiles was the opposite of that promise: the city would fall and their hopes were false. The two prophets were thus effectively allies against the false prophets, whether or not they coordinated.

I tried to read the rest of the chapter (verses 24–29), where Jeremiah is denounced from Babylon by Shemaiah, but the lookup failed. I'm leaving out the details rather than guess them.

## What we can say, and what we can't
- **Convergence (pshat):** Both prophets announce the destruction of the Temple and the exile, and both promise later restoration. Their themes overlap, for example the condemnation of shepherds and false prophets. That is a matter of shared message, not evidence of a relationship.
- **Silence:** Ezekiel never names Jeremiah. In [Ezekiel 14:14] the righteous exemplars are Noah, Daniel, and Job, and Jeremiah is not among them. I'm citing that verse from memory, not from a retrieved text. Nothing in the silence tells us about their feelings.
- **Later tradition:** The Talmud treats both books as canonical, but it ascribes their compilation to different hands. As I recall, [Bava Batra 15a] says Jeremiah wrote his own book, Kings, and Lamentations, while the Men of the Great Assembly wrote Ezekiel. I haven't re-read the passage, so please check it. Rabbinic literature does contain stories that pair the two prophets, but I can't vouch for specific ones without looking them up.

If you'd like, I can retry the lookups and trace how Ezekiel and Jeremiah are paired in the midrash and Talmud, or compare their messages to the exiles.

answer:
Yes, the parallel is real, and the text seems built to invite it. I haven't verified any commentator on this point. What follows is my own reading of the verses, and I mark where I go beyond them.

## Key Takeaways
- Both scenes are periodic gatherings in which a group "comes" together and a hidden danger sits among them.
- Job's worry ("perhaps they have sinned and blessed God in their hearts") matches the Adversary's later claim that Job himself will "bless" God to His face.
- The verb *barakh* ("bless") is used euphemistically in both scenes to mean its opposite, "curse."
- The structure is mirrored. On earth the father stands guard over the feasting children, and in heaven God presides over the heavenly "sons" and the Adversary.
- This is a literary or interpretive observation. I haven't verified that a classical commentator frames it this way.

## The text
The text of [Job 1:4-6] reads:

- Verse 4: "וְהָלְכוּ בָנָיו וְעָשׂוּ מִשְׁתֶּה בֵּית אִישׁ יוֹמוֹ", "His sons would go and hold a feast, each at his house on his day."
- Verse 5: Job sanctifies them and offers burnt offerings, "אוּלַי חָטְאוּ בָנַי וּבֵרְכוּ אֱלֹהִים בִּלְבָבָם", "Perhaps my children have sinned and blessed God in their hearts."
- Verse 6: "וַיְהִי הַיּוֹם וַיָּבֹאוּ בְּנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים לְהִתְיַצֵּב עַל־יְהֹוָה וַיָּבוֹא גַּם־הַשָּׂטָן בְּתוֹכָם", "One day the divine beings came to present themselves before the LORD, and the Adversary also came among them."

## Where the parallel works
1. **Both are recurring, cyclical gatherings.** The feasts rotate "each on his day." The heavenly session is "the day" (*hayom*), with a similar sense of a set occasion. Job's offerings are repeated "all the days" (*kol hayamim*).
2. **Both are "sons" gathering.** The *bnei Elohim* ("sons of God") present themselves before God, and Job's *banav* ("sons") feast. One group is before a divine father and the other before a human father.
3. **Both involve a suspected but unseen failing.** Job suspects an inner sin ("in their hearts") that no one can see. The Adversary likewise questions the hidden motive behind Job's piety: "Does Job fear God for nothing?" [Job 1:9]. Both scenes ask what lies in the heart behind visible conduct.
4. **The use of "bless" for "curse."** Job fears his children *berakhu* God. The Adversary predicts that Job will, in the Hebrew, *yevarekhekha*, "bless You," to Your face [Job 1:11]. The same word returns in [Job 2:9], where Job's wife says "bless God and die." The narrator seems to use this word on purpose to link the scenes.
5. **Job's role mirrors God's.** Job rises early and secures his children's standing by offerings. In heaven God allows the Adversary access and then sets limits. Job's protective care becomes the very thing the Adversary challenges, since [Job 1:10] speaks of a "hedge" around him.

## Where they differ
- Job suspects his children without evidence ("perhaps"). God, by contrast, points to Job as a model of integrity [Job 1:8].
- The feasting is a human celebration where something may be wrong. The heavenly assembly is a court-like setting where the question is put to the test.
- The children's feast is the setting in which the catastrophe later strikes. Job's sons and daughters die while eating and drinking in the eldest brother's house [Job 1:18-19]. So the two scenes are linked in cause as well as in parallel: the heavenly "test" plays out at the earthly "feast."

## A suggestion for further study
It would be worth checking how classical commentators read "sons of God" and the Adversary. They include Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Malbim on [Job 1:6], and the Talmudic discussion in [Bava Batra 15a-16b], which treats Satan's role and Job's offerings. I couldn't retrieve the commentary links just now, so I haven't confirmed what they say about your parallel. I can look them up if you want.

# Parshat Re'eh: "*Patoach Tiftach*", Opening the Hand Again and Again

Sefaria was rate-limiting me, so I could only retrieve [Deuteronomy 15:8]. The Rashi, Talmud and Sifrei points below are from memory, and I mark them as unchecked. Please confirm them before using this in public.

## Direct answer
The Torah doubles the verb, *patoach tiftach*, "you shall surely open", to teach that giving is not a single act. It is a stance that you keep renewing. The same verse also tells us how to give: "whatever is sufficient to meet the need."

## Key Takeaways
- The verse reads: "כִּֽי־פָתֹ֧חַ תִּפְתַּ֛ח אֶת־יָדְךָ֖ ל֑וֹ וְהַעֲבֵט֙ תַּעֲבִיטֶ֔נּוּ דֵּ֚י מַחְסֹר֔וֹ אֲשֶׁ֥ר יֶחְסַ֖ר לֽוֹ" ("Rather, you must open your hand and lend whatever is sufficient to meet the need") [Deuteronomy 15:8].
- The doubled language is traditionally read as "again and again", so the mitzvah has no cap and no "I already gave".
- The verb "open" implies the hand was closed. The Torah assumes our natural instinct is to clench, and it asks us to overcome that instinct.
- The standard is the poor person's *need* ("*dei machsoro*"), not our comfort level.
- The Torah gives this command in the context of a person's worry that the *shemittah* year is near and a loan will never be repaid (the surrounding verses, which I could not retrieve this time).

## The Dvar Torah

### The question
Why does the Torah need a doubled verb? "*Patoach*" alone would command us to open our hand. And why speak of "opening" at all, rather than simply "giving"?

### Pshat: a hand that starts out closed
Just before this verse the Torah warns: "do not harden your heart and do not shut your hand" (v. 7, which I could not retrieve this time). A closed hand is the default. Stinginess seldom looks like cruelty. It looks like prudence, and we tell ourselves that we have to look after our own needs first. So the Torah does not just say "give." It says to *open*, which is a deliberate act against a reflex.

### The doubled verb, from memory and unchecked
As I recall, the Sifrei and Rashi read the doubling as "even a hundred times". The Talmud in *Bava Metzia* (I believe around 31a) is also connected to this idea, but please verify it. The point is that the mitzvah renews itself. When the same person comes back, we must not say "I already did my part." Poverty does not run on our schedule.

### "Whatever is sufficient to meet the need"
My recollection is that Rashi, drawing on the Talmud, says you are commanded to meet the person's lack, but you are not obligated to make him rich. The Talmud also stretches "what he lacks" to the person's own former standard of living. This is unchecked, so please verify it.

Together the two halves of the verse give a balance. The giver is not asked to bankrupt himself, but he also does not get to decide the need. The poor person's actual lack sets the measure, not the giver's mood.

### My own connection (not from a source)
There is a nice symmetry between the two words. A hand opens only by being closed first, and it can only stay open by being opened again. Generosity is not a trait we have once and for all. It is a muscle that we keep exercising. Each time we open the hand, it gets a little harder for it to snap shut. The doubled verb may be teaching that *patoach* is not only what we do for the poor person. It also describes what happens inside the giver.

### Closing message
This week, as Elul approaches, think of one person whom you have helped once and who might need help again. Instead of feeling "I've done enough," hear the doubled verb: *patoach tiftach*. Open the hand once more.

*Sources to check before using this publicly: Rashi on [Deuteronomy 15:8], Sifrei Devarim on this verse, and the Talmudic passage on "what he lacks" (I believe in Ketubot).*

I can look up these sources properly if you'd like. Let me know if you also want a shorter version for the Shabbat table.

answer:
**Short answer:** The Yovel (Jubilee) laws were designed to reverse commercial changes and restore the original distribution. Land sold in a commercial transaction went back to the original family at Yovel. The Torah did allow a few exceptions, and inheritance was a separate matter.

## Key Takeaways
- Sales of ancestral land were treated as leases lasting until Yovel, not permanent transfers.
- The Torah gives the reason: the land belongs to God, and the Israelites are "strangers and sojourners" with Him ([Leviticus 25:23]).
- Yovel restored land to the original family holdings, and the seller or his relatives could also redeem it earlier ([Leviticus 25:24-28]).
- A few exceptions exist: houses in walled cities, and fields that were consecrated and not redeemed.
- Yovel did not undo changes caused by inheritance, such as a daughter's inheritance passing to her husband's tribe. The Torah blocked tribe-to-tribe transfers in that case by other means ([Numbers 36]).

## The main rule
[Leviticus 25:10] commands "each of you shall return to his holding" at Yovel. [Leviticus 25:23] says land may not be sold *latzmitut*, which means permanently, "for the land is Mine". The sale price was therefore calculated by the number of years remaining until Yovel ([Leviticus 25:15-16]). The buyer was in effect buying a number of harvests, not the land itself.

I could not retrieve the text of [Leviticus 25:23-28] in this session, so I am summarizing it from memory. Please check it against the verses.

Redemption (*ge'ulah*) is the companion mechanism. The seller, or a close relative, could buy the land back before Yovel by refunding the buyer for the years left. If no one redeemed it, it went back automatically at Yovel.

## Exceptions
- **Houses in walled cities** ([Leviticus 25:29-30]). The seller had a one-year right of redemption. After that the sale became permanent, and the house did not return at Yovel.
- **Levite cities** ([Leviticus 25:32-34]). Levite property there always remained redeemable and returned at Yovel. The open fields around the cities could not be sold at all.
- **Consecrated fields** ([Leviticus 27:16-21]). If a field was consecrated and not redeemed, it went to the priests at Yovel instead of back to the owner. This is an exception to the rule that fields return to the family.

## Inheritance and the tribal allotments
Yovel reverses *sales*, not inheritance. The case of the daughters of Zelophehad shows this. The concern in [Numbers 36:4] was that if heiresses married into other tribes, then "even when the Israelites observe the jubilee, their share will be added to that of the tribe into which they marry." In other words, Yovel would not restore the land to the original tribe. The solution was that heiresses must marry within their own tribe ([Numbers 36:6-9]), so that "no inheritance shall pass from tribe to tribe."

## Reasoning
The text says outright that the land belongs to God, and the system is built to stop the permanent concentration of land in a few hands. Each family keeps its economic base from generation to generation. Rabbinic law also treats the original division, as made under Joshua, as the baseline for Yovel (see the discussion in Bava Batra 122a). I did not retrieve that passage, so check it before relying on it.

I can also go through the Talmud's laws of Yovel, or how Yovel stopped being observed after the tribes were exiled, if you want either.

answer:
The ceremony is described in [Deuteronomy 27] and [Joshua 8:30-35], and the Mishnah fills in the details. The tribes stood on two mountains and responded "Amen" to blessings and curses recited by the Levites. Its basic purpose was to have Israel accept the covenant and the Torah's moral and religious obligations as soon as they entered the Land.

I could read the Mishnah, but the Sefaria server blocked my attempts to retrieve the verses of Deuteronomy and Joshua. I paraphrase those below from memory and don't quote them. Please check them in your own text.

## Key Takeaways
- Moses commanded the ceremony. Joshua carried it out after Israel crossed the Jordan and came to Shechem.
- Six tribes stood on Gerizim for the blessing and six on Ebal for the curse. The Levites and the Ark stood in the valley between them.
- The people answered "Amen" to each statement, which made each one a binding oath.
- Large stones were plastered and inscribed with the Torah, and an altar was built with offerings.
- The ceremony meant that Israel took on the covenant, with its blessing and curse, as a national and individual responsibility.

## 1. The ceremony

**The biblical outline** (paraphrased, not retrieved):
- Moses commanded that when Israel crossed the Jordan they should set up large plastered stones, write "all the words of this Torah" on them, and build an altar of uncut stones on Mount Ebal. They were to bring burnt offerings and peace offerings and rejoice there.
- The tribes were divided. Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph and Benjamin stood on Gerizim to bless. Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan and Naphtali stood on Ebal for the curse.
- The Levites declared a series of "Cursed be the one who…" statements, and all the people answered "Amen." These cover secret idolatry, dishonoring parents, moving a boundary marker, misleading the blind, perverting justice for the vulnerable, forbidden relations, secret murder, taking a bribe to kill, and a final curse on whoever does not uphold the words of this Torah.
- Joshua carried this out, as [Joshua 8:30-35] records. He built the altar on Ebal, wrote the Torah on stones, and read all the words of the Torah, "blessing and curse," before the whole assembly, including women, children and converts.

**The Mishnah's reconstruction** is in [Mishnah Sotah 7:5]:
- Six tribes went up to the top of Gerizim and six to the top of Ebal. "The priests and the Levites and the Ark are standing below in the middle." The priests surround the Ark, the Levites surround the priests, and the rest of Israel stand on either side.
- The Levites turned toward Gerizim and began with the blessing: "בָּרוּךְ הָאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר לֹא יַעֲשֶׂה פֶסֶל וּמַסֵּכָה" ("Blessed is the man who does not make a graven or molten image"). Both sides answered "Amen."
- They then turned toward Ebal and recited the matching curse, "אָרוּר הָאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר יַעֲשֶׂה פֶסֶל וּמַסֵּכָה" ("Cursed is the man who makes a graven or molten image"). Again both sides answered "Amen."
- They continued this way through all the blessings and curses.
- Afterward they built the altar, plastered it, and wrote the Torah on it "in seventy languages." The Mishnah derives this from the phrase "be'er heitev," "clearly elucidated." Then they took the stones and lodged at Gilgal.

Note that in the Mishnah each curse has a matching blessing for the same act. The verses in Deuteronomy 27 spell out only the curses.

## 2. Basic significance

These points are my explanation, not a quotation of any source.

- **Covenant ratification.** Israel enters the Land as a covenant people. Their "Amen" is an acceptance of the Torah's terms and an oath to uphold them. This is why the curses are phrased as individual acts, such as secret sins, that only the person himself and God know. Each person takes responsibility for them.
- **Two outcomes, one choice.** The same Levites, the same Ark and the same people stand between blessing and curse. This matches the choice Moses sets out in [Deuteronomy 11:26-32]: "blessing and curse," depending on whether Israel keeps the commandments. The Land is given with moral conditions attached.
- **Whole-nation responsibility.** All twelve tribes take part, split evenly between the two mountains, and Joshua stresses that women, children and converts were included. No tribe stands only on the side of blessing.
- **The Torah at the center.** The inscribed stones and the altar make the Torah and the service of God the foundation of life in the Land. The Mishnah's "seventy languages" reflects the idea that the Torah's message is meant for all humanity.

*Consult a teacher or a commentator such as Rashi or Ramban on Deuteronomy 27 for further depth.* I can look them up if you ask again.

answer:
I think your question was garbled in transmission, especially the ending ("released in a semi forum… seventh form of hearing"). I've answered the part I could follow and note below where I'm unsure. I couldn't retrieve Rashi or Ibn Ezra on this verse (the tool was rate-limited), so what follows is my own reading of the text and not a commentator's.

**Short answer:** Eliphaz's "six… seven" is a standard Hebrew numerical proverb. In it the "seventh" is not a new kind of affliction. It is the point at which harm finally stops: "in seven no harm will reach you." Eliphaz means this as a promise to Job if he accepts correction. Read against the book's opening, though, the list uncannily resembles what has already happened to Job.

## Key Takeaways
- Eliphaz holds that suffering is reproof and that the righteous are ultimately protected ([Job 5:17-19]).
- He does not know about the heavenly scene in Job 1–2, so his theology cannot account for Job.
- "Six… seven" is a literary device, not a literal count of seven afflictions.
- The troubles Eliphaz lists (famine, war, the tongue, violence) echo Job's actual losses, which gives the passage a dramatic irony.

## The text
[Job 5:17-19] reads: "See how happy is the person whom God reproves; do not reject the discipline of the Almighty… You will be delivered from six troubles; in seven no harm will reach you" (בְּשֵׁשׁ צָרוֹת יַצִּילֶךָּ וּבְשֶׁבַע לֹא־יִגַּע בְּךָ רָע). The next verses give examples: famine, war, "the scourging tongue" (שׁוֹט לָשׁוֹן), and violence (שֹׁד) ([Job 5:20-21]).

## Eliphaz's world
- Eliphaz argues from experience and from a night vision (Job 4). His principle is that suffering corrects the sinner and God rescues the one who accepts it.
- The reader has seen the prologue, where Job's suffering comes from a heavenly challenge and not from sin ([Job 1:8-12], [Job 2:3]). Eliphaz never learns this. In that sense he lives in a different world from Job.
- Your point about "the curse of Satan" fits the structure. In Hebrew the figure is *ha-satan*, "the accuser," who works under God's permission. Job's friends have no access to that frame.

## The "six and seven"
- The device (x, x+1) appears elsewhere, for example Proverbs 6:16 ("six things the Lord hates, seven are an abomination"). It signals completeness: however many troubles come, you will be saved.
- So "the seventh, which does not touch the person" is not a seventh type of suffering. It is the guarantee of safety, even at the extreme.

## The irony you may be pointing to
Several of Eliphaz's examples match Job's calamities in chapter 1:
- Famine and loss of livelihood: Job's oxen, donkeys, sheep and camels are taken.
- The sword: raiders kill his servants.
- Violence: the great wind kills his children.
- The tongue: his wife and friends later turn on him.

Eliphaz promises that Job will be spared these things. Job has already suffered them, even though he is righteous. Eliphaz's consolation therefore exposes the problem the book is about: the "seventh" protection did not come to a righteous man. That is probably the "indirect reference to the dilemma of Job" you describe.

## Where I need clarification
I can't tell what "released in a semi forum" and "the seventh form of hearing" mean. Do you mean:
1. whether Job is spared in the "seventh" case (the end of the book, where he is restored in [Job 42])?
2. whether "hearing" refers to Job 42:5 ("I had heard of You by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye has seen You")?
3. something else?
