answer:
Retry the failed ones.# The Ark of Words: Noah's Crazy Escape Plan

**Direct answer:** The Torah uses the word *teivah* (תֵּבָה) for Noah's ark. The only other place it appears is the basket that saved baby Moses. In Hebrew, *teivah* also means "word." A well-known Hasidic reading says the Flood is not only ancient history. It describes how a person survives a world that is drowning, and the way through is words: prayer and Torah.

## Key Takeaways
- The Torah introduces Noah by his deeds, not his children, because the real "offspring" of the righteous are their good deeds [Rashi on Genesis 6:9:1].
- The Flood came because the earth was filled with *chamas* (violence or lawlessness) [Genesis 6:11-13].
- *Teivah* means both "ark" and "word," and the Hasidic tradition builds on that double meaning.
- The ark had a *tzohar* (light). Rashi records two opinions on what it was [Rashi on Genesis 6:16:1].
- My own synthesis: you don't survive a flood by being a bigger fish. You survive by building a small, lit space of speech and deeds.

## The Pshat (Plain Meaning)

Right after "These are the generations of Noah," the Torah doesn't list his sons. It says "Noah was a righteous man." Rashi gives two readings of this. One is that mentioning a righteous person is itself a blessing. The other is that "the real progeny of righteous people are their good deeds" [Rashi on Genesis 6:9:1]. This is a midrash (Genesis Rabbah 30:6), not just plain meaning, but it shows the Torah's priorities. Noah's legacy is what he did.

The world around him was the opposite:

> וַתִּשָּׁחֵת הָאָרֶץ לִפְנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים וַתִּמָּלֵא הָאָרֶץ חָמָס
> "The earth became corrupt before God; the earth was filled with lawlessness." [Genesis 6:11-13]

The Torah says the earth was *filled* with *chamas*. The people had no room left for anything else.

## The Crazy Part: A Boat Made of Words

God tells Noah to build a *teivah*. In Hebrew that word also means "word." The only other *teivah* in the Torah is the basket of reeds that carried baby Moses on the Nile.

The Hasidic tradition, usually attributed to the Baal Shem Tov and developed by his students, reads God's command as "Enter the word." I haven't pulled the exact text here, so treat the attribution as a received tradition. Noah is told to step into the words of prayer and Torah and let them surround him. The Flood is any overwhelming force: noise, pressure, cynicism, chaos. The *teivah* is a protected space made of sacred speech. If you live inside the words, the waters rise around you but don't reach you.

## The Light Inside

God also says to put a *tzohar* in the ark. Rashi records two views: "Some say this was a window; others say that it was a precious stone that gave light to them" [Rashi on Genesis 6:16:1]. Both come from Genesis Rabbah 31:11.

The disagreement is interesting. Is the light something you let in from outside, a window? Or is it something you carry inside, a gem? When the world is flooded, you can do either: stay open to heaven, or become a source of light yourself.

## My Own Connection

*This is my own synthesis, not a quotation from a commentator.*

Put the three pieces together:

1. Noah's legacy is his deeds [Rashi on Genesis 6:9:1].
2. The generation's problem is *chamas*, a world of grabbing and violence [Genesis 6:11-13].
3. The solution is a *teivah*, a space of words, with a *tzohar*, a light.

Noah's generation was drowning in *taking*. The ark is a world of *containing*: every animal has its place, and everything is measured, ordered and fed. It is the opposite of *chamas*.

## The Challenge

Where is your flood right now: the news, your phone, work pressure? Can you build a small *teivah* in your day, even ten minutes of real words, whether prayer, learning or an honest conversation? Make sure it has a *tzohar*, something that lights up the dark. Noah didn't change the world around him, but he built something that carried life through it. That is where the world started again.

answer:
Rate-limited; retrying the failed ones.Jeremiah 15 and 16 are a continuous unit. In chapter 15, God says the decree of destruction is final, and Jeremiah complains about his own suffering. In chapter 16, God forbids Jeremiah to marry or to join mourning and feasting, because the nation's doom is certain. The chapter ends with a promise of a future redemption so great that it will overshadow the Exodus.

**Sources note:** The Sefaria tool was rate-limited. I could read the text of both chapters and Rashi on 16 and on 15:1–9 and 15:19. I could not retrieve Radak or Metzudat David, so I haven't attributed anything to them. Rashi's comments on 15:10–18 were cut off, so I haven't cited him there.

## Key Takeaways
- God tells Jeremiah that even Moses and Samuel could not save this generation, and Rashi explains why they could have saved earlier ones.
- Jeremiah's lament (15:10–18) shows a prophet who is isolated and resentful. God answers by telling him to repent and promising to make him a bronze wall.
- In chapter 16, Jeremiah's celibacy and his avoiding mourning and feasting are signs of the coming devastation.
- Rashi reads "I have gathered in My peace" as God withdrawing the kindness He gave Israel because of Abraham.
- Chapter 16 ends with the promise that the future ingathering will overshadow the Exodus, and that the nations will admit their idols were worthless.

## Chapter 15

**Verses 1–9: the decree is final.**
- *Pshat:* God says, "אִם־יַעֲמֹד מֹשֶׁה וּשְׁמוּאֵל לְפָנַי אֵין נַפְשִׁי אֶל־הָעָם הַזֶּה" ("Even if Moses and Samuel were to intercede with Me, I would not be won over to that people") [Jeremiah 15:1].
- The people will meet one of four fates: death, sword, famine, or captivity. Four "kinds" of agents (sword, dogs, birds, beasts) will carry out the punishment (15:2–3). The cause is named as Manasseh's acts in Jerusalem (15:4).
- Rashi explains the choice of Moses and Samuel. Both first brought Israel back to the right path and only then prayed for them. Moses did this at the golden calf, with "שִׂימוּ אִישׁ חַרְבּוֹ" and then "אֶעֱלֶה אֶל ה׳ אוּלַי אֲכַפְּרָה." Samuel did it at Mizpah, where the people removed the Baalim before he prayed. Jeremiah cannot bring this generation back, so he is told not to pray for them [Rashi on Jeremiah 15:1].
- On "לַמָּוֶת… לַחֶרֶב… לָרָעָב… לַשֶּׁבִי," Rashi says each item is harsher than the one before. Famine is worse than the sword, and captivity contains all of them [Rashi on Jeremiah 15:2].
- On "נִלְאֵיתִי הִנָּחֵם" ("I cannot relent"), Rashi says God had planned destruction many times and relented. Now He is "weary of relenting" [Rashi on Jeremiah 15:6].
- On "אֻמְלְלָה יוֹלֶדֶת הַשִּׁבְעָה" ("She who bore seven is forlorn"), Rashi gives two readings. In the first, from Gittin 88a, it is Samaria and the Ten Tribes, from whom seven dynasties of kings arose. The "remnant" is then Judah and part of Benjamin. In the second, from Midrash Tanchuma, it is Jerusalem and seven wicked kings [Rashi on Jeremiah 15:9]. Note that the first reading is from the Talmud and the second is midrashic, and neither is simple *pshat*.

**Verses 10–18: Jeremiah's complaint.**
- *Pshat:* Jeremiah says, "אוֹי־לִי אִמִּי כִּי יְלִדְתָּנִי אִישׁ רִיב וְאִישׁ מָדוֹן" ("Woe is me, my mother, that you ever bore me, a man of conflict and strife"). He has not lent or borrowed, yet everyone curses him [Jeremiah 15:10].
- Rashi says Jeremiah is lamenting about himself. His townspeople hated him because of his rebukes [Rashi on Jeremiah 15:10].
- Jeremiah then asks God to avenge him and says God's words were "joy and delight" when he first took them in. He sat alone, not with revelers, "because of Your hand upon me." His pain is endless, and he accuses God of being "like a spring that fails" (15:15–18).

**Verses 19–21: God's answer.**
- God replies: "אִם־תָּשׁוּב וַאֲשִׁיבְךָ לְפָנַי תַּעֲמֹד וְאִם־תּוֹצִיא יָקָר מִזּוֹלֵל כְּפִי תִהְיֶה." ("If you turn back, I shall take you back and you shall stand before Me. If you produce what is noble out of the worthless, you shall be My spokesman.") [Jeremiah 15:19].
- Rashi says the "turning back" is Israel's return through Jeremiah. "Precious from vile" means bringing a decent person back from wickedness. "You shall be as My mouth" means God decrees and Jeremiah annuls, a Talmudic reading from Bava Metzia 85a. "Let them return to you, but you shall not return to them" means Jeremiah must not be drawn after the people [Rashi on Jeremiah 15:19].
- The chapter ends with God promising to make Jeremiah a bronze wall that his attackers cannot overcome (15:20–21).

## Chapter 16

**Verses 1–9: Jeremiah's life as a sign.**
- Jeremiah may not marry or have children "in this place." Children born there will die gruesome deaths and go unburied (16:2–4).
- He may not enter a house of mourning or a house of feasting (16:5–9). Rashi reads *beit marzeach* as either a feast, citing Sifrei, or, in the Rabbis' reading, a house of mourning (the Rabbis' source is Ketubot 69b).
- God says, "כִּי־אָסַפְתִּי אֶת־שְׁלוֹמִי… אֶת־הַחֶסֶד וְאֶת־הָרַחֲמִים" ("I have withdrawn My favor… My kindness and compassion") [Jeremiah 16:5]. Rashi connects the kindness to Abraham. When Abraham did "tzedakah and mishpat," God gave his descendants kindness and mercy. They turned justice to wormwood, so God took His kindness back [Rashi on Jeremiah 16:5].
- Rashi explains why Jeremiah should not go to mourn: "Since all will die, why should you lament?" He also explains the mourning customs in the verses. Gashing and tonsure are forbidden to Jews and are mentioned only as examples of mourning. "Break [bread]" refers to the mourners' meal in the town square, with the *hamotzi* blessing [Rashi on Jeremiah 16:6–7].
- Verse 9 says God will end the "voice of the bridegroom and bride." Rashi says this is the reason for the earlier prohibition on feasts [Rashi on Jeremiah 16:8].

**Verses 10–13: why it is happening.**
- The people will ask, "What is our sin?" The answer is that their ancestors abandoned God and worshipped other gods, and the current generation is worse, following "the willfulness of their evil heart" [Jeremiah 16:10–12].
- Therefore they will be hurled to a land they do not know, where they will serve other gods day and night (16:13). Rashi cites Targum Jonathan, which reads this as serving nations that worship idols [Rashi on Jeremiah 16:13].

**Verses 14–15: the redemption.**
- God says people will no longer swear "by the God who brought Israel out of Egypt" but "by the God who brought them from the northland and all the lands" [Jeremiah 16:14–15].
- Rashi begins his comment with *lachen*, which he reads as an oath. Even though Israel betrayed God, He swears He will redeem them. He cites the Rabbis (Berakhot 12b) that this does not cancel the Exodus. The final redemption becomes primary and the Exodus secondary [Rashi on Jeremiah 16:14].

**Verses 16–18: fishermen and hunters.**
- God will send "fishermen" and then "hunters" to catch the people out of the mountains and rock clefts. Their sins are not hidden from Him, and they will be repaid "doubly" (16:16–18).
- Rashi reads the fishing image this way. Fishermen take the fish from where it was raised, and a caught fish dies. So enemies will first capture Israel in the city and kill them. The hunters afterward will pursue those who fled to the hills in order to exile them. On "doubly," he says they repeated the sins of their ancestors [Rashi on Jeremiah 16:16–18].

**Verses 19–21: the nations' confession.**
- Jeremiah calls God "my strength and stronghold and refuge." Nations will come to Him from the ends of the earth and say, "Our ancestors inherited only delusion," and "Can mortals make gods for themselves? No-gods are they!" (16:19–20).
- Rashi connects this to the end of days, when the nations will serve God "with one accord." He compares Zephaniah 3:9 and says they will be astonished at how Israel made gods that are not gods [Rashi on Jeremiah 16:19].
- God ends by saying He will make them know His power and "that My name is GOD" (16:21).

If you'd like Radak or Metzudat David on specific verses, such as Jeremiah's complaint in 15:10–18, ask again and I'll try to fetch them.

answer:
**Parshat Lech Lecha** ([Genesis 12:1–17:27](Genesis 12:1-17:27)) tells how God calls Abram to leave his homeland for Canaan. It follows him through famine, war, and the covenants God makes with him. It ends with the birth of Ishmael and the commandment of circumcision. I'm summarizing from my knowledge of the text and didn't look up any sources for this answer.

## Key Takeaways
- God commands Abram to leave his land and promises him a great nation, blessing, and the Land ([Genesis 12:1-3]).
- Abram's journeys include a famine, a descent to Egypt, and a separation from Lot.
- The Covenant Between the Parts ([Genesis 15]) promises descendants and the Land, and foretells exile.
- Sarai gives Hagar to Abram, and Ishmael is born ([Genesis 16]).
- God changes the names to Abraham and Sarah and commands *brit milah* (circumcision) ([Genesis 17]).

## Summary by chapter

**Chapter 12: The call and the journey**
- God says: "לֶךְ־לְךָ מֵאַרְצְךָ וּמִמּוֹלַדְתְּךָ וּמִבֵּית אָבִיךָ" ("Go forth from your land, your birthplace, and your father's house"). He promises, "וְאֶעֶשְׂךָ לְגוֹי גָּדוֹל" ("I will make you a great nation") ([Genesis 12:1-2]).
- Abram, aged 75, leaves with Sarai, Lot, and their household. He arrives in Shechem, where God promises the Land to his offspring, and he builds altars.
- A famine drives him to Egypt. He asks Sarai to say she is his sister. Pharaoh takes her, but God afflicts Pharaoh's house with plagues, and Pharaoh sends them away with wealth.

**Chapter 13: Separation from Lot**
- Their herdsmen quarrel because their flocks have grown too large. Lot chooses the well-watered Jordan plain and settles near Sodom, whose people are wicked.
- God reaffirms the promise of the Land and of countless descendants.

**Chapter 14: The war of the kings**
- Four kings defeat five, including Sodom's, and capture Lot.
- Abram pursues them with 318 men and rescues Lot.
- Malki-Tzedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, blesses Abram. Abram gives him a tenth and refuses any spoils from the king of Sodom.

**Chapter 15: Covenant Between the Parts (*Brit bein HaBetarim*)**
- Abram worries that he has no child. God promises descendants as numerous as the stars. The verse says: "וְהֶאֱמִן בַּה' וַיַּחְשְׁבֶהָ לּוֹ צְדָקָה" ("He believed in the LORD, and He reckoned it to him as righteousness") ([Genesis 15:6]).
- In a covenant ceremony with split animals, God foretells that Abram's descendants will be strangers in a foreign land for 400 years. After that they will leave with great wealth and inherit the Land.

**Chapter 16: Hagar and Ishmael**
- Sarai is childless and gives her maidservant Hagar to Abram. When Hagar conceives, tension arises, and Hagar flees.
- An angel tells her to return, and says her son will be named Ishmael.

**Chapter 17: Names and circumcision**
- When Abram is 99, God appears as *El Shaddai* and changes his name to Abraham, "father of a multitude of nations". Sarai becomes Sarah.
- God commands circumcision of every male on the eighth day as the sign of the covenant.
- God promises that Sarah will bear Isaac within a year. Abraham laughs, and he circumcises himself and his household.

## Themes to explore
- **Faith and trust:** Abram goes without knowing the destination. The text says only "to the land that I will show you."
- **The Land:** The promise is repeated several times, and the Land is tied to the covenant.
- **Tests:** Rashi, following the midrash, counts the tests of Abraham. The commentators differ on how to count them, so I can look up their views if you'd like.

answer:
Ben-deker (*Ben-Deker*, בֶּן־דֶּקֶר) was not the treasurer of Solomon's Temple. The Tanakh describes him as one of Solomon's twelve district officers, and the Temple treasury isn't linked to him anywhere I know of.

## Key Takeaways
- Ben-deker appears only once, in the list of Solomon's district governors in [I Kings 4:9].
- His job was to provision the royal court from his district, not to manage Temple funds.
- His district covered towns in the western lowlands and the Dan/Judah border region.
- The Tanakh gives us no personal details about him, only his title and territory.

## What the text says
[I Kings 4:7] begins the list by saying Solomon had twelve officers (*nitzavim*) over all Israel, and that each one supplied the king and his household for one month of the year. Ben-deker is the third name in the list:

> בֶּן־דֶּקֶר בְּמָקַץ וּבְשַׁעַלְבִים וּבֵית שֶׁמֶשׁ וְאֵילוֹן בֵּית חָנָן
> "Ben-deker, in Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh, and Elon-beth-hanan." [I Kings 4:9]

His role was to collect provisions from those towns and send them to Solomon's court for his assigned month. This is a tax and supply role, not a Temple role. "Ben-deker" may be a patronymic ("son of Deker"), which is why he is listed without a personal name. That is my observation, not something the verse says.

## Where the "treasurer" idea may come from
- **Other officials:** Solomon's cabinet is listed in [I Kings 4:1-6]. It includes Azariah son of Zadok the priest, and Adoniram son of Abda, who was "over the forced labor." Neither of them is called a Temple treasurer either.
- **Temple treasuries:** The Temple's storehouses (*otzrot beit Hashem*) are mentioned elsewhere, for example in [I Kings 7:51]. Ben-deker is not named in connection with them.
- **A different name:** The name *Bidkar* (בִּדְקַר), Jehu's officer in [II Kings 9:25], sounds similar. He lived about a century later and is unrelated.

If you saw "Ben-deker, treasurer of the Temple" in a particular book, website, or game, tell me which one. It may be a later tradition or a fictional adaptation, and I can help you check it. I can also read the other district officers in [I Kings 4] with you, along with the commentators on this passage.

answer:
**Parashat Noach in brief:** God sees a world filled with *chamas* (violence and corruption). He tells Noah, the one righteous man, to build an ark, and a flood destroys everything else. Afterward God makes a covenant with Noah, and the Tower of Babel and the genealogy leading to Avraham follow. I could not retrieve the Aish Kodesh text, so I can't quote him on this parasha. I can give only a general sketch of his approach, which you should check against the book.

## Key Takeaways
- Noach is the story of a world corrupted, a flood, and a new beginning with a covenant.
- Noah is called "righteous and blameless in his generations", and the sages debate whether that is praise or faint praise.
- The Aish Kodesh is the Torah of Rabbi Kalonymus Kalman Shapira of Piaseczno, delivered in the Warsaw Ghetto from 1939 to 1942.
- His sermons were written under catastrophe, so the Flood, suffering and renewal were not abstract topics for him.
- Sefaria's servers were overloaded, so I could not retrieve his actual words. Please don't treat what follows as a quotation from him.

## Summary of the parasha

**1. Noah and the corrupt generation ([Genesis 6:9]).**
The Torah says: "אֵלֶּה תּוֹלְדֹת נֹחַ נֹחַ אִישׁ צַדִּיק תָּמִים הָיָה בְּדֹרֹתָיו אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים הִתְהַלֶּךְ־נֹחַ". In the JPS translation: "This is the line of Noah.—Noah was a righteous man; he was blameless in his age; Noah walked with God."

The earth is full of *chamas*. God tells Noah to build a *teivah* (ark) and to bring in his family and pairs of animals.

**2. The Flood (chapters 7–8).**
The waters rise and everything that lives on dry land dies. The ark rests on the mountains of Ararat. Noah sends out a raven and then a dove, and the dove returns with an olive leaf. Noah then leaves the ark.

**3. Covenant (chapters 8–9).**
Noah offers sacrifices. God promises never to bring a flood on the whole earth again, and the rainbow is the sign of that promise. Human beings are permitted to eat meat, with limits, and murder is prohibited. These commandments are the basis of the Noahide laws.

**4. After the Flood (9:18–11:32).**
Noah plants a vineyard, becomes drunk, and an incident with his sons follows. Next come the Tower of Babel and the dispersal of the nations. The parasha ends with the genealogy from Shem to Terach and Avram.

## The Aish Kodesh

His approach is known from the book. He gave these talks on Shabbat in the ghetto and buried the manuscripts in a milk can. He doesn't offer comfort that avoids the suffering. He asks how a person can remain close to God inside the pain, and he teaches that God also suffers with Israel. Those are the themes his readers would expect in a Flood parasha. I can't say which verse or Rashi he builds them on, and I don't want to invent that.

If you'd like, ask me again in a few minutes. I can retry the Sefaria lookup and bring his actual teaching on Noach, with exact references. If you have the text, you can also paste his passage here and we can study it together.

answer:
The mitzvah of *yibum* (levirate marriage) is stated in **Parashat Ki Teitzei**, in the Book of Deuteronomy: [Deuteronomy 25:5-10]. The same passage also gives the related law of *chalitzah* (the ceremony that releases the widow from the brother-in-law).

I couldn't retrieve the text from Sefaria just now because of a technical error. What follows is from memory, so please check it against the verses.

## Key Takeaways
- The source is Deuteronomy 25:5-10, in Parashat Ki Teitzei.
- The law applies when brothers lived together and one died childless.
- The widow may not marry outside the family. Her husband's brother is to marry her.
- If he declines, the *chalitzah* ceremony in verses 7-10 releases her.
- The first-born son is to carry on the dead brother's name (v. 6).

## The passage
**Verse 5** gives the case and the command. When brothers dwell together and one dies without a son, his widow shall not marry "a strange man" outside the family. Her *yavam* (brother-in-law) shall "come upon her", take her as a wife, and perform *yibum*. The verb *yabem* is the source of the term *yibum*.

**Verse 6** says that the first-born son she bears will "stand upon the name" of the dead brother, so that his name is not erased from Israel.

**Verses 7-10** cover the case where the brother refuses. The widow goes to the elders at the gate. If he still refuses, she removes his shoe and spits before him, and she declares what he has done. His family is then known as "the house of the one whose shoe was removed". This is *chalitzah*.

## Related sources
- The Talmud's main discussion is in tractate *Yevamot*, which is named for this mitzvah.
- Another passage touching on the theme is the story of Judah and Tamar in Genesis 38, which is a precedent for it.
- The Book of Ruth is connected to the theme through Boaz's redemption of the family property and Ruth's marriage.
- In practice, the Ashkenazi ruling is that *chalitzah* is preferred over *yibum*. Many Sephardi communities historically followed the opposite preference. If this is a real situation, consult your rabbi.

I can pull up Rashi, Ramban, or the Talmud's derivation in *Yevamot* if you'd like.

answer:
Genesis 1 describes light on Day 1 and the sun, moon and stars on Day 4. The Torah doesn't state a reason for this order, so the answer comes from the commentators. The main approaches are that the first light was a different kind of light, that God is the source of light and not the sun, and that the sun's job is to mark time.

**Note:** The Sefaria library wouldn't load for me just now, so I'm working from memory and have not re-checked the texts. I'm quoting only the verses I'm sure of. Please verify the commentators' wording before relying on it.

## Key Takeaways
- The Torah gives light on Day 1 [Genesis 1:3] and the luminaries on Day 4 [Genesis 1:14-19], without saying why.
- The Day 4 luminaries are given a specific job: to separate day from night, and to serve as signs for seasons, days and years.
- The rabbis (Chagigah 12a, Bereshit Rabbah) understood the Day 1 light as special, and they say it was stored away for the righteous.
- A more philosophical reading is that light comes from God, so the sun is a tool and not the source.
- These are interpretations, and the *pshat* (plain meaning) is more modest than the midrashic ones.

## Pshat: what the verses say
- On Day 1, "יְהִי אוֹר וַיְהִי אוֹר", "Let there be light, and there was light" [Genesis 1:3]. God then separates light from darkness and names them Day and Night.
- On Day 4, God says "יְהִי מְאֹרֹת בִּרְקִיעַ הַשָּׁמַיִם לְהַבְדִּיל בֵּין הַיּוֹם וּבֵין הַלָּיְלָה", "Let there be lights in the firmament of the heavens to separate between the day and the night" [Genesis 1:14].
- Day 1 creates light itself, and day and night already exist. Day 4 creates the *me'orot* (luminaries), whose role is to carry that light and to regulate time, seasons and signs.
- So the text can be read as light first, then the objects that carry it. The Torah doesn't say how Day 1's light worked before the sun existed.

## Classic interpretive approaches

**1. A special, hidden light (rabbinic tradition).**
- The Talmud [Chagigah 12a] and Bereshit Rabbah teach that the Day 1 light was extraordinary.
- The tradition is that with it one could see from one end of the world to the other. God then concealed it for the righteous in the World to Come.
- Rashi, on Genesis 1:4, brings this idea, as I recall.
- This is *drash* (homiletical interpretation), not pshat. It answers the question by saying the first light was not the sun's light at all.

**2. God, not the sun, is the source of light.**
- Many readers, in the philosophical and homiletical tradition, see the order as a theological statement.
- The sun and moon were worshipped in the ancient world. By creating light first, the Torah shows they are not the source of light or life. They are created things, placed in the sky to serve.
- This is a common explanation, but I haven't verified which commentator says it, so treat it as a general reading and not an attribution.

**3. Light and its vehicles are different things.**
- Some commentators read Day 1 as the creation of light itself, as an energy or a phenomenon. On this reading, Day 4 sets it in specific bodies with specific functions: marking days, seasons and years.
- The point is that the sun's purpose is to serve time-keeping. That also matters for the Jewish calendar, since the moon sets the months.

## Is there tension with science?
Yes, if you read it literally, and the same tension exists between the sun and the plants of Day 3. Jewish tradition has never required one reading, and the commentators above show different ways to approach it. If you'd like, I can look up the actual texts of Rashi, Ramban and others once the library is working again.

answer:
The verse is [Genesis 12:5]. I couldn't retrieve its text from Sefaria, so I'm not quoting it. I did read Rashi and Onkelos. There are two classic readings. The plain sense is that these were servants Avram and Sarai had acquired. The midrashic reading is that they were people Avram and Sarai brought to faith in God.

## Key Takeaways
- The Hebrew phrase is literally "the souls that they *made* in Haran." The verb is *asu* (עָשׂוּ), not "bought."
- Rashi gives the *pshat* (plain sense): the phrase means servants, male and female, that they acquired.
- Rashi also brings the midrash: Avraham converted the men, Sarah converted the women, and the verse credits them as if they had "made" them.
- Onkelos translates the phrase as people "who were subjected to the Torah" in Haran. That puts him with the conversion reading.

## Pshat: servants and household
Rashi says "the real sense of the text is that it refers to the men-servants and to the maidservants whom they had acquired for themselves." He supports this from other uses of the verb *asah* (עשה) for gaining wealth:
- "he has acquired (*asah*) all this wealth," from [Genesis 31:1].
- "And Israel acquires (*oseh*) wealth," from [Numbers 24:18].

He calls it "an expression for acquiring and amassing." *Nefesh* (נפש, "soul") often means a person, as in "seventy souls." So "souls acquired" means people who came into their household. This fits the verse's context: Avram is leaving with his family and his property. [Rashi on Genesis 12:5]

## Drash: "making" souls through conversion
The midrash is in Genesis Rabbah 39:14, as Rashi cites it. Rashi says the phrase means "The souls which he had brought beneath the sheltering wings of the Shechinah. Abraham converted the men and Sarah converted the women, and Scripture accounts it unto them as if they had made them."

- This reads *asu* as "made." The idea is that someone who brings another person to God has, in a sense, created that person anew.
- This is a midrashic reading. It isn't the plain meaning, and Rashi labels it separately from the *pshat*.
- **Onkelos** reflects this tradition. He translates the phrase as "the souls that they had made [converted] in Charan" (my wording of the Sefaria translation). The Aramaic is *nafshata de-shaabidu le-oraita* (נַפְשָׁתָא דְּשַׁעְבִּידוּ לְאוֹרַיְתָא), "souls they subjected to the Torah." [Onkelos Genesis 12:5]

## How the two fit
The two readings aren't necessarily opposed. Many people read them together: the household members were acquired as servants and also became Avraham's followers. Rashi, though, presents them as two separate explanations. The *pshat* is about acquisition. The midrash makes the verse a statement about Avraham and Sarah as the first to spread belief in one God.

I didn't retrieve other commentators such as Ramban, so I can't say how they treat the verse.

answer:
**Genesis 1:1 says that God is the source of all that exists.** The plain sense is that the heavens and the earth came into being through God's act of creation. Commentators disagree on the grammar, and that disagreement affects the meaning. One reading is "In the beginning, God created." The other is "When God began to create…"

## Key Takeaways
- The verse opens the Torah by presenting God as Creator of "heaven and earth," meaning the whole ordered world.
- The word *bereshit* (בְּרֵאשִׁית, "in the beginning") can be read as an absolute or as a construct ("in the beginning of…"). Ibn Ezra and the JPS translation take the construct reading.
- Ramban calls creation the root of faith. He also says its deeper details are a mystery learned through tradition.
- Rashi, as Ramban cites him, says the Torah opens with creation to affirm that the whole world belongs to God, who gives each land to whom He wishes.
- Rabbi Yitzchak's midrash, which Ramban quotes, ties creation to Israel's claim to the Land.

## The verse (pshat)
> בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים אֵת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֵת הָאָרֶץ
> "When God began to create heaven and earth—" [Genesis 1:1] (Sefaria's JPS translation)

The words break down like this:
- *Bereshit* comes from the root ראש (*rosh*, "head" or "first"). It means "at the beginning."
- *Bara* (בָּרָא, "created") is used in the Torah only with God as its subject. The root can mean to bring something into being or to form it.
- *Elohim* (אֱלֹהִים) is a name of God that denotes might and judgment.
- "The heavens and the earth" is a Hebrew way of saying "everything," the whole cosmos.

The JPS translation quoted above reads verse 1 as a subordinate clause: "When God began to create… the earth being unformed and void… God said, 'Let there be light.'" The traditional rendering is "In the beginning God created heaven and earth." Both translations are grammatically defensible.

## Ibn Ezra on the grammar
Ibn Ezra surveys several views of the word *bereshit* [Ibn Ezra on Genesis 1:1:1]:
- Some say the *bet* (בּ) is superfluous, like the one in *ba-rishonah*. Ibn Ezra objects that the vowel would then be a long *kamatz*.
- Others say it means "in the beginning of the evening or night or darkness." Ibn Ezra objects with the verse "And he chose a first part for himself" (Deuteronomy 33:21).
- Others say the *bet* is a plain preposition. On this view the Torah is ruling out the idea that heaven and earth had no beginning.
- Ibn Ezra's own view is that *bereshit* is in the construct state, as in "In the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim" (Jeremiah 26:1). He compares verbs that follow a construct noun, such as Hosea 1:2.

## Ramban: why does the Torah begin here?
Ramban quotes Rashi's comment, which builds on Rabbi Yitzchak. A book of laws should have started with the first commandment, "This month shall be for you…" (Exodus 12:2). The Torah starts with creation so that, if the nations call Israel robbers for taking the Land of Canaan, Israel can answer: "The whole world belongs to the Holy One, blessed be He. He gave it to whom He pleased… and gave it to us." [Ramban on Genesis 1:1:1]

I couldn't retrieve Rashi's own text just now, so I'm relying on Ramban's quotation of it. Ramban then raises an objection. Creation is "the root of faith," and someone who believes the world is eternal "has no Torah at all." He answers that the process of creation is "a deep mystery" that is not fully understood from the verses. It is known through tradition going back to Moses. On Ramban's account, the Torah therefore tells the story mainly to show a pattern: lands are held on condition of conduct.

## Layers beyond pshat
- **Midrash.** Rabbi Yitzchak's reading is *aggadic* (homiletic), not a plain-sense claim about the grammar. Ramban says as much when he calls it "a homiletic exposition."
- **Faith.** In Ramban's view, the verse affirms that the world has a beginning and a Creator. He treats this as foundational.
- **Kabbalah.** Ramban hints that creation has hidden depths. I haven't laid out those teachings here.

I can go further into Rashi's own comment, Bereshit Rabbah, or the "creation from nothing" question if you'd like.

answer:
Let me retry.I couldn't retrieve the texts from Sefaria just now (the service was rate-limiting me). What follows comes from my own knowledge of these sources, and I haven't checked the wording against the texts. I paraphrase the commentators and don't quote them.

**Short answer:** The plain text of Genesis 1 doesn't say that water was created first. Verse 1 says God created "the heavens and the earth," and verse 2 then describes water already present. Because of this, the commentators split on the question. Rashi says the verses don't give the order of creation, and he reads verse 1 as an introduction. Ramban and others hold that the first matter was created before the heavens and earth took their final form.

## Key Takeaways
- Verse 2 mentions water ("the face of the deep," "the face of the waters") without saying when it was created.
- Rashi says the Torah doesn't teach chronological order here, so "water first" isn't a settled reading.
- Rashi cites the proof that water isn't described as created before the heavens: the heavens are made from fire and water, so the water was already there.
- Ramban says God first created a primordial substance, and the heavens and earth were formed from it.
- Midrash and the *Tosafot* tradition also discuss the question, and the rabbis don't agree on what was created first.

## The text
[Genesis 1:1-2] reads: "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. And the earth was *tohu va-vohu* (formless and void), and darkness was on the face of the deep, and the spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters."

The difficulty is that verse 1 seems to describe the whole creation, yet verse 2 begins with the earth already unformed and with water already present. The Torah never says "God created the water." The verb *bara* (created) isn't used for water anywhere in the chapter. On the second day, God separates the waters.

## The main approaches
**Rashi** ([Rashi on Genesis 1:1:1]): As I remember it, Rashi says the verse is not teaching the order of creation. If it were, it would say *barishonah* ("at first"). He says the word *bereshit* is in the construct form, so the verse means "In the beginning of God's creating the heavens and the earth, when the earth was formless…" On this reading, water and the formless earth were part of the opening state, and the Torah isn't saying they came before or after the heavens. Rashi also notes that the verses don't give a clear order, since the Torah doesn't say whether heaven or earth came first.

**Ibn Ezra** ([Ibn Ezra on Genesis 1:2:1]): I recall that he, too, treats verse 2 as describing the first condition of matter, and that he reads the water as already existing as part of that matter. I haven't verified his exact wording, so treat this as approximate.

**Ramban** ([Ramban on Genesis 1:1:2]): As I remember it, Ramban reads verse 1 as the creation of a primordial substance from nothing (*yesh me-ayin*). He says everything else was formed from that substance, with water among the earliest forms. This reading puts water before the final heavens and earth.

**Midrash:** [Bereshit Rabbah 1] discusses the order of creation and the role of water. The midrash says, for example, that the heavens and earth were created first, and it also records views that the earth, or water and fire, came earlier. I haven't verified the details here.

## Summary of the debate
- **Water first:** supported by verse 2 and by the view that the heavens and earth were formed from a primordial substance.
- **Heavens and earth first:** supported by the plain order of verse 1, with verse 2 describing a later state.
- **No order stated:** Rashi's approach, since the Torah is not giving a chronology here.

answer:
The standard tradition counts 304,805 letters in the Torah (some say 304,807). The word count is usually given as about 79,976 (some sources say 79,847), and there are 5,845 verses (the common figure is 5,845, though 5,888 also appears in some sources). I'm giving these from memory and haven't checked them against Sefaria. The exact figures vary by source because of differences in spelling and in counting.

## Key Takeaways

- The commonly cited letter count of the Torah is 304,805. Another count is 304,807.
- The word count is commonly given as 79,976, though a few sources give other figures.
- The verse count is usually 5,845.
- The differences come from *ḥaser* and *malei* (defective and full) spellings. Because of these, no count is perfectly fixed.
- Any statement of a fixed count is a tradition, not something I can verify in a specific text.

## Background

**Counting by the *Soferim*.** The Talmud says that the early scholars were called *Soferim* (counters) because they counted all the letters of the Torah [Kiddushin 30a]. The Gemara there mentions that the middle letter of the Torah is the *vav* in *gachon* (גחון), in [Leviticus 11:42]. It also says the middle verse is [Leviticus 13:33], and the middle word is *darosh darash* (דרש דרש) in [Leviticus 10:16]. I haven't re-read the passage here, so check the text if you need the exact wording.

**Why the numbers differ.** Torah scrolls differ in a few words that can be written fully (*malei*) or defectively (*ḥaser*), such as with or without a *vav* or *yod*. Each such difference changes the letter count slightly. Because of this, the Talmud notes that "we are not experts" in *ḥaser* and *malei* [Kiddushin 30a]. In practice, the commonly cited letter total is the tradition's rough figure. Do not treat it as exact.

**In practice.** A scribe (*sofer*) does not rely on these totals to check a scroll. He follows the established text, such as the Masoretic tradition and the *Tikkun Soferim*.

If you'd like, I can look up the Kiddushin 30a passage in full, or the Masoretic notes on the middle of the Torah.

answer:
The idea of an eternal covenant (*brit olam*) between God and Israel runs through the whole Tanakh. It is not in one place. The main passages are the covenant with Abraham, the Sabbath, the Sinai covenant and the prophets' promises. The Talmud builds on these but doesn't have one passage devoted to the theme. The Sefaria lookup failed (rate limit) while I was writing this, so I'm working from memory. I paraphrase below and don't quote word for word, so check the verses yourself.

## Key Takeaways
- The covenant with Abraham, including circumcision, is called a *brit olam* in [Genesis 17:7] and [Genesis 17:13].
- The Sabbath is called a *brit olam* between God and the children of Israel in [Exodus 31:16-17].
- Leviticus and the prophets say God will not break the covenant even when Israel sins: [Leviticus 26:44-45], [Jeremiah 31:34-36], [Isaiah 54:10] and [Ezekiel 37:26].
- The Talmud takes this up in other places, for example in discussions of Israel's acceptance of the Torah at Sinai ([Shabbat 88a]) and of Israel's enduring chosenness.

## Tanakh sources

**The Abrahamic covenant.** [Genesis 17:7-13] says God will establish His covenant with Abraham and his descendants as a *brit olam*, an everlasting covenant, to be God to them. The flesh covenant of circumcision is also called a *brit olam*. [Psalms 105:8-10] and [1 Chronicles 16:15-17] recall this covenant as one God remembers forever.

**The Sabbath.** [Exodus 31:16-17] says Israel shall keep the Sabbath "as an everlasting covenant" (*brit olam*). It is "a sign forever" between God and Israel.

**The covenant survives Israel's failures.** [Leviticus 26:44-45] says that even when Israel is in exile, God will not reject them so completely as to break His covenant. He will remember the covenant with their ancestors.

**The prophets.**
- [Jeremiah 31:30-36] (in some editions 31:31-35) speaks of a new covenant with the Torah written on the heart. It then compares the permanence of Israel to the fixed order of sun, moon and stars.
- [Isaiah 54:10] says the mountains may move, but God's kindness and "covenant of peace" will not.
- [Isaiah 59:21] and [Isaiah 55:3] speak of an everlasting covenant.
- [Ezekiel 37:26] promises a "covenant of peace," an everlasting covenant, after the restoration.

**Other verses.** Priestly and Davidic everlasting covenants also appear, in [Numbers 25:12-13] (Pinchas) and [2 Samuel 23:5], but those concern specific families.

## Talmud and Midrash
The Talmud doesn't use a single "eternal covenant" passage, but several discussions bear on it:
- [Shabbat 88a] discusses Israel's acceptance of the Torah at Sinai, including the teaching that God held the mountain over them "like a barrel." Rava says they re-accepted the Torah willingly in the days of Ahasuerus. The passage is about how binding the covenant is.
- [Sanhedrin 44a] says "Israel, though they have sinned, are still Israel." Rashi and others use it to show that sin doesn't dissolve the covenant.
- [Mishneh Torah, Laws of Repentance 3:5], Maimonides' code, rules on Israel's status and on those who deny the covenant. It is a later halachic source, not Talmud.

## Interpretive differences
- **Plain reading:** the verses describe a covenant that is permanent on God's side and lasts for all generations.
- **"New covenant" in Jeremiah:** Jewish commentators generally read it as God renewing and internalizing the same Torah. It is not a replacement covenant. This is the mainstream Jewish reading, and some other traditions read it differently.

If you tell me whether you're interested in the covenant's permanence, its conditions or its relationship to the nations, I can look up specific commentators such as Rashi, Ramban and Radak on these verses.

answer:
# The Torah Opens with a Legal Defense

**Direct answer:** The "craziest" thing about Bereshit is Rashi's first question. Why does the Torah start here at all? Rashi, quoting Rabbi Yitzchak, says a book of law should have opened with the first commandment. Creation is there as a courtroom defense: it is the title deed to the Land of Israel. (The framing as a "crazy" dvar Torah is mine. The sources are real.)

## Key Takeaways
- Rashi's opening comment asks why the Torah begins with Creation instead of with the first mitzvah.
- His answer, from Rabbi Yitzchak, is that Creation establishes God's ownership of the whole earth, and so Israel's right to the Land.
- Genesis 1:1–2 begins "mid-sentence" with a world of chaos, which suggests creation is a beginning and not a finished product. This second point is my own reading.
- The two ideas combine: the world is God's property, but it is handed over unfinished and given to us to work with.

## The question: why Bereshit?
[Rashi on Genesis 1:1:1] opens with Rabbi Yitzchak: "לֹא הָיָה צָרִיךְ לְהַתְחִיל אֶת הַתּוֹרָה אֶלָּא מֵהַחֹדֶשׁ הַזֶּה לָכֶם" ("The Torah should have commenced with 'This month shall be unto you…'"). That verse, from Exodus 12:2, is the first commandment given to Israel as a nation.

His answer cites Psalms 111:6, "כֹּחַ מַעֲשָׂיו הִגִּיד לְעַמּוֹ לָתֵת לָהֶם נַחֲלַת גּוֹיִם". In the translation I retrieved: "He declared to His people the strength of His works, in order that He might give them the heritage of the nations."

Rashi then imagines a hostile claim: the nations will say to Israel, "You are robbers, because you took by force the lands of the seven nations of Canaan." Israel's reply is that "כָּל הָאָרֶץ שֶׁל הַקָּבָּ"ה הִיא, הוּא בְרָאָהּ וּנְתָנָהּ לַאֲשֶׁר יָשַׁר בְּעֵינָיו". In the retrieved translation: "All the earth belongs to the Holy One; He created it and gave it to whom He pleased. When He willed He gave it to them, and when He willed He took it from them and gave it to us."

So the first page of the Torah is a legal brief. Before we hear any commandment, we learn who owns everything.

## The "crazy" part: a defense written before anyone attacked
The Torah wrote this defense roughly 2,500 years of history before the Canaanite conquest it was defending. The first word of the Torah was drafted with a cross-examination in mind. A moral claim has to be anchored in something deeper than power. That is why the Torah goes back to the very beginning.

## The text itself starts in the middle of things
[Genesis 1:1-2] reads in the JPS translation: "When God began to create heaven and earth— the earth being unformed and void, with darkness over the surface of the deep and a wind from God sweeping over the water—". The Hebrew is "וְהָאָרֶץ הָיְתָה תֹהוּ וָבֹהוּ". Note that the JPS rendering "When God began…" reflects the reading of *bereshit* as a construct form, a grammatical point that Rashi's commentary also discusses. I did not manage to retrieve that part of Rashi, so I am not quoting it here.

## My own connection (not from a source)
Put the two ideas together:
1. **God owns the world.** That is Rashi's point.
2. **The world He owns arrives as *tohu vavohu*,** formless and unfinished, with a wind hovering over it.

Ownership in the Torah's picture is a **stewardship deed**, not a trophy. The land is given to Israel as raw material, and the claim is only as strong as what is built on it. The nations' accusation, "you are robbers," is answered by the opening verse. Whether the answer holds up in every generation is answered by how the people live.

## A closing thought
The Torah starts with Creation to tell us the world is not ours by default and not anyone's by force. It is lent by its Owner, and He left it open for us to build. Shabbat Shalom.

answer:
**תשובה קצרה:** לא הצלחתי לשלוף את המקורות מספריא (השרת החזיר שגיאה), ולכן אני עונה מהידע הכללי ומציין איפה לא הצלחתי לאמת. לפי ההלכה המקובלת, אין דרך לטבול ביום העשירי מהראייה. המינימום המקובל הוא יום 12 מהראייה לפחות, אם ההפסק טהרה נעשה ביום החמישי. לפי הקולא של הרב עובדיה בשעת הדחק, המינימום הוא יום 11. הצירוף שהצעת, שני היתרים יחד, לא מוכר לי כהלכה למעשה. אני לא מכיר פוסק שמתיר אותו.

## נקודת המוצא

- **מהתורה:** נידה היא 7 ימים מהראייה. זבה היא 7 נקיים אחרי הפסקת הדם (ויקרא טו).
- **הגזרה הרבנית:** חכמים החמירו שכל ראייה, גם של נידה רגילה, מצריכה 7 נקיים אחרי שהדם פסק. לכן הימים של הראייה והימים הנקיים הם שני שלבים נפרדים ולא חופפים. "הפסק טהרה" הוא הבדיקה שמסיימת את שלב הראייה.
- **המינימום להפסק טהרה:** לפי המנהג המקובל, בעיקר אצל האשכנזים, הוא יום 5. בשלב הזה אין פחות מ-5 ימים כי ימי הנידה הם לפחות 5 (הלכה הנגזרת מהספרות סביב שו"ע יו"ד קצו). את מספר הסעיף ואת הנוסח המדויק לא הצלחתי לאמת, אז אל תסתמך עליו בלי בדיקה.

## החישוב

אם ההפסק טהרה נעשה בסוף יום 5, ימי הספירה הם 6 עד 12. הטבילה היא בליל יום 12, כלומר אחרי 12 יום מהראייה. עם ההקלה על הפסק טהרה ביום 4 של הרב עובדיה בשעת הדחק, הספירה היא יום 5 עד 11, והטבילה בליל יום 11 או ביום 11.

## הבעיה בהצעה שלך

1. **ההקלה של הרב עובדיה:** נאמרה בשעת הדחק ולמקרים מסוימים, ולא כהיתר כללי. עליה אפשר לסמוך רק עם שאלה לרב.
2. **"שישה נקיים" בשם הבן איש חי:** לא מצאתי ולא אימתתי שהוא התיר לספור שישה נקיים. אני לא מכיר הוראה כזו, והיא נראית לי בעייתית.
   - שבעה נקיים הם דין גמור. הוא מפורש במקרא, והפסוק על הזבה הוא מקור שבעה הנקיים (ויקרא טו, כח).
   - הקולות על ימי הפסק הם קולות בגזרה רבנית. ספירת פחות משבעה נקיים היא ביטול של דין ברור, ולא נעשה בזה שימוש מעשי.
   - אם יש לך מקור לדעה כזו, שלח לי אותו ואבדוק אותו. כרגע אין לי אפשרות לאשר אותו.
3. **שילוב קולות:** גם אם כל קולא קיימת בפני עצמה, פוסקים לא מקבלים צירוף של כמה קולות יחד. זה בדיוק מה שהנחיות ההלכה מזהירות ממנו.

## מסקנה מעשית

- לפי השיטה המקובלת ביותר, הטבילה היא בלילה של יום 12 לפחות. לפי הקולא של הרב עובדיה בשעת הדחק, היא ביום 11.
- שישה נקיים אינם מקובלים להלכה למעשה. אם יש מקרה קונקרטי, למשל חשש לזמן הטבילה, צריך לשאול רב.

אשמח לדעת מה העדה שלך (ספרדית, אשכנזית או חב"ד), ואם המקרה הוא תיאורטי או מעשי. אם תרצה, אנסה שוב לשלוף את המקורות. בכל מקרה, שאלות של טהרת המשפחה צריכות להישאל לרב או לרבנית מוסמכת, שיכולים לשאול שאלות המשך.

**Короткий ответ.** Галаха не устанавливает верхнего предела числа раз за ночь. Она определяет другое: минимальную обязанность мужа перед женой (*она*) и пределы дозволенного, то есть скромность, взаимное согласие и отсутствие вреда. Вопрос о «лимите» поэтому в основном практический. Он зависит от согласия супругов, их сил и от того, разрешено ли им быть вместе в этот день.

## Основные выводы
- Верхней границы в галахе нет. Есть нижняя: муж обязан давать жене *она* в соответствии со своими силами и занятием.
- Обязанность и дозволенность относятся к дням, когда супруги не в состоянии *нидда*. Правила семейной чистоты надо уточнять у раввина.
- Нельзя ни принуждать жену, ни отказывать ей ради того, чтобы причинить боль.
- Скромность и святость важны и в этой сфере. Не следует искать чрезмерного или неуместного.
- Конкретный случай лучше обсудить с раввином.

## Источники

**Обязанность.** В [Shulchan Arukh, Even HaEzer 76:1] сказано: «каждый мужчина обязан давать *она* по своим силам и по своему занятию». Периодичность зависит от рода занятий. Для людей, не занятых тяжёлой работой, обязанность выше. Это нижняя норма. Предела «сверху» в этом месте нет.

**Нельзя отказывать.** В [Shulchan Arukh, Even HaEzer 76:11] сказано: «אסור לאדם למנוע מאשתו עונתה» («Запрещено человеку отказывать жене в её *она*»). Тот, кто отказывает, чтобы причинить ей боль, нарушает запрет «עונתה לא יגרע» («*она* её не уменьшит», Исход 21:10).

**Ограничения.** Я не смог открыть соответствующие места Шулхан Аруха, Орах Хаим 240, и Рамбама, Законы запретных связей, глава 21. Поэтому их содержание излагаю по памяти, без цитат. Общий принцип в них такой: близость должна быть по обоюдному желанию, без принуждения и без стремления к чрезмерной страсти. Муж не должен принуждать жену. Нужны скромность и сдержанность, а супруги должны осознавать святость супружеских отношений.

## Практическое замечание
Супруги определяют это по взаимному согласию, с учётом здоровья, усталости и желания друг друга. Если у вас есть вопросы о конкретных днях, о состоянии *нидда* и *тевила* (погружении в микву) или о здоровье, обратитесь к своему раввину. Он сможет задать уточняющие вопросы.

answer:
Die kurze Antwort: Die Tora verbietet Männern, den Bart „zu verderben“. Das ist ein Gebot (*mitzwa*, Verbot), kein bloßer Brauch. Verboten ist aber nur das Rasieren oder das rasierähnliche Abschneiden an bestimmten Stellen. Ein Bart ist nicht grundsätzlich unantastbar. Beim Wie und Womit unterscheiden sich die Gemeinschaften.

Hinweis: Die Sefaria-Abfrage wurde bei einigen Quellen wegen Überlastung blockiert. Den Tora-Vers und die Mischna habe ich deshalb aus dem Gedächtnis zitiert und nicht neu geprüft. Verse und Mischna-Nummern gebe ich nur an, wo ich mir sicher bin.

## Key Takeaways
- Quelle ist Levitikus 19:27: „Und du sollst den Rand deines Bartes nicht verderben.“
- Das Verbot gilt nur für Männer und betrifft das Rasieren, nicht jedes Kürzen.
- Nach der Talmud-Tradition (Makkot) gibt es fünf Stellen am Gesicht, an denen man nicht rasieren darf.
- Rasierklinge: verboten. Schere: erlaubt, solange sie nicht rasierähnlich nah an der Haut schneidet.
- Elektrorasierer sind umstritten. Chabad und viele Sephardim sind strenger, manche aschkenasische Poskim erlauben sie.

## Die Quelle in der Tora
In Levitikus 19:27 heißt es: „לֹא תַקִּפוּ פְּאַת רֹאשְׁכֶם וְלֹא תַשְׁחִית אֵת פְּאַת זְקָנֶךָ“. Das heißt: „Ihr sollt den Rand eures Kopfes nicht rundum abschneiden, und du sollst den Rand deines Bartes nicht verderben.“ (Meine Übersetzung.)

Der Talmud (Traktat Makkot, 3. Kapitel) versteht „verderben“ (*haschchata*) als Entfernen der Haare mit einer Rasierklinge. Er nennt fünf Stellen im Gesicht: zwei an den Schläfen (Koteletten), zwei am unteren Kiefer und eine am Kinn.

Der Schulchan Aruch behandelt die Gesetze in [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 181]. Sein erster Abschnitt, [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 181:1], definiert zuerst die *pe'ot* (Ecken) des Kopfes. Er sagt, sie liegen dort, wo der Kopf an den Kiefer anschließt, rechts und links. Die Regeln zum Bart folgen im selben Kapitel.

## Was ist erlaubt, was nicht?
- **Rasierklinge:** Nach allen Ansichten verboten, an den fünf Stellen.
- **Schere:** Erlaubt, wenn sie nicht wie eine Rasierklinge direkt an der Haut schneidet. Im Prinzip darf man den Bart also kürzen.
- **Elektrorasierer:** Das hängt davon ab, ob er wie eine Schere (Scherwirkung zwischen Klinge und Schutzgitter) oder wie eine Klinge arbeitet.
  - Manche Poskim, besonders im aschkenasischen Raum, erlauben ihn unter Bedingungen. Dazu gehört Rav Moshe Feinstein, wenn ich ihn richtig im Gedächtnis habe.
  - Chabad und viele chassidische Kreise sowie viele sephardische Poskim sind strenger.
  - Das gilt auch für Chemikalien oder Enthaarungscreme. Dort gehen die Meinungen auseinander.

## Warum? Die Gründe
Die Tora nennt keinen Grund. Es ist ein *chok*, ein Gebot ohne ausdrückliche Begründung. Die Tradition kennt aber Erklärungen:
- **Abgrenzung von Götzendienst:** Rambam sieht darin eine Abkehr von heidnischen Priesterbräuchen (siehe Mischne Tora, Hilchot Avoda Sara, und Führer der Unschlüssigen III:37). Diese Stelle habe ich hier nicht neu abgerufen.
- **Kabbala:** Im Zohar und beim Arizal steht der Bart für die „13 Eigenschaften der Barmherzigkeit“. Deshalb schneiden viele Chassidim und Chabad den Bart gar nicht.
- **Würde:** Viele sehen im Bart ein Zeichen jüdischer Identität und Männlichkeit. Das ist ein späterer Gedanke und keine Begründung des Verbots.

## Gemeinschaften im Überblick
- **Aschkenasisch (litauisch/modern-orthodox):** Es gibt Bärte verschiedener Länge. Viele Männer benutzen eine Schere oder einen als schergleich anerkannten Elektrorasierer.
- **Chassidisch/Chabad:** Man schneidet den Bart gar nicht oder kaum. Chabad ist hier strikt.
- **Sephardisch:** Vom Schulchan Aruch her gilt das Verbot der Klinge. Viele folgen strengeren Ansichten, etwa des Ben Ish Chai. Die genauen Bedingungen für Elektrorasierer sind hier umstritten.

Wenn du mir sagst, welcher Gemeinschaft du angehörst und welches Gerät du benutzt, kann ich gezielter antworten. Für deinen persönlichen Fall frag bitte deinen Rabbiner.

answer:
El movimiento masorti (conservador) no tiene una única postura. La posición oficial más influyente, adoptada en 1950 en Estados Unidos, permite conducir a la sinagoga en shabat, pero no para otros fines recreativos o comerciales. Esa postura es muy discutida dentro del propio movimiento, y la halajá ortodoxa tradicional prohíbe viajar en vehículo en shabat.

## Puntos clave
- La decisión del Comité de Leyes y Normas Judías (CJLS) de 1950 permitió conducir a la sinagoga, y la decisión fue discutida.
- Su argumento es que el motor de combustión interna no implicaría una prohibición de la Torá, y que la asistencia a la sinagoga fortalece el shabat.
- Hubo opiniones de minoría que rechazaron esa conclusión, por ejemplo la del rabino Joel Roth en la década de 1980.
- Las comunidades masortíes difieren según el país y el rabino. En Israel la práctica es en general más estricta.
- La halajá ortodoxa (askenazí, sefardí y jabad) prohíbe viajar en vehículo en shabat.

## Posición del movimiento masorti
- **La decisión de 1950.** Fue un responsum de los rabinos Morris Adler, Jacob Agus y Theodore Friedman. Se aprobó por mayoría en el CJLS, no por unanimidad. Permitía usar un vehículo para ir al templo cuando la distancia hace difícil asistir a pie. No es una autorización general para pasear o hacer compras.
- **Su razonamiento.** Sostiene que encender un motor no es necesariamente la melajá (labor prohibida) de "encender fuego", que la Torá prohíbe en [Exodus 35:3]. Lo ve como mucho una prohibición rabínica. Esa prohibición, según este razonamiento, cede ante valores como el *oneg shabat* (deleite del shabat), la oración en comunidad y la cohesión comunitaria. Esta es mi síntesis de la postura, no una cita textual.
- **Voces en contra.** Dentro del movimiento hay rabinos que consideran que conducir contradice el espíritu del shabat, y que la excepción para la sinagoga se amplió demasiado en la práctica.
- **Variación local.** El Masorti en Israel y algunas comunidades de otros países, incluida Latinoamérica, suelen desalentar más el uso del coche. En la práctica, cada rabino y cada comunidad deciden. No puedo verificar aquí las posturas actuales de cada comunidad.

## Posición tradicional (ortodoxa)
- La mayoría de los poskim (decisores halájicos) prohíbe viajar en vehículo en shabat. Algunos lo consideran una prohibición de la Torá, por encender o avivar un fuego, o por la electricidad. Otros lo consideran una prohibición rabínica. Todos coinciden en que está prohibido.
- Aparte de eso, existe el límite de desplazamiento en shabat (*tejum shabat*), que restringe la distancia que se puede recorrer fuera de la ciudad.
- Esto vale para las tradiciones askenazí, sefardí y jabad. No conozco diferencias relevantes entre ellas en este punto.
- Si hay peligro de vida (*pikuaj nefesh*), se permite e incluso se exige viajar, por ejemplo para llegar al hospital.

Si me dices tu comunidad, puedo detallar más. Para tu caso concreto, consulta con tu rabino.

answer:
**Resposta curta:** Um gentio não tem a obrigação da sucá. Se quiser sentar nela, não comete nenhuma transgressão, mas isso não conta como mitzvá no sentido haláchico. Os Sábios derivam essa exclusão do versículo que fala em "todo cidadão em Israel". Não consegui abrir as fontes na Sefaria agora porque as consultas falharam. Por isso cito só o que sei com segurança e aviso onde falta verificação.

## Principais pontos
- A obrigação da sucá recai sobre o povo judeu: "todo cidadão em Israel" ([Leviticus 23:42]).
- Um não judeu não está obrigado a ela, e ela não faz parte das sete leis de Noé.
- Um gentio pode sentar na sucá ou até ajudar a construí-la. Não é proibido.
- Se um gentio construiu a sucá, isso não a invalida. O que importa é que o judeu cumpra a mitzvá dentro dela.

## Fonte e raciocínio
O versículo diz: "בַּסֻּכֹּת תֵּשְׁבוּ שִׁבְעַת יָמִים כָּל הָאֶזְרָח בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשְׁבוּ בַּסֻּכֹּת" ("Em sucot habitareis sete dias; todo cidadão em Israel habitará em sucot") ([Leviticus 23:42]). Segundo o Talmud (Tratado Sukkah, por volta da página 28a, que não consegui reabrir agora), a expressão "todo cidadão em Israel" delimita quem está obrigado. A leitura simples é que o texto se dirige ao povo de Israel, e não às nações.

## Distinção prática
Os Noaítas (as sete leis de Noé) não recebem as mitzvot específicas de Israel. A tradição vê um risco quando um gentio cria um "ritual novo" e o apresenta como mitzvá da Torá. Por isso, em geral:
- **Permitido:** visitar uma sucá, comer nela, aprender sobre ela. Isso é feito como experiência ou estudo, e não como "cumprimento de mitzvá".
- **Evitar:** fazer a bênção judaica *leshev basucá* ("…que nos ordenou habitar na sucá"). Ela fala de um mandamento dado a "nós", Israel.
- **Questão de conversão:** quem está se preparando para se converter deve perguntar ao seu rabino como proceder.

Não verifiquei as discussões dos poskim sobre os detalhes, como o gentio que quer sentar na sucá "como mitzvá", nem sobre a validade de uma sucá construída por gentio. Posso tentar abrir o Talmud e o Shulchan Arukh (Orach Chayim, simanim 625–640) quando a Sefaria voltar a responder.

Consulte o seu rabino para o seu caso pessoal.

Elle ne dit jamais clairement que le jus et le ketchup sont Chéhakol. Elle affirme même qu'« en sauce » la tomate garde Haadama et renvoie le reste à un rav. Elle omet aussi la règle de la salade, et l'affirmation qu'on mange rarement un kazayit de tomate est trompeuse, une tomate moyenne dépassant largement cette quantité. answer:
**Réponse directe :** sur une tomate, on récite *Boré péri haadama* (בורא פרי האדמה), car elle pousse sur une plante annuelle et non sur un arbre. C'est la pratique courante des communautés ashkénazes et sephardes. Après avoir mangé, la bénédiction finale est *Boré néfashot*, si l'on a mangé la quantité requise.

## Points clés
- Bénédiction initiale : **Haadama**.
- La tomate est un légume, donc elle n'entre pas dans la catégorie *Haétz* (fruit d'arbre).
- Cuite, en sauce ou en salade, elle garde en principe la bénédiction **Haadama**.
- Le jus de tomate se traite lui aussi selon les règles des jus de légumes. Les cas particuliers (concentré, ketchup, purée très lisse) sont à demander à un rav.
- Si la tomate est mangée dans un repas avec du pain, le *Hamotsi* la couvre.

## Explication

**Principe.** La Michna et le Talmud distinguent les fruits de l'arbre (*Haétz*) des produits de la terre (*Haadama*), voir [Berakhot 35a]. Les légumes relèvent de *Haadama*, ce qui est établi dans [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 203]. La tomate est une plante herbacée qui meurt chaque année et ne repousse pas depuis un tronc. Elle suit donc la règle des légumes.

Je n'ai pas pu relire le texte du Shulchan Arukh à l'instant, car l'accès à Sefaria a échoué. Les références ci-dessus sont donc données de mémoire et sans citation exacte.

**Bénédiction finale.** Pour un légume, on récite *Boré néfashot* après avoir mangé, seulement si l'on a consommé au moins un *kazayit* (environ 27 g selon certains, environ 14 à 19 g selon d'autres). En pratique, on mange rarement cette quantité en tomate seule, donc on ne dit souvent pas de bénédiction finale.

**Tomate cuite ou en sauce.** La cuisson ne change pas la bénédiction d'un légume, qui reste *Haadama*. Pour une purée ou une sauce très lisse, certains posquim discutent de la changer en *Chéhakol*. Cette question dépend de la texture et de l'usage, donc elle est à poser à un rav.

**Ordre de priorité.** Si l'on mange plusieurs aliments, la tomate passe après un fruit d'arbre (*Haétz*) et avant les aliments en *Chéhakol*.

N'hésitez pas à consulter votre rabbin pour votre cas personnel.

answer:
Esta es la secuencia habitual de la cena del viernes por la noche. Las variantes de *minhag* (costumbre) se indican por comunidad. Las fuentes de Sefaria dieron error de límite de consultas, así que solo pude leer completos los encabezados de [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 262:1] y [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 271:1]. Lo demás lo expongo según la práctica conocida, sin citar números de *se'if* que no verifiqué.

## Puntos clave
- El orden básico es: velas, rezo en la sinagoga, canciones en casa, *Kidush*, lavado de manos, *Hamotzi* sobre dos panes, comida con *zemirot* y *Birkat Hamazon*.
- Las bendiciones propias de la noche son: encender las velas, *Kidush* (sobre el vino) y *Hamotzi* (sobre dos panes enteros).
- El *Kidush* se hace sobre vino (o jugo de uva) y se completa con la bendición *mekadesh haShabbat*.
- Las costumbres varían entre ashkenazíes, sefardíes y Jabad en detalles como cuándo cubrir los ojos con las velas, si se está de pie o sentado en el *Kidush*, y el orden de los cantos.

## 1. Preparación (antes del atardecer)
- **La mesa puesta.** El *Shulchan Arukh* indica preparar la mesa, arreglar la casa y vestir ropa limpia para encontrarlo todo en orden al volver de la sinagoga [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 262:1]. El Rema añade que la mesa se deja puesta durante todo Shabbat.
- **Encendido de velas** (*Orach Chayim* 263). Se hace antes del atardecer, según el horario local de tu ciudad.
  - Bendición: *Baruj Atá Ado-nai, Elo-heinu Mélej haolam, asher kideshanu bemitzvotav vetzivanu lehadlik ner shel Shabbat.* Significa: "Bendito eres, Eterno, nuestro Dios, Rey del universo, que nos santificó con Sus preceptos y nos ordenó encender la vela de Shabbat".
  - **Ashkenazíes y Jabad:** primero se enciende, luego se cubren los ojos y se dice la bendición.
  - **Sefardíes:** en general se hace la bendición antes de encender, con la mano apartada, y después se enciende.
  - Una vez encendidas las velas, quien las encendió ya aceptó el Shabbat y no puede hacer *melajá* (labores prohibidas).

## 2. Sinagoga
*Kabalat Shabbat* (*Lejá Dodí*, salmos) y *Maariv*. En muchas comunidades ashkenazíes se dice *Kidush* en la sinagoga al final. Su origen es para los huéspedes que comían allí, y no exime a quien lo escucha de hacerlo en casa.

## 3. Al llegar a casa (el orden de estos cantos varía)
1. **Shalom Aleijem**, canción a los ángeles de servicio.
2. **Eshet Jayil** (Proverbios 31), en honor a la mujer de la casa.
3. **Bendición a los hijos.** Es una costumbre, con *Yesimjá Elo-him keEfráyim vejiMenashé* para los varones y *Yesimej Elo-him keSará, Rivká, Rajel veLeá* para las niñas, seguida de *Yevarejejá Ado-nai veyishmerejá...* (la bendición sacerdotal).

## 4. Kidush
Se hace con la mesa puesta y los dos panes cubiertos. El tema de *Orach Chayim* 271 es "las leyes del *Kidush* sobre el vino" [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 271:1].

1. **Vayejulú** (Génesis 2:1-3, precedido por "Yom hashishí" en el rezo). Muchos lo dicen de pie, y Jabad también. Muchos sefardíes lo dicen sentados. Depende de la costumbre familiar.
2. **Bendición del vino:** *Baruj Atá Ado-nai, Elo-heinu Mélej haolam, borei peri hagáfen.*
3. **Bendición del día:** *...asher kideshanu bemitzvotav vertzá banu, veShabbat kodsho beahavá uvratzón hinjilanu, zikarón lemaasé bereshit... Baruj Atá Ado-nai, mekadesh haShabbat.* Esta es la forma abreviada. El texto completo está en cualquier *sidur*.
4. Se bebe al menos un trago grande de la copa. Quien dirige bebe la mayor parte, y los presentes responden *Amén*.

## 5. Lavado de manos y Hamotzi
1. **Netilat yadáyim.** Se lavan las manos con un vaso (dos veces en la mano derecha y luego en la izquierda, según la costumbre) y se dice: *...asher kideshanu bemitzvotav vetzivanu al netilat yadáyim.* Después no se habla hasta comer el pan.
2. **Hamotzi.** Se bendice sobre dos panes enteros (*lejem mishné*), que recuerdan el doble maná del viernes.
   - Se descubre el pan y se corta o se marca la rebanada.
   - Bendición: *Baruj Atá Ado-nai, Elo-heinu Mélej haolam, hamotzí lejem min haáretz.*
   - Se moja en sal (o se espolvorea), se come y se reparte a los comensales.

## 6. La comida
- Se come en el orden habitual, normalmente pescado, sopa, plato principal y postre.
- Se cantan **zemirot** (por ejemplo *Yah Ribón*, *Shabbat Hayom laShem*) y se dicen palabras de Torah.
- Los alimentos que forman parte de la comida quedan cubiertos por *Hamotzi*. Algunos alimentos, como la fruta de postre o el vino que se bebe aparte, pueden requerir su propia bendición. Si tienes un caso concreto, pregunta a tu rabino.

## 7. Cierre
1. **Birkat Hamazón** (bendición después de la comida), con *Shir Hamaalot* (Salmo 126) antes en Shabbat.
2. En la tercera bendición se añade **Retzé**: *Retzé vehajalitzenu...* (agrega Shabbat). Y en *Harajamán* se dice: *Harajamán hu yanjilenu yom shekulo Shabbat.*
3. Si olvidaste *Retzé*, hay reglas específicas que dependen de en qué momento lo notas, así que consulta a tu rabino.
4. Algunas comunidades dicen **Mayim Ajaronim** (lavado final de los dedos) antes de la *Birkat Hamazón*. Es costumbre de muchos, pero no de todos.

Si me dices tu comunidad (ashkenazí, sefardí, Jabad u otra), te preparo el orden exacto con los textos completos. Para tu caso concreto, consulta a tu rabino.

answer:
Bonjour. Il n'existe pas de moyen de rendre ce mariage « licite ». La Torah et la halakha l'interdisent, et la loi civile l'interdit aussi.

## Réponse directe
Un garçon de 3 ans et 7 mois ne peut pas contracter de *kiddushin* (sanctification du mariage), car un mineur n'a pas de capacité juridique en la matière. Si l'enfant est une fille, les sources reconnaissent un cas où le père peut la marier mineure. Les Sages l'ont toutefois interdit : on ne marie pas sa fille tant qu'elle est petite. On attend qu'elle ait grandi et qu'elle dise : « Je veux celui-ci ». Je n'ai pas pu consulter Sefaria à l'instant (erreur technique). Ce qui suit vient donc de ma connaissance des sources, sans citation textuelle.

## Points clés
- **Garçon :** les *kiddushin* d'un mineur (avant la majorité religieuse, 13 ans) n'ont aucune valeur.
- **Fille :** le père a un pouvoir théorique de la marier avant sa majorité. Les Sages l'ont interdit, d'après [Kiddushin 41a], repris dans [Shulchan Arukh, Even HaEzer 37:8].
- **Consentement :** le mariage juif repose sur la volonté réelle des deux conjoints. Une enfant de 3 ans n'en a aucune.
- **Loi du pays :** la *halakha* demande de respecter la loi civile non contraire à la Torah (*dina de-malkhuta dina*). Marier un jeune enfant est un crime dans pratiquement tous les pays, et il met l'enfant en danger.

## Explication
**1. Le principe talmudique.** Le Talmud [Kiddushin 41a] enseigne qu'il est interdit de marier sa fille mineure avant qu'elle soit en âge de choisir. Le *Shulchan Arukh* en fait une règle de pratique. Les autorités font de cette interdiction une restriction forte, pas un simple conseil. Le cas d'une fille mineure mariée par son père existe surtout dans des situations extrêmes et très exceptionnelles, que les sources traitent à part. Il ne concerne pas un projet de mariage planifié pour un enfant de cet âge.

**2. La maturité comme condition.** Dans la tradition, le mariage est une alliance entre deux adultes, avec des devoirs conjugaux et familiaux. Un enfant de 3 ans ne peut ni comprendre ni assumer cela. Sa protection est une valeur centrale de la Torah.

**3. Ce que vous pouvez faire à la place.**
- Si vous pensez à une famille précise, à un projet de *shidoukh* (proposition de mariage) ou à un engagement entre deux familles, il faut attendre que les enfants soient adultes. Ils décideront alors librement.
- Si ce projet vient d'une pression familiale ou communautaire, parlez-en à un rabbin de confiance. Il pourra vous aider à y répondre.
- Si quelqu'un exerce une contrainte sur vous ou sur l'enfant, ou si vous craignez pour la sécurité de l'enfant, contactez les services de protection de l'enfance ou la police de votre pays.

Pour votre situation personnelle, consultez un rabbin.

answer:
**Respuesta corta:** No. En Shabat está prohibido encender fuego, ya sea una vela, un fósforo, una estufa o una chispa. Sí se puede disfrutar de un fuego que se encendió antes de Shabat, y hay excepciones por peligro de vida.

*Nota: las herramientas de consulta no respondieron (error 429), así que cito de memoria. No pude verificar el texto de cada fuente en esta sesión.*

## Puntos clave
- La Torá prohíbe encender fuego en Shabat: [Exodus 35:3].
- Es una de las 39 *melajot* (labores prohibidas), llamada *mav'ir* (encender): [Mishnah Shabbat 7:2].
- La prohibición incluye encender luz o calor, y también el fuego eléctrico de una bombilla incandescente, según la mayoría de los poskim. Hay discusión sobre la razón exacta.
- Se puede encender antes de Shabat para tener luz y calor, y por eso se encienden las velas de Shabat.
- Si hay peligro de vida (*pikuaj nefesh*), se permite e incluso se debe hacerlo.

## Fuente y alcance
**Fuente bíblica.** La Torá dice: "No encenderéis fuego en ninguna de vuestras moradas en el día de Shabat" (*lo tebaaru esh*) [Exodus 35:3]. La Mishná incluye *hamav'ir* entre las labores principales de Shabat [Mishnah Shabbat 7:2].

**Qué incluye en la práctica**
- Encender una vela, un fósforo o un encendedor.
- Prender una hornalla o un horno de gas.
- Subir la llama de un fuego ya encendido. Esto es una forma de encender y se prohíbe.
- Acercar combustible a una llama para que arda más.

**Qué no es lo mismo**
- **Apagar el fuego** es una labor distinta (*mejabeh*), también prohibida, salvo en casos de peligro.
- **Aprovechar un fuego que ya estaba encendido** antes de Shabat está permitido. Por eso se dejan velas encendidas y se usa un *plata* o una olla preparada de antemano. Hay reglas adicionales sobre cocinar y mantener la comida caliente.
- **Aparatos eléctricos.** Muchos poskim prohíben encenderlos, ya sea por *mav'ir*, por *boneh* (construir) u otra razón. En la práctica, las comunidades ortodoxas no usan electricidad en Shabat, y se usan temporizadores (*Shabbat clocks*) puestos antes de Shabat.

## Excepciones
- **Peligro de vida.** Se enciende fuego si es necesario para salvar una vida, por ejemplo por frío extremo o una emergencia médica. Esto anula casi todas las prohibiciones de Shabat. No lo consultes antes de actuar: primero actúa.
- **Enfermos.** Hay reglas especiales, y es mejor preguntar a un rabino.
- **Un no judío.** Pedirle que encienda fuego por uno mismo está prohibido en principio (*amirah le-nojri*). Hay excepciones limitadas en casos de enfermedad o necesidad grande. No lo apliques sin consultar.

## Diferencias entre comunidades
En lo básico (no encender fuego) no hay diferencia entre ashkenazíes, sefardíes y jabad. Las diferencias aparecen en los detalles, como el uso de luz eléctrica y de temporizadores, o la manera de dejar la comida caliente.

Si me dices tu comunidad y qué situación concreta tienes (por ejemplo calefacción, cocina o una emergencia), puedo ser más específico. Consulta a tu rabino para tu caso personal.

A non-Jew does not count, and without a minyan the devarim shebikdusha are not said. It misses some nuances: the contrast with the stricter proof required for marriage, a respectful welcome for the non-Jew, and the explicit presence of non-Jews in Tel Aviv. Sourcing is honest and the quote of SA OC 55:11 is accurate, but 55:1 and Yevamot 47a are missing, and the meta remarks about the limited tools plus the vague mention of community variations weaken the presentation somewhat.

answer:
**Réponse courte :** n'additionnez pas quelqu'un au quorum (*minyan*) sur une simple impression. Demandez-lui directement s'il est juif. En général, on croit sa déclaration, et il peut alors compter dans le minyan, même s'il n'est pas pratiquant. S'il ne sait pas, ou s'il n'est pas juif, il ne compte pas. Les outils de Sefaria ont été limités pendant cette recherche : je n'ai donc pu vérifier qu'une partie des sources, et je le signale ci-dessous.

## Points essentiels
- Seuls des Juifs adultes (hommes de plus de 13 ans) comptent dans le minyan. Un non-Juif ne compte pas, même s'il prie avec vous.
- Le doute sur le judaïsme de quelqu'un ne suffit pas pour le compter. Il faut une raison valable de le considérer comme juif.
- À Tel Aviv, la majorité des passants sont juifs, mais l'apparence ou la probabilité statistique ne remplace pas une réponse claire de l'intéressé.
- Un Juif non pratiquant compte, tant qu'il n'a pas été mis en *herem* (excommunication).
- Si le doute persiste, mieux vaut chercher une autre personne que de dire *Kaddish*, *Barekhou* ou la *Kedoucha* avec un minyan douteux. Si cela n'est pas possible, demandez à un rabbin.

## Le raisonnement

**1. Seuls des Juifs comptent.** Le minyan est appris du verset « *Je serai sanctifié parmi les enfants d'Israël* » (Lévitique 22:32), d'où l'on déduit qu'il faut dix membres de la communauté d'Israël. C'est l'enseignement de la tradition talmudique (je cite ici de mémoire, sans avoir pu consulter la page). Un non-Juif ne peut donc pas compléter le quorum.

**2. Le Juif qui ne pratique pas.** Le *Choulkhan Aroukh* dit : « עבריין שעבר על גזירת הצבור או שעבר עבירה אם לא נידוהו נמנה למנין עשרה » (« Un transgresseur qui a enfreint un décret de la communauté ou commis une faute, s'il n'a pas été excommunié, est compté dans le minyan de dix ») [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 55:11]. Ce n'est donc pas son niveau d'observance qui importe, mais son statut de Juif.

**3. Que faire face au doute ?** Voici le raisonnement habituel, tel que je le comprends. Je n'ai pas pu relire les décisionnaires à ce sujet, donc ce n'est pas une citation de leur texte :
- Le plus simple est de lui demander : « Es-tu juif ? ». En matière de statut personnel, la parole d'une personne sur elle-même est généralement crue.
- S'il répond oui, il compte.
- S'il ne sait pas, ou s'il hésite parce qu'un seul de ses parents est juif, il y a un vrai doute. Selon la halakha orthodoxe, le statut se transmet par la mère (ou par une conversion valide). Pour un doute de ce genre, il faut consulter un rabbin.
- S'il vous dit qu'il n'est pas juif, il ne compte pas.

## Pratique
- Ne comptez pas sur lui si le doute est réel.
- Cherchez un dixième homme dans une synagogue voisine. À Tel Aviv, il y en a beaucoup, et c'est souvent plus simple que de s'arrêter à un passant.
- Si le minyan reste incomplet, priez seul avec les prières individuelles, sans les parties qui demandent un quorum (*Kaddish*, *Barekhou*, *Kedoucha*, lecture de la Torah). Vous pouvez aussi rattraper plus tard ce qui peut l'être.
- Ces règles peuvent varier un peu selon les communautés (séfarades, ashkénazes, Habad). Dites-moi la vôtre si vous voulez une réponse plus précise.

Pour votre cas concret, consultez votre rabbin.
