El Salmo 42 es la voz de alguien que anhela a Dios como un ciervo sediento, y que vive ese anhelo en el exilio y en la angustia. Se repite un estribillo de esperanza: «¿Por qué te abates, alma mía?». Es el primer salmo del segundo libro de los Salmos y está dedicado a los «hijos de Coraj».

## Puntos clave
- El salmo expresa sed de la presencia de Dios, comparada con la de un ciervo junto a un arroyo seco.
- El autor recuerda con dolor cuando subía en peregrinación a la casa de Dios entre multitudes festivas.
- Tres veces se interpela a sí mismo: «¿Por qué te abates, alma mía?» (vv. 6, 12 y también 43:5).
- Se alternan el recuerdo, la angustia y la esperanza.
- Nota de numeración: en el texto hebreo el título es el versículo 1, así que el salmo propiamente dicho empieza en el v. 2. Muchas Biblias cristianas lo numeran un versículo menos.

## Traducción (numeración hebrea)

1. Para el director del coro. *Maskil* de los hijos de Coraj.
2. Como el ciervo que brama por las corrientes de agua, así mi alma te anhela a ti, oh Dios.
3. Mi alma tiene sed de Dios, del Dios vivo. ¿Cuándo vendré y me presentaré ante Dios?
4. Mis lágrimas han sido mi pan de día y de noche, mientras me dicen todo el día: «¿Dónde está tu Dios?».
5. Estas cosas recuerdo y derramo mi alma dentro de mí: cómo pasaba entre la multitud, avanzando con ellos hasta la casa de Dios, con voz de júbilo y alabanza, el gentío en fiesta.
6. ¿Por qué te abates, alma mía, y te turbas dentro de mí? Espera en Dios, porque aún le alabaré por la salvación de su presencia.
7. Dios mío, mi alma está abatida dentro de mí; por eso te recuerdo desde la tierra del Jordán y de los Hermones, desde el monte Mizar.
8. Un abismo llama a otro abismo, al estruendo de tus cascadas; todas tus olas y tus ondas han pasado sobre mí.
9. De día el Eterno ordenará su bondad, y de noche su canto estará conmigo, una oración al Dios de mi vida.
10. Diré a Dios, mi roca: «¿Por qué me has olvidado? ¿Por qué ando de luto, oprimido por el enemigo?».
11. Como quebrantamiento en mis huesos, me afrentan mis adversarios, diciéndome todo el día: «¿Dónde está tu Dios?».
12. ¿Por qué te abates, alma mía, y por qué te turbas dentro de mí? Espera en Dios, porque aún le alabaré: salvación de mi presencia y Dios mío.

## Comentarios breves
- **Pshat (sentido simple):** el orante está lejos del Templo. El v. 7 menciona la región del Jordán y del Hermón, que sugiere un lugar de exilio al norte de la tierra de Israel. Su dolor es doble: la ausencia de Dios y la burla de quienes preguntan «¿dónde está tu Dios?».
- **El estribillo:** el diálogo consigo mismo (vv. 6 y 12) muestra que la fe aquí no es ausencia de angustia, sino una decisión de esperar en medio de ella.
- **Liturgia:** de memoria recuerdo que el v. 3 y otros versículos de este salmo se usan en la oración, pero no pude verificarlo y prefiero no darte referencias que no he comprobado.

Si quieres, puedo volver a intentar la consulta en Sefaria para citar a Rashi, Ibn Ezra o Radak sobre versículos concretos, como el ciervo (v. 2) o «abismo llama a abismo» (v. 8).

**Salmo 41** (traducción mía, a partir del hebreo; Sefaria no ofrece versión en español de este texto). Es [Psalms 41], de Tehilim.

**1** Para el director del coro. Salmo de David.

**2** Dichoso el que se ocupa con inteligencia (*maskil*) del pobre; en el día malo lo librará el Eterno.

**3** El Eterno lo guardará y le dará vida, y será tenido por dichoso en la tierra; no lo entregarás al deseo de sus enemigos.

**4** El Eterno lo sostendrá en el lecho del dolor; todo su lecho transformarás en su enfermedad.

**5** Yo dije: «Eterno, ten piedad de mí, sana mi alma, porque he pecado contra Ti».

**6** Mis enemigos dicen mal de mí: «¿Cuándo morirá y perecerá su nombre?».

**7** Si uno viene a visitarme, habla falsedad; su corazón junta maldad; sale afuera y lo cuenta.

**8** Juntos murmuran contra mí todos los que me odian; contra mí maquinan el mal:

**9** «Algo perverso se ha derramado sobre él; ya que yace, no volverá a levantarse».

**10** Incluso el hombre de mi paz, en quien confiaba, el que comía mi pan, ha levantado el talón contra mí.

**11** Pero Tú, Eterno, ten piedad de mí y levántame, y les pagaré.

**12** En esto sabré que me quieres: en que mi enemigo no cante victoria sobre mí.

**13** Y a mí, por mi integridad me sostuviste y me estableciste ante Ti para siempre.

**14** Bendito sea el Eterno, Dios de Israel, desde el mundo hasta el mundo. Amén y amén.

**Notas breves**
- El versículo 3 tiene una variante de lectura. El texto escrito (*ketiv*) dice *ye'ushar* y la lectura tradicional (*kri*) dice *ve'ushar*: «y será dichoso».
- El versículo 14 no pertenece al contenido del salmo. Es la doxología que cierra el Libro I de los Salmos (capítulos 1–41).
- *Maskil* (v. 2) puede entenderse como «el que actúa con sensatez o consideración» hacia el necesitado.

Si quieres, puedo añadir el comentario de Rashi, Radak o Metzudat David sobre este salmo.

El Salmo 77 es un salmo de Asaf. Un hombre angustiado clama a Dios de noche. Duda de que Dios lo haya abandonado y encuentra consuelo al recordar el Éxodo y el cruce del mar. La traducción es mía, porque Sefaria no ofrece una versión en español de este texto. Sigo la numeración hebrea, en la que el versículo 1 es el encabezado [Psalms 77:1-21].

## Puntos clave
- El salmo avanza de la queja (vv. 2-10) al recuerdo de las obras de Dios (vv. 11-16) y a la imagen del mar y de la redención (vv. 17-21).
- La pregunta central es si Dios rechazará para siempre y si su bondad se habrá acabado (vv. 8-10).
- El salmista se consuela recordando los milagros pasados, en especial el Éxodo.
- El salmo termina de repente, con Moisés y Aarón guiando al pueblo "como a un rebaño".

## Traducción (mía)

**1** Para el director; sobre Yedutún. De Asaf. Salmo.

**2** Mi voz clama a Dios, y gritaré; mi voz a Dios, para que me escuche.

**3** En el día de mi angustia busqué al Señor; mi mano de noche se extendía sin cansarse; mi alma rehusaba consuelo.

**4** Me acuerdo de Dios y me conmuevo; medito, y mi espíritu desfallece. *Sela.*

**5** Tú sujetaste los párpados de mis ojos; estoy turbado y no puedo hablar.

**6** Pensé en los días de antaño, en los años de los siglos pasados.

**7** Recuerdo mi canto en la noche; converso con mi corazón, y mi espíritu indaga:

**8** ¿Rechazará el Señor para siempre y no volverá a complacerse?

**9** ¿Se habrá agotado para siempre su bondad? ¿Ha cesado su promesa por todas las generaciones?

**10** ¿Habrá olvidado Dios tener piedad, o habrá encerrado en su ira sus compasiones? *Sela.*

**11** Y dije: "Mi debilidad es que la diestra del Altísimo haya cambiado."

**12** Recordaré las obras de Yah; sí, recordaré tus maravillas de antaño.

**13** Meditaré en toda tu obra y hablaré de tus hazañas.

**14** Oh Dios, santo es tu camino. ¿Qué dios es grande como Dios?

**15** Tú eres el Dios que hace maravillas; has dado a conocer tu poder entre los pueblos.

**16** Con tu brazo redimiste a tu pueblo, a los hijos de Jacob y de José. *Sela.*

**17** Te vieron las aguas, oh Dios, te vieron las aguas y temblaron; también se estremecieron los abismos.

**18** Las nubes derramaron aguas, los cielos dieron su voz; también tus saetas iban de un lado a otro.

**19** La voz de tu trueno estaba en el torbellino; los relámpagos iluminaron el mundo; la tierra se estremeció y tembló.

**20** En el mar fue tu camino, y tu sendero en las aguas inmensas; tus huellas no fueron conocidas.

**21** Guiaste a tu pueblo como a un rebaño, por mano de Moisés y de Aarón.

## Notas sobre el texto
- **Estructura (explicación mía).** Los vv. 2-4 describen el clamor y el insomnio. Los vv. 8-10 formulan la duda con tres preguntas retóricas. El v. 11 es el punto de giro, y desde ahí el salmista cambia el recuerdo de su dolor por el recuerdo de los milagros.
- **v. 11, "jalotí hi".** Es un versículo difícil y se traduce de varias maneras. La lectura que seguí entiende "mi debilidad" o "mi dolencia es esta", es decir, el salmista se duele de que la diestra de Dios haya cambiado. Otra lectura entiende "mi herida / mi flaqueza", con matices distintos. No he consultado aquí los comentaristas, así que no atribuyo ninguna lectura a uno en concreto.
- **v. 16, "Jacob y José".** José se menciona junto a Jacob, quizá por ser quien sostuvo a la familia en Egipto. Esto es una observación mía, no de una fuente.
- **vv. 17-20.** Evocan la salida de Egipto y el cruce del mar. La frase "tus huellas no fueron conocidas" subraya que el camino de Dios es misterioso, igual que lo es en el sufrimiento del salmista.

Si quieres, puedo leer contigo los comentarios clásicos (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak, etc.) sobre los vv. 11 y 20. También puedo darte el texto hebreo verso por verso.

I assume you mean Chol HaMoed (the intermediate days of Pesach and Sukkot), since that is where this question usually comes up. As I remember it, those who wear tefillin on Chol HaMoed generally take them off before Hallel, or say Hallel without them. This is a community custom, not a universal rule.

## Key Takeaways
- Whether tefillin are worn on Chol HaMoed at all depends on community.
- Where they are worn, the common Ashkenazi practice is to remove them before Hallel.
- The reason is the dispute over whether Chol HaMoed has the status of a "sign" (*ot*) that makes tefillin unnecessary.
- Ashkenazim in Israel, most Sephardim, and Chabad don't wear tefillin on Chol HaMoed, so the question doesn't arise for them.
- This is not about Hallel being incompatible with tefillin on an ordinary weekday. It is specific to Chol HaMoed, and a separate Rosh Chodesh custom applies at Musaf.

## The background (as I recall it)
- **Who wears them on Chol HaMoed:**
  - Ashkenazim outside Israel generally do wear tefillin.
  - The Vilna Gaon's students and Ashkenazim in Israel generally don't.
  - Sephardim following the Shulchan Arukh and the Kabbalists (the Arizal) don't.
  - Chabad doesn't.
- **Why remove them for Hallel:** Chol HaMoed is a time when tefillin may not be needed, because the day itself is a sign. For that reason, those who wear tefillin treat Hallel, with its Yom Tov character, as a point to take them off. Another version of the custom is to put them on after Hallel is finished, or to skip the blessing. I'm unsure of the exact wording of the Shulchan Arukh and Rema on this, and of the Mishnah Berurah's conclusion. They are in [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 31:2] and [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 423] as far as I recall, but I haven't confirmed that.
- **Rosh Chodesh is different:** tefillin are worn all day. Some people remove them before Musaf, because Musaf has a Yom Tov-like character. They don't remove them for Hallel. This is a separate custom.

I paraphrase rather than quote at length, and you should confirm exact wording and references before you put them in a printed handout.

## Direct answer

The strongest sources for a Rosh Hashanah drasha on community are the Nitzavim passage, "You are standing today, all of you" [Deuteronomy 29:9]. It is usually read shortly before Rosh Hashanah. Add Hillel's "Do not separate yourself from the community" [Pirkei Avot 2:4]. Add Rambam's teaching that someone who separates from the community loses a share in the World to Come [Mishneh Torah, Repentance 3:11]. The liturgy itself supports the theme, because the confessions and petitions are all in the plural. Together they let you argue that the Days of Awe are a judgment of the individual, but that we stand for it as a community.

## Key Takeaways

- Nitzavim presents the covenant as made with everyone together, from "heads of tribes" to "water-drawers."
- Hillel and Rambam treat staying connected to the community as a precondition of repentance.
- The Rosh Hashanah liturgy speaks in the first-person plural (*Ashamnu*, *Avinu Malkeinu*, "Zochrenu lechayim").
- The shofar's *teruah* and *shevarim* are often read as a broken cry, which fits a community that gathers around its brokenness.
- Each source can be paired with a question about your own congregation's practice.

## Sources and how to use them

**1. Nitzavim: "Atem nitzavim hayom kulchem" [Deuteronomy 29:9-14]**
- Pshat: Moses gathers everyone, from leaders to the woodchopper and water-drawer, and also those "not here with us today" (v. 14). They enter the covenant together.
- Commentators to check: Rashi and Ramban on the verse. Rashi (as I recall) connects the gathering to Israel's survival after the curses of Ki Tavo. Verify this before citing.
- Midrash and later ideas: the Zohar and Hasidic readings treat "kulchem" (all of you) as meaning that each person completes the others. I haven't verified these, so check them before using them.
- Drasha angle: we are judged individually, yet we stand together. Who is "not here with us today" in your own community?

**2. Hillel: "Al tifrosh min hatzibbur" [Pirkei Avot 2:4]**
- Hillel's instruction is not to separate yourself from the community. Look at the neighboring clauses on not trusting yourself until the day of death.
- Drasha angle: self-improvement alone is not enough. Teshuvah in isolation is incomplete.

**3. Rambam on those who separate [Mishneh Torah, Repentance 3:11]**
- Rambam lists people who lose their share in the World to Come. Among them is one who separates from the community's ways, even without sinning. This is a strong text for the idea that community is a religious obligation.
- Related text: [Mishneh Torah, Repentance 2:4] says that teshuvah includes praying for one's fellow. Check the exact wording before citing it.

**4. Individual vs. community judgment [Rosh Hashanah 16a-18a]**
- The sugya discusses the judgment on Rosh Hashanah and the three books, including the "beinonim" (middling people) whose fate is held in suspense until Yom Kippur. Pay attention to the idea that the middling person's balance can be tipped.
- Drasha angle: your own mitzvah or kindness may tip the balance for a community that is evenly balanced. Rambam develops this in [Mishneh Torah, Repentance 3:4]. Verify the wording.

**5. Liturgy**
- Viddui (*Ashamnu, Bagadnu*) is said in the plural, as are *Avinu Malkeinu* and *Unetanneh Tokef*, which Ashkenazi and Conservative machzorim include. The Conservative *Machzor Lev Shalem* has commentary you could draw on.
- Drasha angle: we confess sins we may not personally have committed, because we are responsible for one another. The Talmud's *kol Yisrael arevim zeh bazeh* (all Israel are guarantors for each other) is found at [Shevuot 39a]. Verify the reference.

**6. Shofar**
- Teruah and shevarim are traditionally linked to Sisera's mother's cry (Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 33b). The ritual of blowing is done together, and hearing it is the mitzvah. Hearing from another person is itself a communal act.

## Suggested structure

1. Open with a question: if teshuvah is personal, why do we say it together?
2. Use Nitzavim for the covenant and Hillel for the principle.
3. Add Rambam as the strong, challenging text.
4. Add the beinoni idea for a hopeful close: you matter to the balance.
5. Close with the shofar, which does not work for anyone who isn't listening together.

answer:
Yes. Jewish tradition distinguishes between a person being **responsible** for their own choices and another person **praying or acting on their behalf**. The two don't conflict. Praying for a child's thoughts doesn't remove the child's accountability. It asks God to help, forgive, or strengthen them.

## Key Takeaways
- Responsibility is individual, but prayer and atonement for others are a recognized part of the Tanakh.
- Job's offering asks for forgiveness for a possible sin. It doesn't claim to take over his children's free will.
- The Tanakh has many examples of parents and leaders praying for the inner life of those they love.
- The Tanakh and later tradition see a parent's role as supporting a child's choices, not replacing them.

## What Job actually does
The verse reads: "Job would send word to them to sanctify themselves, and, rising early in the morning, he would make burnt offerings, one for each of them; for Job thought, 'Perhaps my children have sinned and blasphemed God in their thoughts.' This is what Job always used to do." [Job 1:5]

Three details matter:
- **Job doesn't act alone.** He first sends for his children to "sanctify themselves." They take part in their own purification, and the offering follows.
- **He says "perhaps."** He knows of no actual sin. The offering is precautionary, a way of saying "if anything went wrong, let it be forgiven."
- **It is an offering, not a verdict.** He doesn't claim to decide whether they sinned. He asks that any sin be pardoned.

I couldn't retrieve Rashi or other commentators on this verse just now, so I'm not quoting them. I'd be glad to look at them if you ask again.

## The principle of individual responsibility
The Torah and Prophets state that each person answers for their own sins. Ezekiel 18 is the classic text, and Deuteronomy 24:16 says the same about human courts. I'm citing these from memory because the lookup failed. Ezekiel's point is that no one is condemned *automatically* for a parent's sin, and the reverse also holds.

That doesn't mean one person can't intercede for another. Nothing in these passages says prayer for someone else is pointless. It says the other person's own deeds still count.

## Other examples of praying for others' hearts
- **David for Solomon.** He prays that God give Solomon "a whole heart" to keep the commandments [1 Chronicles 29:19]. I'm citing this from memory.
- **Moses for Israel.** After the golden calf, Moses pleads for the people, who had sinned of their own will [Exodus 32:32].
- **Abraham for Ishmael.** He says, "If only Ishmael might live by Your favor!" [Genesis 17:18].
- **Jacob's blessing of Ephraim and Manasseh.** It is the source of the custom of blessing children on Friday night [Genesis 48:20].

## Reconciling the two ideas
- **Free will stays intact.** A prayer doesn't force anyone to change. It can ask for circumstances, clarity, or inner strength that make good choices easier. Rambam's view of free will [Mishneh Torah, Repentance 5:1] leaves room for this, since God can still shape the setting in which we choose.
- **Prayer and atonement can help even when the other person's own repentance is still needed.** Job's practice looks like that. He prompts the children to sanctify themselves and also offers on their behalf.
- **Sin "in the heart."** Job worried about thoughts, which no court could judge. Only the person and God know them, so a parent's prayer is the only way to address something like that.

If you'd like, I can look at how specific commentators read Job's worry, or at the classic discussions of whether one person's merit can help another.

answer:
Rosh Hashanah's prayers are less about asking for things than about crowning God as King and standing honestly before Him. Below are four prayers, each with an insight you can share. I could only retrieve one Talmudic source today because the library was rate-limited, so I've marked what I did and didn't verify.

## Key Takeaways
- The Musaf *Amidah* (standing prayer) is built on three themes, *Malchuyot* (Kingship), *Zichronot* (Remembrance), and *Shofarot* (Shofar), and the Talmud treats them as the heart of the day.
- Kingship comes first because the day is about relationship and responsibility, not only judgment.
- *Unetaneh Tokef* pairs a frightening picture of judgment with a hopeful turn: repentance, prayer, and charity "avert the harsh decree."
- *Avinu Malkeinu* combines intimacy (Father) and authority (King), and its Talmudic origin is a prayer made in a time of drought.
- The shofar's cry is a prayer without words.

## 1. The three themes of Musaf: Malchuyot, Zichronot, Shofarot

**Source.** The Mishnah gives the order of the Rosh Hashanah Musaf blessings: the usual first three, then Kingship, Remembrances, and Shofarot, with the shofar sounded after each, and then the closing blessings [Rosh Hashanah 32a]. The Gemara asks where we learn that we say them. Rabbi Eliezer derives it from "a solemn rest, a memorial of blasts" (Leviticus 23:24): *zikhron* points to Remembrances and *teruah* points to Shofarot [Rosh Hashanah 32a]. Rabbi Yosei bar Yehudah, in the same passage, links Kingship to the verse "I am the Lord your God."

**Insight for your audience.**
- Each theme answers a different question. Kingship asks who we answer to. Remembrance asks whether we are known and remembered. Shofar asks how we are awakened.
- The Mishnah's debate about whether to blow the shofar after Kingship (Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri against Rabbi Akiva) shows the sages cared about the structure of the day.
- Each section is built from ten verses, drawn from the Torah, Writings, and Prophets. The Gemara raises the question of why ten, which suggests the number is itself meaningful. The service is anchored in Scripture, not in new poetry.

## 2. Unetaneh Tokef: "Who shall live and who shall die"

**What it says (my paraphrase, not retrieved today).** It describes God as Judge, witness, and record-keeper. The books are opened, the great shofar is sounded, and a "still small voice" is heard. It then lists the possible fates of the year ahead. It ends with the refrain *Teshuvah, Tefillah, u-Tzedakah ma'avirin et ro'a ha-gezeirah*: repentance, prayer, and charity avert the severity of the decree.

**Background.** The Talmud teaches that on Rosh Hashanah "three books are opened": one for the fully wicked, one for the fully righteous, and one for the in-between, whose judgment is suspended until Yom Kippur [Rosh Hashanah 16b]. I couldn't reload that text today, so check the exact wording before quoting it. The tradition that Rabbi Amnon of Mainz composed the prayer is a medieval legend, and scholars debate the prayer's origin.

**Insight.**
- The prayer doesn't deny that the future is uncertain. It says we can respond to it.
- The three responses cover three relationships: *teshuvah* is with oneself, *tefillah* is with God, and *tzedakah* is with other people.
- A question to ask the room is why the prayer names no specific sin. One answer is that it invites each person to fill in their own.

## 3. Avinu Malkeinu: "Our Father, our King"

**Source.** The Talmud tells of Rabbi Eliezer, who led a series of prayers during a drought and was not answered. Rabbi Akiva then prayed "Avinu Malkeinu, we have no king but You... have mercy on us," and rain came [Taanit 25b]. I couldn't retrieve the text today, so I'm giving the story from memory and you should confirm it before quoting.

**Insight.**
- The two titles are held together. A king can feel distant, and a father can feel too lenient. Saying both lets us approach God with awe and with trust.
- Many congregations say it as a list of requests, such as "write us in the book of life" and "have mercy on us." Many Ashkenazi communities begin it with the confession "we have sinned before You."
- It is usually omitted on Shabbat, since requests are not made on Shabbat. Where the day falls on Shabbat, customs vary on this point.

## 4. The shofar as prayer

**Source.** The Gemara above connects *teruah* (the broken blasts) to Shofarot and to the verse "a memorial of blasts" [Rosh Hashanah 32a]. Rambam describes the shofar as a call to wake up, in his laws of repentance, but I did not retrieve his text today. Cite it only after checking.

**Insight.**
- The shofar is wordless and has no translation. It is the sound of a person with no more words.
- A practical exercise is to ask the audience to listen to the first blast and think of one thing they want to change.

## Suggested format for the service
1. Open with a short question, such as "What does it mean to crown someone king?"
2. Read one passage (for example, the Mishnah on the three themes).
3. Ask the congregants what Kingship, Remembrance, and Shofar each mean to them.
4. End with the shofar.

## Note on sources
I'd recommend reading the Mishnah and Gemara directly, since I could only retrieve them in part. If you tell me your community (Ashkenazi, Sephardi, or Chabad), I can adjust the customs. I can also write a full 500–900 word dvar Torah on any one of these prayers once the library is available again.

answer:
The *Amidah* (literally "standing") is the central prayer of every Jewish service. It is also called *Shemoneh Esreh* ("Eighteen," after the original eighteen blessings) or simply *HaTefillah* ("the Prayer"). It is said silently, standing, with feet together and facing Jerusalem. It consists of blessings of praise, petition, and thanksgiving. This answer draws on my general knowledge of the prayer and its sources. I did not look up the texts in this session, so I cite no specific references.

## Key Takeaways

- The Amidah is the core prayer of Jewish worship, said at every weekday, Shabbat, and festival service.
- Weekday versions have 19 blessings (originally 18), and Shabbat and festival versions have 7.
- It follows a three-part structure: praise, requests, and thanksgiving.
- Its origins are tied to the Men of the Great Assembly and to the patriarchs, and the Talmud connects it to the daily offerings.
- It is said quietly and standing, and in many communities it is then repeated aloud by the prayer leader.

## Structure

**1. Praise (*Shevach*), the first three blessings**
- *Avot* (Patriarchs): God as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who remembers the kindness of the fathers.
- *Gevurot* (God's might): God sustains the living and revives the dead. In winter we add mention of rain.
- *Kedushat HaShem* (God's holiness).

**2. Requests (*Bakashah*), the middle blessings**
On weekdays there are 13 petitions. They cover:
- wisdom and understanding
- repentance and forgiveness
- redemption
- healing
- prosperity (blessing of the years)
- the ingathering of exiles
- justice
- the downfall of wrongdoers
- support for the righteous
- the rebuilding of Jerusalem
- the Davidic kingdom
- the acceptance of prayer

On Shabbat and festivals these weekday requests are replaced by a single blessing about the sanctity of the day. This is so that we do not trouble ourselves with personal needs on a day of rest.

**3. Thanksgiving (*Hoda'ah*), the final three blessings**
- *Avodah* (desire for the service to be accepted)
- *Modim* (gratitude for daily miracles)
- *Birkat Shalom* (peace)

Many people add personal prayers at the end, before taking three steps back.

## Origins and Meaning

According to the Talmud, the Men of the Great Assembly established the Amidah, and Rabban Gamliel's court later arranged the nineteenth blessing (against slanderers and heretics). The Talmud also teaches that the three daily prayers correspond to the patriarchs (Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob) and to the daily offerings in the Temple. That is why there are three daily Amidot: Shacharit (morning), Minchah (afternoon), and Ma'ariv (evening). Additional Amidot are said on Shabbat, festivals, and Rosh Chodesh (*Musaf*), and on Yom Kippur (*Ne'ilah*).

## Customs of Practice

- **Standing with feet together:** this is meant to resemble angels, who are described as having a single straight leg.
- **Bowing:** one bows at the beginning and end of the first blessing, and at *Modim* and the end of the prayer.
- **Silent prayer:** this follows Hannah, who prayed with her lips moving but her voice unheard (1 Samuel 1).
- **Steps:** before starting, take three steps forward, like approaching a king. At the end, take three steps back.

Details vary between Ashkenazi, Sefardi, and Chabad customs, so ask a rabbi about your own tradition.

If you'd like, I can go through the text of any blessing in a particular siddur (Ashkenaz, Sefard, or Edot HaMizrach) and explain it phrase by phrase.

answer:
The "thank you, Hashem" prayer you mean is most likely **Modeh Ani**. It's the short thanks a Jew says on waking up each morning. I couldn't reach the library to check the text just now, so this is from memory and I've left out citations.

**Modeh Ani** (said on waking, before washing hands):

> מוֹדֶה אֲנִי לְפָנֶיךָ מֶלֶךְ חַי וְקַיָּם, שֶׁהֶחֱזַרְתָּ בִּי נִשְׁמָתִי בְּחֶמְלָה, רַבָּה אֱמוּנָתֶךָ.

"I gratefully thank You, living and eternal King, for You have returned my soul within me with compassion; great is Your faithfulness."

## Key Takeaways
- Modeh Ani is the standard Jewish "thank you, God" prayer for the morning.
- It thanks God for returning the soul after sleep, so each day is treated as a gift.
- It is short, and it has no divine Name in it. That is why it can be said right on waking, before washing hands.
- Other "thank you" prayers exist, such as *Modim*, *Birkat HaGomel*, and *Birkat HaMazon*.

## Meaning
- **Modeh** means both "thank" and "acknowledge." You are admitting that your life is not something you own by right.
- **"Returned my soul"**: the tradition sees sleep as a small taste of death, so waking is a renewal of life.
- **"Great is Your faithfulness"** echoes the verse in Lamentations 3:23. It means that God trusts us with another day.
- The prayer is a later custom, not part of the Talmudic liturgy. It is widely accepted among Ashkenazim and Sephardim alike.

## Other "thank you" prayers
- **Modim**: the "we thank You" blessing in the Amidah, the central standing prayer. It is said three times a day.
- **Birkat HaMazon**: Grace after Meals, the Torah's commandment to thank God after eating and being satisfied (Deuteronomy 8:10).
- **Birkat HaGomel**: a blessing of thanks after surviving danger, such as illness, travel, or childbirth.
- **Hodu**: the Psalms of thanksgiving at the start of morning prayers, such as Psalm 100, "A Psalm of Thanksgiving."

answer:
Kaddish is an ancient prayer, written mostly in Aramaic, that praises and sanctifies God's name and asks for His kingdom to be established soon. It isn't a prayer *about* death. It is best known as the Mourner's Kaddish, which mourners say after the death of a close relative. In fact, Kaddish has several forms that mark transitions in the prayer service.

## Key Takeaways
- Kaddish is a public declaration of God's greatness and holiness, not a prayer about death.
- Its central line is the congregation's response: *Yehei shmei rabba mevorach le'olam ule'olmei olmaya* ("May His great name be blessed forever and for all eternity").
- It is said only with a *minyan* (a quorum of ten adults), because it is a public sanctification of God's name.
- There are several versions: Half Kaddish, Full Kaddish, Rabbis' Kaddish and Mourner's Kaddish.
- Mourners say it to honor the deceased by leading the community in praise of God, even in grief.

## What it says
It opens: *Yitgadal v'yitkadash shmei rabba* ("Magnified and sanctified be His great name"). It then asks that God's kingdom be revealed "in your lifetime and in your days." The congregation answers with *Yehei shmei rabba*.

The text then piles up words of praise: blessed, praised, glorified, exalted. It ends with a request for peace: *Oseh shalom bimromav…* ("He who makes peace in His heights, may He make peace upon us and upon all Israel").

The Mourner's Kaddish doesn't mention death at all. In the face of loss, the mourner publicly affirms God's greatness.

## Sources and background
- **The response to Kaddish is treated as very significant.** [Berakhot 3a] records a teaching in the name of Elijah. When Israel enters synagogues and study houses and answers *Yehei shmei hagadol mevorach*, the Holy One, Blessed be He, "shakes His head" (*menaanea rosho*). The passage continues past what I could read here, so I'm not reconstructing the rest. Even so, it shows how weighty the Sages considered the response.
- **Its roots are probably biblical.** The phrases echo verses such as [Ezekiel 38:23] ("I will magnify Myself and sanctify Myself") and [Daniel 2:20]. I couldn't pull up Daniel just now, so treat that comparison as my own observation.
- **The Aramaic** was the everyday language of the Jewish masses when the prayer took shape. That is a common explanation for the language, though scholars and commentators give other reasons too.

## The forms of Kaddish
- **Half Kaddish** (*Chatzi Kaddish*) separates sections of the service, such as before the Amidah.
- **Full Kaddish** (*Kaddish Shalem*) ends a major section. It adds a request that our prayers be accepted.
- **Rabbis' Kaddish** (*Kaddish d'Rabbanan*) is said after studying Torah. It includes a prayer for teachers and students.
- **Mourner's Kaddish** is said by mourners. Tradition holds that it helps elevate the soul of the departed, since a child's public sanctification of God's name brings merit to the parent. This understanding developed in the medieval period, so it is a later custom, not a Talmudic law.

## Practice
Ashkenazi custom is for a child to say Kaddish for a parent for eleven months, and for other close relatives for thirty days. Details vary by community, including who may say it and whether mourners say it together. Those details are matters of halacha and minhag, so consult your rabbi for your personal situation.

answer:
Je ne vous donnerai pas de vocalisation pour prononcer ce Nom, parce que la tradition juive ne le prononce pas comme il est écrit. Je n'ai pas pu rouvrir les sources à l'instant (Sefaria ne répondait pas), donc je les résume de mémoire, sans citation littérale.

## Key Takeaways
- Les voyelles de יְהוָה dans le texte massorétique ne sont pas celles du Nom lui-même.
- Elles viennent de *Adonaï* (אֲדֹנָי), et elles signalent au lecteur de dire « Adonaï ».
- La voyelle que vous cherchez est le *holam* (ֹ). Elle donnerait יְהֹוָה, d'où la forme « Jéhovah », qui est une construction hybride et non une prononciation authentique.
- La vraie prononciation du Nom (le Tétragramme) ne s'est pas transmise publiquement. La pratique est de lire « Adonaï », et hors de la prière ou de l'étude, de dire « HaShem » (« le Nom »).

## Explication

**Ce que montre la vocalisation.** Dans la Bible, le Nom est écrit יְהוָה, avec un *shva* sous le י et un *kamats* sous le ו. Ces signes rappellent ceux de אֲדֹנָי. Le *holam* de אֲדֹנָי, le « o » du milieu, n'est pas reporté. On voit alors que ces voyelles servent de rappel de lecture (*qeré*, ce qu'on lit). Elles ne notent pas une prononciation (*ketiv*, ce qui est écrit). En ajoutant le *holam*, on obtient יְהֹוָה. C'est cette forme, mélange des consonnes du Nom et des voyelles de *Adonaï*, qui a donné « Jéhovah » à la Renaissance.

**Ce que dit la tradition.**
- Le Talmud, au traité Kiddoushin 71a, rapporte, si ma mémoire est bonne, que le Nom n'est pas lu comme il est écrit : il s'écrit avec *yod-hé* et se lit avec *alef-dalet*, c'est-à-dire *Adonaï*. Cet enseignement est à vérifier dans le texte.
- La Michna (Sota 7:6) et Sanhédrin 90a limitent la prononciation du Nom : à l'époque du Temple, il n'était dit que dans le service sacré, et l'on mettait en garde contre son usage ordinaire.
- Aujourd'hui, la pratique universelle est la suivante. À la prière et à la lecture de la Torah, on dit *Adonaï*. Dans la conversation et l'étude, on dit *HaShem*.

**Pourquoi on ne peut pas « reconstituer » la prononciation.** La vocalisation d'origine n'est pas connue avec certitude. Les reconstitutions modernes (« Yahvé » et autres) sont des hypothèses de chercheurs, sans autorité dans la tradition juive. On évite aussi de prononcer par jeu les formes reconstituées, comme « Jéhovah », parce que le respect dû au Nom s'applique à tout essai de le prononcer.

Pour une question pratique, par exemple comment lire ce Nom dans une prière ou un texte précis, consultez votre rabbin.

Je ne reconnais pas « Alef-Hei-Vav-Yud » (אהוי) comme un nom divin classique. Je ne veux donc pas inventer une explication. Vous pensez peut-être à *Ehyeh* (אהיה, Alef-Hei-Yud-Hei), ou à un nom de la tradition kabbalistique qui combine ces lettres. Pouvez-vous me dire où vous l'avez rencontré ?

## Points clés
- Les lettres A-H-V-Y n'ont pas, à ma connaissance, de statut de nom sacré à part entière dans les sources classiques que je peux vérifier.
- Le nom le plus proche est *Ehyeh* (אֶהְיֶה), « Je serai », révélé à Moïse au buisson ardent.
- Les lettres א-ה-ו-י ressemblent aussi à celles du Tétragramme (י-ה-ו-ה), avec un *alef* à la place du second *hei*.
- La tradition déconseille de prononcer les noms divins et d'expérimenter avec eux sans maître.

## Ce que je peux dire avec certitude

**1. Ehyeh (אהיה).** Dans [Exodus 3:14], Dieu répond à Moïse : « Ehyeh asher Ehyeh » (« Je serai ce que je serai »). Ce passage est la source de ce nom. Je n'ai pas pu relire le verset ni Rashi à l'instant, car l'accès à la bibliothèque est limité. Je le cite donc de mémoire, sans détailler les commentaires.

Dans la Kabbalah, *Ehyeh* est généralement associé à la sefira *Keter* (la « couronne »). Je le dis de mémoire, sans source vérifiée ici.

**2. Un lien avec le Tétragramme.** Les lettres *yod, hei, vav* sont celles du nom de quatre lettres (*Havayah*). Dans les écrits kabbalistiques, ce nom est « rempli » de différentes façons, et chaque remplissage donne un total numérique différent. Un *alef* y apparaît parfois. Mais je ne peux pas affirmer que « אהוי » est l'un de ces noms, et je ne veux pas inventer.

**3. Une précaution.** La tradition recommande de ne pas prononcer les noms divins en dehors de leur usage prévu. Elle recommande aussi de ne pas utiliser les noms kabbalistiques comme formules ou méditations sans enseignant. Je me limite donc à l'étude des sources.

- où vous avez vu ce nom (livre, prière, amulette, cours) ;
- si vous pensiez à *Ehyeh* (אהיה) ou à un autre nom.

Je pourrai alors chercher la source exacte et vous l'expliquer.

answer:
Oui, c'est une observation de type *gematria*/notarikon, donc un jeu de lecture (*drash*) et non une preuve. Elle repose sur le fait que אִילָן (*ilan*, « arbre ») contient les lettres אין (*ayin*, « rien, néant »), plus ל et un second mot.

## Key Takeaways

- אילן s'écrit א-י-ל-ן, et les lettres א-י-ן y forment אין, « rien ».
- Le mot est donc אין avec un ל ajouté entre le י et le ן.
- C'est une lecture homilétique, sans valeur de preuve linguistique.
- La racine réelle de *ilan* est en araméen et en hébreu mishnaïque, sans lien avec *ayin*.

## Ce que l'on voit dans le mot

Les lettres sont **א** (1), **י** (10), **ל** (30) et **ן** (50), soit 91 au total. Si l'on retire le ל, il reste **אין**, « il n'y a pas ». Une lecture possible est que l'arbre a en lui un « néant ». C'est le point de départ d'où naît la croissance, comme la graine qui doit « disparaître » pour donner l'arbre.

Le ל peut aussi se lire comme un élan vers le haut. Le ל est la lettre la plus haute de l'alphabet, qui dépasse la ligne. Il s'élève donc au-dessus du « rien ». Ce point est mon interprétation, et je n'ai pas vérifié qu'une source classique le dise.

Il y a aussi un lien de valeur numérique : 91 est la valeur de אמן et de יהוה × אדני (26 + 65). Ce lien relève lui aussi du jeu homilétique.

## Pshat (sens simple)

Le mot אילן vient de l'araméen et de l'hébreu mishnaïque. En hébreu biblique, « arbre » se dit עץ (*ets*). On trouve אילן dans la Mishna, par exemple dans les lois de *orlah* et de *shevi'it*. Il est apparenté à l'araméen de Daniel (אִילָנָא, Daniel 4), où il désigne l'arbre du rêve de Nebuchadnetsar. Aucun lien d'étymologie avec אין n'est établi. Je n'ai pas fait de recherche dans Sefaria pour cette réponse, donc je ne cite pas de référence précise.

## Pour aller plus loin

Dans la pensée hassidique et kabbalistique, *ayin* (le néant) désigne la source divine, au-delà de toute définition. La lecture « l'arbre contient le *ayin* » rejoint cette idée, mais je ne peux pas affirmer qu'une source précise fasse ce lien pour le mot *ilan*. Si cela t'intéresse, je peux chercher dans les textes hassidiques pour voir si cette lecture y apparaît.

**Réponse courte :** je n'ai trouvé aucun rapport traditionnel entre ces deux expressions et les 22 lettres de l'alphabet. Un lien existe seulement par un calcul de lettres, que je donne ici comme jeu homilétique (*drash*) et non comme source. Les outils Sefaria ont échoué à l'instant (erreur 429). Je n'ai donc pas pu relire le verset ni chercher dans les sources, et je cite le texte de mémoire.

## Points clés
- Les deux expressions sont dans [Exodus 3:1] : « וּמֹשֶׁה הָיָה רֹעֶה **אֶת־צֹאן** יִתְרוֹ… וַיִּנְהַג **אֶת־הַצֹּאן** אַחַר הַמִּדְבָּר ».
- Je ne connais aucun commentateur qui relie ces deux expressions aux 22 lettres. Je n'invente donc pas de source.
- Le calcul des lettres donne un résultat curieux : 5 + 6 = 11, et 11 × 2 = 22.
- Ce calcul est ma propre remarque, pas une tradition. Il ne prouve rien.

## Le sens simple (*pshat*)
Le verset dit d'abord que Moïse est berger du troupeau de Jéthro. Il dit ensuite qu'il mène « le troupeau » au-delà du désert. Le « ha- » (הַ) de la deuxième mention est un article défini : le troupeau est déjà connu, parce qu'il vient d'être nommé. Il n'y a donc là aucun signe d'un message sur l'alphabet.

## Le calcul des lettres (mon observation)
- **אֶת־צֹאן** compte 5 lettres : א, ת, צ, א, ן.
- **אֶת־הַצֹּאן** compte 6 lettres : א, ת, ה, צ, א, ן.
- Total : 11 lettres, soit la moitié de 22.

Si l'on compte les lettres finales comme des lettres distinctes, l'alphabet en compte 27 (22 + 5 formes finales). Cela affaiblit encore le rapprochement.

## Si l'on cherche un lien thématique
Le *Midrash* (je crois dans *Shemot Rabbah* 2, à vérifier) décrit Moïse comme un bon berger. Il y raconte que Moïse a porté un chevreau fatigué, et que D.ieu en a conclu qu'il était digne de faire paître Israël. Une lecture homilétique pourrait dire que ce berger recevra ensuite la Torah, écrite avec les 22 lettres. Ce serait une idée à développer, pas une explication connue du verset.

answer:
Réessayons avec une seule requête.Dans [Exodus 3:15], « זֶה־שְּׁמִי לְעֹלָם » désigne le Nom divin de quatre lettres (le Tétragramme, י-ה-ו-ה). Dieu le présente à Moïse comme son nom propre, valable « pour toujours ». La tradition rabbinique ajoute que ce nom ne se prononce pas comme il s'écrit.

**Précision :** le serveur de Sefaria a refusé mes requêtes (erreur 429). Je n'ai donc pas pu relire les textes en direct. Les citations ci-dessous viennent de ma mémoire et les traductions sont les miennes. Les références sont à vérifier. Je ne mets entre guillemets que ce dont je suis sûr.

## Key Takeaways

- Le verset donne à Moïse la réponse à la question « quel est son nom ? » : le Nom de quatre lettres, appelé « mon nom pour toujours ».
- Le mot *le'olam* (לְעֹלָם) est écrit sans *vav* dans le texte de la Torah. Le Talmud y lit une allusion à la dissimulation du Nom (*le'alem*, « cacher »).
- Le Talmud enseigne que ce Nom s'écrit י-ה-ו-ה mais se lit autrement, et que cela changera dans le monde à venir.
- Les commentateurs divergent sur le sens du nom : présence de Dieu auprès d'Israël, ou Être absolu et nécessaire.

## Le contexte (pshat)

Au buisson ardent, Moïse demande comment répondre si les enfants d'Israël lui demandent le nom de Celui qui l'envoie. Dieu répond d'abord *Ehyeh asher Ehyeh* ([Exodus 3:14]). Il enchaîne ensuite, au verset 15, en disant à peu près ceci :

> « כֹּה תֹאמַר אֶל־בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵי אֲבֹתֵיכֶם … שְׁלָחַנִי אֲלֵיכֶם, זֶה־שְּׁמִי לְעֹלָם וְזֶה זִכְרִי לְדֹר דֹּר »

« Tu diras ainsi aux enfants d'Israël : l'Éternel, Dieu de vos pères… m'a envoyé vers vous. Tel est mon nom pour toujours, et tel est mon souvenir de génération en génération. »

Les deux membres du verset sont parallèles :

- *shemi* (« mon nom ») correspond à *zikhri* (« mon souvenir »). Le nom est ce par quoi Dieu est invoqué et rappelé.
- *le'olam* (« pour toujours ») correspond à *le-dor dor* (« de génération en génération »). Ce nom ne sera pas remplacé.

Le verset relie ainsi le Nom à l'identité de Dieu comme « Dieu des pères ». Il y a une continuité entre les patriarches et la rédemption qui commence.

## Le mot לְעֹלָם : écrit « caché »

Dans la Torah, ce mot est écrit sans *vav* (לעלם). On peut donc le lire *le'alem*, « pour cacher ». C'est la lecture que fait le Talmud, notamment dans [Kiddushin 71a]. Selon cette lecture, le verset dit : « Voici mon nom, à cacher ». Rashi signale lui aussi cette orthographe défective dans son commentaire sur ce verset ([Rashi on Exodus 3:15]). Cette lecture relève de la *drash* (interprétation homilétique). Elle ne remplace pas le sens simple « pour toujours », elle s'y ajoute.

## Écrit autrement qu'il n'est lu

Le Talmud, dans [Pesachim 50a], enseigne que dans ce monde le Nom s'écrit avec *yod-hé* (י-ה) puis *vav-hé* (ו-ה), mais se lit avec *aleph-dalet* (*Adonaï*). Dans le monde à venir, il sera lu comme il est écrit. D'où l'usage de dire *Adonaï* dans la prière et la lecture, et *HaShem* (« le Nom ») dans la conversation. Dans le Temple, selon la Mishna (Yoma, Sota), le Nom était prononcé dans des circonstances particulières, notamment par le Grand Prêtre à Yom Kippour. Cette prononciation s'est perdue.

## Le sens du nom : deux lectures classiques

- **Rashi (sur Exodus 3:14)** : *Ehyeh* signifie « je serai avec eux dans cette détresse, comme je serai avec eux dans les oppressions futures ». Le Nom exprime donc une présence auprès d'Israël. C'est un enseignement qu'il rapporte du Talmud (Berakhot 9b).
- **Maïmonide (Guide des égarés I, 63)** : ce Nom exprime l'existence absolue, l'Être dont l'existence est nécessaire. Il est aussi le seul nom qui ne désigne pas Dieu à travers une action ou un attribut, et c'est pourquoi on l'appelle *shem ha-meforash*.

Ces deux lectures ne se contredisent pas forcément. L'une met l'accent sur la relation de Dieu avec Israël, l'autre sur sa nature propre. Je cite Maïmonide de mémoire, donc la formulation exacte reste à vérifier.

## Conséquence pratique

Ce verset est la source habituelle du respect dû au Nom : on ne le prononce pas tel qu'il est écrit, et on prend soin des écrits qui le contiennent. Pour les règles précises (écriture, effacement, usage dans la conversation), consultez votre rabbin.

Si vous voulez, je peux relire les textes cités dès que Sefaria répond à nouveau, ou approfondir un angle précis : Rashi, Ramban, Maïmonide ou la Kabbale.

answer:
Gematria equivalence doesn't claim that two words are the same thing. It claims that their *numerical values* match, and the tradition treats that match as a hint that the two concepts are connected at a deeper level. The match is a pointer for interpretation, not a proof.

## Key Takeaways

- Gematria compares the numerical value of letters, not the meaning of the words.
- Two words with the same value stay distinct in meaning. The tradition reads the shared value as a hint of a hidden link.
- The sages treat gematria as a homiletic tool (*drash*), not a source of proof.
- Your question is a good one: a number is a quantity, while a concept is a quality. The mystics answer that letters are more than labels.

## The plain point: it is a tool, not an identity

In Hebrew the letters double as numbers (א=1 … י=10 … ק=100 … ת=400). Every word therefore has a numerical sum. Take *chai* (חי, "life"): ח=8 and י=10, so 18. This is why 18 is a number of blessing.

Two words that share a sum are not the same word. Gematria just says: "Look at these two together. Why might they share a value?" Its role is similar to a pun or a wordplay in a sermon. It points toward an insight, and the insight has to stand on other grounds.

The tradition is explicit about this limit. Gematria is counted among the interpretive tools of the sages, and the classic principle is that one does not derive law from it. The Torah's own methods of reading (*middot*) include it as a lesser, supportive tool. The Talmud itself uses gematria as a hint (*asmachta*), not as a proof. I am stating this from general knowledge and have not looked up a specific passage here. If you want, I can find the source for you.

## Your deeper question: how can number relate to concept?

You are right that magnitude and meaning are different categories. Here are three traditional answers.

- **Letters are not only symbols.** In Kabbalah the Hebrew letters are the building blocks of creation. *Sefer Yetzirah* describes God creating the world through the letters. If the letters are the real structure behind things, then a number carried by them is part of that structure. It is not a random label.
- **The numerical value is a "root".** On this view, a word's value shows the root energy or channel of the thing it names. Two words with the same value can share a root, while remaining different expressions of it. They are like two branches of one tree.
- **Number as a language of relationship.** Some writers use number the way music uses ratio. Two different notes can be related by an interval without being the same note. Equal value is one kind of relationship, and the interpreter has to ask what the relationship teaches.

A caution applies here. These are mystical and homiletic readings. They are not claims that the words are equal in meaning, and different schools use gematria with very different degrees of seriousness. I have given you the general ideas and have not quoted particular texts.

## A practical way to think about it

When someone shows you a gematria match, ask three questions:

1. Is the arithmetic correct? Different methods exist, such as standard value, reduced value and ordinal value, and they give different results.
2. Does the link illuminate something that is already supported by the verse or the teaching?
3. Is it presented as a hint, or as a proof? Only the first is traditional.

answer:
**The most direct word for "mountain" is *har* (הַר) itself.** It is the standard word in the Torah and in modern Hebrew. Its sense of "elevation" comes from its being a mountain, so the word's basic meaning is not metaphorical. Where *har* seems to point to something "elevated," that is usually because mountains are the high places in the biblical landscape.

## Key Takeaways
- *Har* (pl. *harim*, הרים) is the plain Hebrew word for "mountain," in the Torah and today.
- Words like *givah* (hill) and *ramah* (height) are related to *har* but are not synonyms for it.
- The "elevated" connotations of *har* are extensions of the literal meaning, such as Temple Mount, holy ascent, or a lofty place.
- In Mishnaic Hebrew and Aramaic, *tur* (טוּר) is a further word for "mountain."

## Plain meaning: *har*
The word *har* is the ordinary word for a mountain. Examples:
- *Har Sinai* (הר סיני), the mountain of the giving of the Torah.
- *Har Ararat* (הרי אררט), where the ark rested, in [Genesis 8:4]. I couldn't retrieve the verse text just now, so I'm citing it from memory.
- *Har HaZeitim*, the Mount of Olives, and *Har HaCarmel*, Mount Carmel. Both names are still in everyday use.

The usual scholarly view is that the root is ה-ר-ר. Related words from the same root include *harari* (הררי, "mountainous") and *harar* (הרר, "mountain-range," poetic).

## Related words that are not quite "mountain"
- **גִּבְעָה (*givah*)**: a hill. It often appears paired with *har* to mean "mountains and hills." An example is Isaiah 40:4, *kol har v'givah*. I couldn't fetch the verse for this answer.
- **רָמָה (*ramah*)** and **בָּמָה (*bamah*)**: a height or high place. *Bamah* is also a cultic "high place," so it has a religious sense as well as a geographic one.
- **סֶלַע (*sela*)** and **צוּר (*tzur*)**: a rock or cliff, not a mountain.
- **תֵּל (*tel*)**: a mound, usually the remains of an ancient city.
- **טוּר (*tur*)**: Aramaic and Mishnaic Hebrew for "mountain." The Targumim often render *har* as *tura*, as in *Tur Sinai*. It is also used in Hebrew for "mountain" in some names, such as *Tur Malka*.

## Why *har* seems to mean more than "mountain"
Because mountains are high places, the Tanakh uses *har* for:
- A place of divine encounter, such as Sinai and Moriah.
- The elevated place of the Temple, *Har HaBayit* or *Har Hashem*.
- Spiritual ascent. The verse "Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord?" (*mi ya'aleh b'har Hashem*, Psalms 24:3) is the classic example. I'm citing it from memory.

The Sages and later commentators often draw on this connotation of lofty holiness. That is a layer of *drash* (homiletic interpretation), built on the plain meaning "mountain."

If you want, I can look up a specific verse, or the wording of Rashi or Radak on *har*, once the library is reachable again.

answer:
The standard term is *Or Ein Sof* (אוֹר אֵין סוֹף, "light without end"), and it is spelled only with an *aleph*. Spelling it with an *ayin* doesn't give an alternate version of the same phrase. It gives a different word.

## Key Takeaways
- *Ein* (אֵין, "there is not / without") starts with *aleph*, so *Ein Sof* means "without end."
- *Ayin* spelled with an *ayin* (עַיִן) means "eye" or "spring," so "Ayin Sof" would not mean "infinite."
- A similar-sounding word, *Ayin* (אַיִן, "nothingness"), is spelled with an *aleph*. Kabbalah uses it for the highest divine level, and it is a separate concept from *Ein Sof*.
- Kabbalists do connect these terms, but through wordplay on the *aleph* spelling.

## The words
- **אֵין** (*ein*) is built on the root א-י-ן. It means "there is not," and in *Ein Sof* it means "without." Its numerical value is 1+10+50 = 61.
- **עַיִן** (*ayin*) is the "eye" or "spring" root, ע-י-ן. Its value is 70+10+50 = 130. It has no negative sense of "without," so it can't carry the meaning "infinite."
- **אַיִן** (*ayin*, "nothingness") is spelled like אֵין, with an *aleph*. Only the vowels differ, and the vowels are why people confuse the two.

## Where the confusion comes from
In Kabbalah, *Ayin* (nothingness) is a name for the highest level, *Keter*, or the divine "no-thing" beyond any description. *Ein Sof* is the Infinite itself, which has no limit. Because the two are spelled almost the same, later writers often link them. The link is in the *aleph* spelling, not in an alternate *ayin* spelling. Treat gematria and letter play like this as homiletic (*drash*), not as proof.

The question looks incomplete, and it also has a problem. No single Hebrew letter equals 63. The letters run 1–9, then 10–90 in tens, then 100–400 (א=1 … ט=9, י=10 … צ=90, ק=100 … ת=400). So 63 can only be a combination of letters, such as ס״ג (Samekh 60 + Gimel 3).

**Key Takeaways**
- No single letter has the value 63.
- 63 is written with two letters: ס״ג (60 + 3).
- ס״ג is the Kabbalistic name of the world of *Beriah* and the "Sag" level of the Divine Name (Name of 63).
- Perhaps you meant 60 (*Samekh*, "support") or 6/3 (*Vav* "hook/nail", *Gimel* "camel/kindness").

**What 63 can be**

**Deker (דֶּקֶר)** is a rare Hebrew name. It comes from a root meaning "to pierce" or "to stab." It is not a common given name in the Torah and has no well-known spiritual tradition attached to it.

## Key Takeaways
- Deker comes from the root ד־ק־ר (*d-k-r*), "to pierce or stab."
- In the Bible it appears only in the name "Ben-Deker" ("son of Deker"), one of King Solomon's district officers.
- I know of no classic commentary that interprets the name symbolically, so any "significance" beyond its meaning is modern or personal.
- In modern Hebrew, *dekar* is related to words for stabbing, and the name is used mostly as a surname or in Western settings.

## Meaning and root
The root ד־ק־ר means to pierce through. Related forms appear in Tanakh, for example *midkerot* (מַדְקְרוֹת), "piercings" or "stabbings," in Proverbs 12:18. Biblical Hebrew uses it for a physical thrust, such as a spear or sword. Modern Hebrew uses it the same way: *dakar* means "he stabbed." I did not retrieve those examples here, so check them before relying on them. The name Deker therefore literally means "a piercing" or "a stab." It may originally have described a sharp, spear-bearing, or strong person, but that is my inference. The sources I found don't explain the name.

## Biblical appearance
Deker appears only once, as the father of one of Solomon's twelve officials who supplied the royal court:

> "בֶּן־דֶּקֶר בְּמָקַץ וּבְשַׁעַלְבִים וּבֵית שָׁמֶשׁ וְאֵילוֹן בֵּית חָנָן"
> "Ben-deker, in Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh, and Elon-beth-hanan" [I Kings 4:9]

Nothing more is said about Deker himself. The verse only places his son's district in the territory of Dan and Judah, near Beth-Shemesh. Some translations render "Ben-Deker" as a personal name and others as "son of Deker." The Hebrew can be read either way.

## Significance
- **Textual:** The name shows how Solomon's administration was organized by district (see the surrounding verses, I Kings 4:7–19).
- **Spiritual or traditional:** I found no midrash or classic commentary that expounds the name. Names meaning "piercing" are not typical Jewish given names, which is probably why it is rare.
- **Gematria (homiletic only, not proof):** דקר = ד(4) + ק(100) + ר(200) = 304.

answer:
**Short answer:** The Hebrew *nachash* (נָחָשׁ, "snake") is usually linked to the root נ-ח-ש. That root is tied to hissing or whispering, and to the practice of divination or "reading omens" (*nichush*). There is no single agreed etymology, and the sources below are drawn from memory. I did not look them up in this conversation. The Hebrew roots and the Genesis 3:1 wording are well established, but check the details against the texts before you rely on them.

**Key Takeaways**
- *Nachash* is a three-letter root noun, נחש, meaning "snake."
- The same letters give *nichush* (divination, omen-reading) and *menachesh* (a diviner).
- Many scholars connect the root to a hissing or whispering sound, which would make the word onomatopoeic.
- Related Semitic words include Arabic *ḥanash* (snake) and Aramaic *nachsha*, though the cognate details are debated.
- Chazal and the commentators also read the word homiletically, which is not etymology in the linguistic sense.

## Pshat and linguistic background

**Root and meaning.** The noun נָחָשׁ is the standard biblical word for a snake. It appears first in [Genesis 3:1], which describes the snake as "עָרוּם מִכֹּל חַיַּת הַשָּׂדֶה," "more cunning than any beast of the field."

**The verb.** The same root gives the verb נִחֵשׁ, "to practice divination" or "to take an omen." Joseph's steward says of the goblet, "הֲלוֹא זֶה אֲשֶׁר יִשְׁתֶּה אֲדֹנִי בּוֹ וְהוּא נַחֵשׁ יְנַחֵשׁ בּוֹ" ([Genesis 44:5]). Laban says "נִחַשְׁתִּי וַיְבָרֲכֵנִי ה׳" ([Genesis 30:27]). The prohibition appears in [Deuteronomy 18:10] ("מְנַחֵשׁ").

**Two proposed explanations**
1. **Sound-based (onomatopoeic).** The word imitates a hiss or whisper. A related Hebrew word is *lachash* (לָחַשׁ, "to whisper"), which is also used for snake-charming. The snake's hiss and the diviner's muttering would then share a source.
2. **Omen-based.** Some scholars say the snake gave its name to divination because snakes were widely used for omens in the ancient Near East. Others say it runs the other way and the snake is named for its association with omens. The direction is uncertain.

**Cognates.** Arabic has *ḥanash* for a snake, and Aramaic and Syriac have *chivya* and *nachash*. Scholars debate how close these relations are. A different noun, *nechoshet* (נְחֹשֶׁת, "copper/bronze"), is spelled with the same letters. It is probably a separate root, though the "bronze serpent" (*nechash hanechoshet*, [Numbers 21:9]) plays on the two words.

## Traditional readings (drash, not etymology)
- Chazal and the commentators connect the snake's cunning to its role in [Genesis 3]. The Rabbinic word-play on *nichush* is homiletic.
- Rashi on [Genesis 3:1] explains the snake's "cunning" (*arum*) and its plot to cause Adam's death. I have not re-read the comment here, so check it before quoting it.

I can pull the actual texts of [Genesis 3:1], [Genesis 44:5] and the commentators if you want them verified and quoted.

Yes. The word *Ivri* (עִבְרִי, "Hebrew") is commonly linked to the root ע-ב-ר (*avar*, "to cross over, pass"), and that link is one of the main classic explanations of the term. It is not the only one, though. The other main explanation ties the word to the name Ever.

I'm answering from memory here and haven't pulled the texts in this session. I'm confident about the sources named below, but check the exact wording before quoting any of them.

## Key Takeaways

- The root ע-ב-ר means "to cross, pass over," and *Ivri* can mean "one from the other side."
- Bereshit Rabbah gives the reading "the whole world on one side, and he on the other side."
- The other classic reading derives *Ivri* from Ever (עֵבֶר), Shem's descendant, as in [Genesis 10:21].
- Abraham is first called *Ivri* in [Genesis 14:13].

## Pshat: the first appearance

[Genesis 14:13] says "וַיָּבֹא הַפָּלִיט וַיַּגֵּד לְאַבְרָם הָעִבְרִי", "A fugitive came and told Abram the Hebrew." The text does not explain the word here, which is why commentators offer several explanations.

## The "crossed over" reading

- **Geographic:** Abraham came from across the river, the Euphrates (*ever hanahar*). The root is used this way in [Joshua 24:2-3], which says the ancestors lived "בעבר הנהר" (beyond the river).
- **Midrashic/ideological:** Bereshit Rabbah 42:8 on this verse quotes Rabbi Yehudah: "כל העולם כולו מעבר אחד והוא מעבר אחד", "the whole world was on one side (*ever*) and he on the other." So *Ivri* means one who stands apart from the surrounding culture, in his faith and way of life. This is drash, not pshat.

## The "descendant of Ever" reading

- [Genesis 10:21] introduces Shem as "אֲבִי כׇּל־בְּנֵי־עֵבֶר", "father of all the children of Ever."
- Rashi on [Genesis 14:13] gives both explanations: Abraham came from the other side of the river, and he descended from Ever. I'd check Rashi's exact wording on Sefaria before quoting him.
- Ibn Ezra and others lean toward the Ever lineage. The objection is that Ever had other descendants besides Abraham's line. Those who accept this reading answer that Abraham's line preserved Ever's tradition, a point the Talmud also makes in discussing Ever's study hall.

## Which is right?

The two readings can coexist, since Hebrew often layers meanings. Many Jewish teachers combine them: Abraham was both a descendant of Ever and a person who "crossed over," in place and in worldview. If you'd like, I can pull up Rashi and Bereshit Rabbah in full.

answer:
**Direct answer:** Below is Ramban on [Genesis 9:5], using Sefaria's English translation (Chavel's), lightly tightened. Ramban explains the phrase "your blood *lenafshoteichem*" and the problem of the extra letter *lamed*.

## Ramban on Genesis 9:5

**Verse:** "דִּמְכֶם לְנַפְשֹׁתֵיכֶם" ("Your blood, of your lives…").

**Ramban's comment [Ramban on Genesis 9:5:1]:**

> דִּמְכֶם לְנַפְשֹׁתֵיכֶם – דִּמְכֶם נַפְשׁוֹתֵיכֶם, כְּלוֹמַר דִּמְכֶם שֶׁהוּא נַפְשׁוֹתֵיכֶם...

**Translation:**

1. **First explanation.** *Lenafshoteichem* means the same as *nafshoteichem*, with no *lamed*. It means "your blood, which is your lives." The *lamed* is redundant, as in "*lechol* (to all) the instruments of the tabernacle" [Exodus 27:19], meaning "all the instruments." Likewise "the third, *l'Avshalom*" [I Chronicles 3:2] means "the third, Absalom."

2. **Second explanation.** *Lenafshoteichem* can also mean *benafshoteichem* ("in your souls"). The verse says "the life of all flesh is its blood, in its life" [Leviticus 17:14]. A parallel is "You shall eat no manner of blood in any of your dwellings, *la'of velabehemah*" [Leviticus 7:26]. That phrase means "in fowl or in beast."

3. **Ramban's own preferred reading ("the correct interpretation").** The verse says, "the blood which is the life in you I will require." It declares that the blood is the life. It hints that the death penalty applies to someone who spills the blood on which life depends. It does not apply to spilling the blood of limbs on which life does not depend.

4. **The Rabbis' reading.** Our Rabbis [Bava Kamma 91b] expounded the verse as a prohibition of suicide: "I will require your blood from your own souls."

**Notes:**
- The bracketed grammatical glosses in point 1 come from the Sefaria translation.
- I added the verse references for the Exodus and Leviticus parallels from Ramban's Hebrew. The Talmud reference is given in the Hebrew as "ב״ק צא."

answer:
**Torah** (תּוֹרָה) is usually translated as "teaching" or "instruction." It is often rendered "law," but that is narrower than the Hebrew. The word has two main meanings. In the narrow sense it is the Five Books of Moses (Genesis through Deuteronomy). In the broad sense it is the whole body of Jewish teaching, including the Prophets, the Writings, the Talmud, and later Torah study.

## Key Takeaways
- *Torah* comes from the root י-ר-ה, "to teach, direct, shoot (like an arrow)." Its core meaning is "instruction" or "guidance."
- "Law" comes from the Greek *nomos* in the Septuagint. It is a common but limited translation.
- Narrowly, Torah means the Five Books of Moses, also called the Pentateuch or the Written Torah.
- Broadly, it includes the Oral Torah (Mishnah, Talmud, Midrash) and all Torah learning.
- Good English Torah translations include the JPS Tanakh, Robert Alter's *The Five Books of Moses*, and the Artscroll Stone Chumash. All are available on Sefaria.

## Meaning of the word

**Root and basic sense.** *Torah* is generally derived from the root י-ר-ה (*y-r-h*), which means "to throw or shoot" and, in the causative form, "to point the way" or "to teach." The related word *moreh* (מוֹרֶה) means "teacher." So Torah is what points you in the right direction, which is closer to "guidance" than to "legislation."

**Use in the Tanakh.** The word appears for a parent's teaching, as in "Do not forsake the Torah of your mother" (Proverbs 1:8). It also appears for a particular set of laws, as in "This is the Torah of the burnt offering" (Leviticus 6:2). It also refers to the whole Mosaic teaching, as in "the book of the Torah of Moses" (Joshua 8:31).

**Written and Oral Torah.** Jewish tradition speaks of two parts. The Written Torah (*Torah she-bi-khtav*) is the Five Books. The Oral Torah (*Torah she-be-al peh*) is the tradition of interpretation that was later written down in the Mishnah and Talmud. Colloquially, "learning Torah" can mean studying any of these.

**Why "law" falls short.** The Torah contains commandments, but it also contains narrative, genealogy, poetry, and ethics. Much of Genesis is story. "Teaching" or "instruction" covers all of this, which is why modern translations such as JPS often use it.

If you'd like, I can pull up a verse in a few different translations to compare, or explain the five books and their Hebrew names.

**Translation:** "that they trampled (or trod) with their heels."

**Breakdown**

- דָּשׁוּ is the past tense, third person plural, of the root ד־ו־ש / ד־ו־שׁ (*dush*). It means "they trod," "they trampled," or "they threshed." The root is used for treading grain to separate it, as in oxen threshing. It is also used more broadly for trampling something underfoot.

**Sense:** Taken literally, it means people trampled something down by stepping on it with their heels. The sentence could be completed as "…the grain/ground that they trampled with their heels."

answer:
The Hebrew morning prayer is called *Shacharit* (שַׁחֲרִית), from *shachar*, "dawn". It is the first of the three daily prayer services, and it is longer than the other two. If you meant the short prayer said on waking, that is *Modeh Ani*, which I give below.

## Key Takeaways
- *Shacharit* is the daily morning service, and Jews traditionally pray it after dawn, ideally with a minyan (quorum of ten).
- Its core is the *Shema* with its blessings, followed by the *Amidah* (the silent standing prayer).
- Before the core, there are waking-up blessings, psalms, and Torah passages. After it, there are supplications, the Torah reading on certain days, and closing prayers.
- Wording differs somewhat between Ashkenaz, Sefard, and Edot HaMizrach, and so does the order of some parts.

## Upon waking: *Modeh Ani*
Before anything else, many Jews say this one-line prayer:

מוֹדֶה אֲנִי לְפָנֶיךָ מֶלֶךְ חַי וְקַיָּם, שֶׁהֶחֱזַרְתָּ בִּי נִשְׁמָתִי בְּחֶמְלָה, רַבָּה אֱמוּנָתֶךָ

"I give thanks before You, living and eternal King, for You have returned my soul within me with compassion. Your faithfulness is great." (My translation.)

## The structure of *Shacharit*
1. **Morning blessings (*Birkot HaShachar*).** These thank God for waking, sight, clothing, and the other ordinary gifts of the day. They also include *Elohai Neshamah*, "My God, the soul You placed in me is pure."
2. **Verses of Praise (*Pesukei DeZimra*).** These are psalms, especially Psalms 145–150, and they build up to *Baruch SheAmar* and *Yishtabach*.
3. **The *Shema* and its blessings.** This is the declaration "Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is one" ([Deuteronomy 6:4]). It is framed by blessings on creation (light), on God's love for Israel, and on redemption.
4. **The *Amidah* (also called *Shemoneh Esrei*).** This is a silent prayer said standing. It has blessings of praise, then requests, then thanks. The first three blessings begin with the Patriarchs, "God of Abraham, God of Isaac, and God of Jacob."
5. **Concluding sections.** These include *Tachanun* (supplication) on ordinary days, the Torah reading on Mondays, Thursdays, Shabbat, and holidays, *Aleinu*, and the Psalm of the Day.

## Why we pray in the morning
The Talmud connects the three daily prayers to the Patriarchs and also to the Temple offerings. Shacharit corresponds to the morning *tamid* (daily) offering ([Berakhot 26b]). I'm citing this from memory and haven't pulled up the text here, so check it if you want the exact wording.

## Where to read it in English
Sefaria has full siddurim, with Hebrew and English side by side, for Ashkenaz, Sefard, and Edot HaMizrach. I can walk you through any part phrase by phrase, or give a full English translation of one section, such as the *Amidah* or the *Shema*. Tell me which nusach (tradition) you use, if you know.

Practical questions, such as how to start praying or what to do if you miss the time, are best put to your rabbi.
